News.title: Nepal floods live: Girl, 13, among 33 Brits missing near Tibet as avalanche causes flood
News.content:
A 13-year-old girl is among 33 British tourists missing in Nepal after an avalanche led to major flooding along the Bhotekoshi River - hundreds of tourists are missing in total

At least 157 people are dead and as many as 341 tourists, including 33 Brits, are thought to be missing after sudden flooding in Nepal today.

An avalanche of ice and rock triggered massive flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border which killed at least eight people and caused massive damage to villages and infrastructure along the Bhotekoshi River, which has now swelled.

Officials said 403 people from countries including India, the United States, the United Kingdom and Malaysia were missing following the floods. One of the missing Brits is a 13-year-old girl.

Officials have issued warnings to residents living across several districts of Nepal, telling them to stay away from the banks of Bhotekoshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers. Several villages as well as roads and hydropower projects have been obliterated in the floods, authorities said.

News.title: Nepal flash floods: Rescuers search for dozens of Britons as death toll rises to 157
News.content:
Nepal flash floods: Rescuers search for dozens of Britons as death toll rises to 157

The number of missing people has risen to 403, with 33 UK citizens among 341 foreign nationals unaccounted for after devastating flash floods struck the Rasuwa region

View 6 Images Flash floods in Nepal have killed 157 people so far (Image: Skanda Gautam/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Rescuers are frantically searching for dozens of British nationals among those missing and feared dead in Nepal following catastrophic flash floods that have claimed more than 150 lives.

‌



Nepal Police confirmed on Wednesday evening that 157 bodies had been retrieved after devastating flooding in the Rasuwa region of Nepal, which shares a border with China's autonomous region of Tibet.

‌



The Nepal Tourist Board reported on Wednesday that the tally of missing individuals had climbed from 384 to 403, with 33 UK citizens amongst 341 foreign nationals whose whereabouts remain unknown.

‌



View 6 Images An area affected by flash floods in Nuwakot District, Nepal. (Image: Xinhua/Shutterstock)

Dad of innocent student shot dead by police in Pennsylvania shares heartbreaking last moments READ MORE :

Flash floods caused rivers to burst their banks, spreading thick mud across inhabited areas, engulfing homes and creating treacherous conditions for rescue teams.

Footage shared on social media captured massive flood waters tearing through valleys as people screamed in fear, with bridges swept away by the deluge. Additional footage showed people desperately scrambling uphill to outrun the advancing muddy torrent.

‌



The United States Geological Survey (USGS) reported that a magnitude 5.2 seismic event struck near the Nepal-China border on Wednesday at 8.37am local time. It stated that a "glacial collapse and debris flow" triggered "subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream".

Kalpana Malla, from Nepal's Nuwakot district, told BBC News: "My family members were swept away by the flood in front of my eyes." Ms Malla said her father, mother, sister and her sister's children were all carried away by the floods.

View 6 Images An aerial view shows buildings and infrastructure damaged along the swollen Trishuli River following a massive flash flood (Image: Skanda Gautam/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

‌



She added: "They could not escape the flood, there was no chance at all. This flood took everything, but my son and I climbed the rooftop of a house and survived, but couldn't explain how."

Rajan Shrestha, the mayor of Bidur municipality, told The Times that he had "never seen such a massive flood in my life" and estimated that about 400 people may have been swept away. He added: "And it came so fast. We could not evacuate all the people from the main town."

‌



Sunil Sharma, a tourism board spokesman, revealed that 133 of those missing were from India on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet – a sacred site for Hindus.

View 6 Images Damaged houses and vehicles are seen in the aftermath of flash floods (Image: AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha)

Also amongst the missing were 47 people from the US, 34 from Australia, and 24 from Canada, he added. According to the tourist board, 203 of the missing are male and 200 female.

‌



Tour operator Alpine Eco Trek confirmed that a 13 year old girl was amongst the missing British nationals, along with two Irish citizens.

Travel logs obtained by the Press Association reveal that the missing British nationals include three men aged 65, 64, and 52, and seven women aged 44, 47, 51, 60, 63, 63, and 65.

The firm, which provides guided tours and expeditions throughout Nepal, also confirmed that four of its Nepalese tour guides – aged 38, 35, 45 and 29 – are unaccounted for.

‌



View 6 Images Rescuers transport an elderly woman rescued from a Devighat old age home following a flash flood in Trishuli Bazar (Image: NARENDRA SHRESTHA/EPA/Shutterstock)

Kumar Adhikari, the manager of Alpine Eco Trek, told the Press Association: "I feel so sad. We are just thinking about what to do next. We are in pain at the moment, deep pain."

Mr Adhikari explained the tour group, who were on a nine-day tour to Mount Kailash, were entering Tibet from Nepal when they became stranded at the border as the flash floods hit.

‌



He revealed he maintained contact with his tour guides until 8.40am when their phones went dead, by which time the group would have been within Tibet's immigration office.

"We were hoping that inside it was safe," he said. "But later the video came from China's government which (showed) even Tibet's side was hit by the flood."

View 6 Images A massive flood swept through Nepal's northern Rasuwa district on August 26, damaging roads and power infrastructure (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Article continues below

In its assessment, the USGS stated: "This event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake. Additional analysis of nearby seismic stations, long period seismic waves, and satellite imagery led to the determination that the seismic event was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow, and that no earthquake had occurred."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced on Wednesday that the Government will do "everything we can" to support British nationals in Nepal following the floods.

The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office confirmed it was "deeply saddened by the loss of life and devastation caused by the floods in Nepal". It continued: "British nationals in Nepal should follow local authority advice and exercise caution while travelling. For consular assistance call (+44) (0)207 008 5000 or (+977) (0)14237100."

News.title: Dad of innocent student shot dead by police in Pennsylvania shares heartbreaking last moments
News.content:
Dad of innocent student shot dead by police in Pennsylvania shares heartbreaking last moments

Glen Pysher believes his son mistakenly tried to enter what he thought was his friend's house after a night out - the mistake lead to him being shot dead by police

View 3 Images Glenwood Pysher IV had been on a night out with friends but one mistake had fatal consequences (Image: FACEBOOK)

The father of a 22-year-old college student who was shot dead by police has shared the fatal decision that lead to his innocent son being killed.

‌



Glenwood Pysher IV had been on a night out with friends and visited several bars on Sunday and were splitting up to spend the night in two homes when his son took a wrong turn in the woods. Based on what he has been told by his son's friends, Pysher believes his son mistakenly tried to enter what he thought was his friend's house.

‌



Pysher's father, Glen Pysher, said he wasn't carrying any weapons, just a phone and backpack containing clothing and a few beers. Glen said: “He tried to open the doorknob and obviously startled the homeowner. From what we understand, he announced, ‘Hey! Open the door!’ because he thought he was at his friend's house.”

‌



View 3 Images Pysher realised he was in the wrong house but it was too late (Image: eyJpdiI6IjBkdmZ3WXNmWngwV3RiOGlIdU5lNmc9PSIsInZhbHVlIjoiRVZJMStwaHkwcUd5T09IS01MTFlBNWdYQ08vZGU0Vng3NUtXZGNyWllWenpFZW4zNmluN3VGblNLQTJVVXh0UVYzZFN2R1ZPd3E3RFJaTllnVjlhTWc9PSIsIm1hYyI6ImU4OTRiNDYzOTFm)

Pysher then sat down on the back porch and contacted his friends, who realized he was in the wrong place and started to go find him. But minutes later, they saw police and emergency vehicles and figured their friend would be arrested for public drunkenness. Instead, he was shot.

“At 12:32 a.m. my son was on a FaceTime call with his friends that were coming to get him,” he said. “We were told that my son was shot at 12:35 a.m.. So what kind of encounter could have ensued? What kind of communication could that officer have given him?”

‌



A Montgomery County Department of Public Safety dispatch record shows police were dispatched at 12:30 a.m. and arrived at 12:34 a.m. following reports of a possible burglary, according to the Montgomery County district attorney's office.

Upper Pottsgrove Township Police Chief Al Werner declined to release any further information, including the names of any officers involved in the shooting, until the investigation is complete. The Montgomery County Detective Bureau is investigating the shooting, the district attorney’s office said.

View 3 Images A GoFundMe page has been set up to help raise funds for Pysher's family (Image: GoFundMe)

‌



Pysher was about to begin his senior year at St. Elizabeth University in New Jersey, where he planned to play baseball. His goal was to become a high school history teacher and coach after graduation.

His father described him as a kind-hearted, loving kid who could be a “knucklehead” but enjoyed helping others. Since the shooting, former teammates, coaches and others have been texting his father to share heartbreaking memories.

“One young man in particular texted me and said, ‘I was going through a lot of really difficult things in my life. I was going the wrong way. And your son is the one who helped me put my life on track,’ " the father said. “He will be sadly missed in his community.”

News.title: Middlesbrough fire live: Girl, 7, and aunt die in house fire as police probe gangland revenge theory
News.content:
Two men have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a house fire in Grangetown, Middlesbrough, left two people - including a child - dead and four others injured

A seven-year-old girl and her aunt have been named locally as the two victims of a fatal house fire in Middlesbrough, as police investigate whether the blaze could be linked to a 'gangland dispute' that led to a crash on the A66 on Saturday.

Valentina Foster, seven, and her aunt, Natalie McDonald, 34, died in the devastating fire at a house on Birchington Avenue in Grangetown this morning, according to reports.

Two men, aged 23 and 31, have been arrested on suspicion of murder and remain in custody. Cleveland Police said officers were called to the property shortly before 5.30am.

The force said officers "cannot rule out any links to wider organised crime at this time" as they investigate the circumstances surrounding the blaze. One woman remains in a critical condition at the Royal Victoria Infirmary (RVI), while three others are in hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

The house fire occurred less than a mile from the scene of the A66 crash that killed seven people - five young males and two police officers - in the early hours of Saturday. The tragedy happened when a Volkswagen Passat, which was travelling the wrong way along the dual carriageway while evading police, collided with a police car.

News.title: Cases of liver disease linked to type 2 diabetes and obesity have soared in the past decade
News.content:
Cases of liver disease linked to type 2 diabetes and obesity have soared in the past decade

Researchers at Queen Mary University of London and the University of Glasgow looked at the GP records of nearly 12million people and discovered a five-fold leap in a type of liver disease over the past ten years

View 3 Images A study has found the a type of liver disease has soared in the UK (Image: Getty Images)

Cases of a type of liver disease linked to type 2 diabetes and obesity have risen five-fold in the past 10 years, a new study has revealed.

‌



Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), previously known as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, happens when fat builds up in the liver. Researchers said that despite a "growing recognition" of the chronic condition a large "diagnostic gap persists".

‌



People who are overweight, not active, have type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure or are over 50 years old are more likely to develop MASLD. Symptoms of the condition include feeling very tired or generally unwell, as well as pain in the abdomen.

‌



View 3 Images MASLD happens when fat builds up in the liver (Image: Getty Images/Science Photo Library RF)

NHS reminder for women who may have 'missed' out READ MORE :

Shingles vaccine on NHS could cut risk of stroke and prevent thousands of deaths READ MORE :

The study, by researchers at Queen Mary University of London and the University of Glasgow, looked at GP records from almost 12 million people in the UK between 2003 and 2022. The researchers found that recorded diagnoses of MASLD were 0.02% of adults in 2003, the equivalent of 1,300 people but this then jumped up to 0.5% in 2012, around 60,000 people.

These figures skyrocketed to 2.4% in 2022, or 283,762 people. New diagnoses of the condition doubled from 2012 to 2022, and those diagnosed with MASLD were three times as likely to have type 2 diabetes.

‌



Researchers also found that people of south Asian ethnicity were also "overrepresented" in MASLD diagnoses. Despite this, they were least likely to have a score used to estimate liver scarring despite higher levels of type 2 diabetes.

View 3 Images Researchers from the University of Glasgow (pictured) and Queen Mary University of London led the study (Image: Getty Images)

The researchers said that "more progress is needed to reach public health goals in this disease". They added: "Equally urgent is the need for additional research to identify and mitigate any risks of compounding health disparities among different ethnic groups especially in the era of medicines with specific indications in this space."

‌



An "opportunity to detect advanced fibrosis" would be through blood test that enables doctors to estimate liver scarring, according to the team behind the study. The study also found there was a "substantial diagnostic gap" in the UK, based on estimated cases of MASLD cases in Europe.

Researchers said: "The current data demonstrate that while UK prevalence has risen substantially to 2.42%, the diagnostic gap remains large compared to expected rates."

They suggest that, to close the gap, "at-risk groups such as those living with type 2 diabetes and obesity should be identified and case-finding actively pursued".

Article continues below

It is estimated that almost six million people in the UK are living with diabetes, almost 1.3 million of which may be living with undiagnosed type 2 diabetes. The latest NHS data also shows that in 2024, 30% of adults aged 16 and over were obese.

News.title: Two dead and eight injured as car drives into crowd in Caen 'after argument in bar'
News.content:
Two dead and eight injured as car drives into crowd in Caen 'after argument in bar'

Eyewitnesses claim they saw a man, who had been in an earlier barfight nearby, getting behind the wheel of a car which he used to ram through the bus stop nearby

View Image Eyewitnesses say a man was seen ramming the bus stop with his car (Image: Getty Images)

Two people are dead, and a further eight are injured after a car drove into a crowded bus stop in France.

‌



According to the French news network BFMTV, the incident followed a fight that broke out in a nearby bar in the port city of Caen.

‌



Witnesses told the publication that one of the people involved in the incident, which occurred at around 10:30 pm local time, was then seen getting into the vehicle that struck several people.

Article continues below

One man has been taken into police custody.

More to come.

News.title: Two killed in horror gyrocopter crash in Italy as vehicle strikes cable car lines
News.content:
Two killed in horror gyrocopter crash in Italy as vehicle strikes cable car lines

Emergency services rushed to the scene of the incident as the vehicle burst into flames

View Image Horror as gyrocopter 'erupts into fireball after hitting cable car lines' The small vehicle crashed to the ground near a dam. Two people died in the incident (Image: Facebook) (Image: Facebook)

Two people have died in a horror gyrocopter incident.

‌



The vehicle crashed at around 11.30am local time (10.30am BST) in the northern Italian region of Piedmont.

‌



The small vehicle struck cable car lines in the upper Antrona Valley, on the border between Ossola and Switzerland.

‌



Several helicopters intervened in the incident, including a 118 vehicle which departed from Borgosesi.

Emergency services including the fire brigade, rescue personel, law enforcement and the Alpine Rescue Service of the Guardia di Finanza all rushed to the scene.

‌



After the collision the aircraft came down near the shores of Lake Campliccioli, on a grassy area beside the dam.

The pair were travelling in a gyrocopters, a lightweight, typically two-seat recreational aircraft popular in mountainous terrain for low-altitude sightseeing flights.

Investigations into the circumstances of the crash remain ongoing.

This is a breaking story, updates to follow.

News.title: DWP chief hails 'early fruits' of job guarantee to tackle UK's Neets crisis
News.content:
DWP chief hails 'early fruits' of job guarantee to tackle UK's Neets crisis

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden hailed the 'early fruits' of the government's jobs guarantee scheme for Neets who claiming Universal Credit as he met the first wave at Boots HQ in Nottingham

View 4 Images Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden, with Broxtowe MP Juliet Campbell and employee Kai (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire)

Labour's work and pensions chief says he is "seeing the early fruits" of a drive to guarantee jobs for unemployed young people as he hailed the impact on their lives.

‌



Pat McFadden warned the number of 16 to 24 year olds who are not earning or learning is too high - and said it is right that the government is ploughing cash into finding them placements. A new scheme to secure jobs for all young people who are not in education, employment or training - known as Neets - claiming Universal Credit and seeking work for over 18 months is expected to employ 90,000 by 2029.

‌



Under the programme, announced by former Chancellor Rachel Reeves last year, the government fully funds up to 25 hours of paid work a week for six months. Mr McFadden said it is ministers' responsibility to step in as he met some of the first workers to be taken on at Boots' national headquarters in Nottingham.

‌



The Work and Pensions Secretary told reporters: "I think for us to stand back, fold our arms and say, 'This has nothing to do with us'... Well, that's what was happening." And he added: "I think we've got a responsibility."

View 4 Images Mr McFadden hailed the impact of the scheme on young workers at Boots (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire)

Calling for big businesses to get involved, he said: "I want this agenda of youth opportunity to be a national cause. And I strongly believe the government has its part to play, but it can't only be government."

‌



On Thursday the latest Neets figures will be released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS), with the number expected to be hovering around one million. Former health study Alan Milburn, who is carrying out a review on the crisis, previously described it as a generational catastrophe.

Asked how low he wants the number of Neets to be by the next general election, Mr McFadden declined to give a figure but said: "Well, I want the numbers to come down.

"I think they're too high. They've been too high for some years. This has been a long-term problem for the UK, it's not a short-term problem. But the really steep rise in recent Neet numbers came after Covid, where the numbers went up by quarter of a million between 2021 and 2024. We now have about a million young people who are Neet."

‌



The government has said there will be sanctions for those who do not engage. Mr McFadden spoke to several young people who have been taken on by Boots. Many told him they had been unemployed for two years or more, despite applying for jobs.

View 4 Images Mr McFadden said he is intent on tackling the number of Neets (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire)

He said: "I always say that the Department for Work and Pensions is where policy meets life. And it was just amazing for me to hear their stories.

‌



"These are young people who have been out of work for one, two, up to four years at 20 years old, maybe a bit more. They got their first job here.

"Most of them have only been working here for a matter of weeks. And you can already see how it's changed their confidence in themselves, their sense of belief in themselves."

He said he had been told by Boots that all those taken on would get permanent jobs unless there were performance issues. Mr McFadden said: "When we create opportunities like the ones that you've seen today, we expect young people to engage with those opportunities. That seems to me a fair deal from the point of view of the state, the individual, the taxpayer.

‌



"So, it is a package, but I think we're seeing some very early fruits of it, and I think we'll have to do more of this in the future."

View 4 Images Mr McFadden with Sir Sadiq Khan and Andy Burnham at a Sainsbury's branch on Wednesday morning (Image: Richard Pohle/The Times/PA Wire)

So far the scheme has been rolled out in six areas with the highest levels of unemployment among young people - Birmingham and Solihull, the East Midlands, Greater Manchester, Hertfordshire and Essex, Central and East Scotland and South East and South West Wales.

‌



It will expand to all eligible 18 to 24 year olds later this year. Asked if this would have an impact on older people looking for work, Mr McFadden said: "We have over 50s work coaches, too. And we're not neglecting anyone.

"But I would say there is a good reason to focus on the young, which is the very obvious one that their whole future is in front of them. And let me give you a startling fact. If someone aged 20 signs on to long-term sickness benefits at that age, they are more likely to celebrate their 30th birthday and still be on that benefit than to have had a steady job in between."

The government has pledged £2.5billion investment in employment support for young people. Figures published in May showed nearly one in seven young people aged 16-24 were neither working nor learning, with the figure exceeding one million for the first time since 2013 in the three months from January to March.

Article continues below

It comes as Andy Burnham called on businesses to step forward to offer work experience to young people on a visit to Sainsburys, after the retailer announced 10,000 work placements for youngsters. He said: “We need a national drive to challenge youth unemployment and give more opportunities for our young people, and I would ask other businesses to do the same. We have a huge challenge: too many young people are out of work – but it can be fixed.”

News.title: BBC visits hospital in Kathmandu as families wait for news
News.content:
A deadly flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border has killed at least 150 people, with hundreds still missing.

The missing include more than 100 from India, 54 from the US, and 33 from the UK, as well as more than 100 from Nepal itself, according to Nepal's tourist board.

The BBC Nepali's Shreejana Shrestha is in a hospital in Kathmandu, where some survivors are being flown in by helicopter for treatment.

News.title: Meta to pay up to $18bn to settle claims its platforms harm children
News.content:
As a jury trial kicked off last week in an Oakland, California, federal court, state lawyers argued the tech company knew that millions of 11- and 12-year-old users were on Instagram and Facebook over the years, yet "did little to keep them off" the platforms.

Although the trial had only gone on for five days, state lawyers relied heavily on information found in millions of internal Meta documents provided in the case. They included internal research, employee emails, and chat logs that went all the way up to chief executive Mark Zuckerberg.

One piece of internal research on Instagram stated: "Teens have an addict's narrative about use." Still, the states argued, Meta targeted young users.

"The trial did not go well for Meta," Bonta said on Wednesday.

Meta maintained throughout the brief trial that it had worked extensively over the years to make its platforms safer for its youngest users, pouring resources into testing and research, and building new features.

"We're always working on teen safety," head of Instagram Adam Mosseri said during an hour of court testimony on Tuesday.

The case was settled and court adjourned before he could reappear before a jury.

Before Mosseri's testimony, a former researcher at Meta, George Volichenko, appeared and with lawyers went over various internal communications he had been a part of regarding Meta's work on safety.

Volichenko said he struggled to understand when he was at the company in 2022 why the team he worked on wasn't given more freedom to better test and implement new safety features.

One of those was "quiet mode", which muted notifications for teen users during the night. His team knew such a feature would be much more widely adopted if Meta turned it on by default.

He recalled his manager telling him he "shouldn't worry too much about the adoption figures being low, because the team exists partially to protect the company against the upcoming lawsuits".

As part of the Wednesday settlement, however, a feature called "night mode", which blocks notifications between midnight and 6am, will now be on by default - meaning they will be turned on automatically. The settings are also designed only to be turned off by a parent or guardian.

"The framework we've negotiated will empower parents to easily manage how their children access our platforms," CJ Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said.

Other features for teen users being implemented as part of the deal include:

A default two-hour daily time limit (cumulative across Instagram and Facebook) that teens can only turn off with a parent's permission.

Likes will be hidden, on teens' profiles and those that they interact with.

"School mode", or a mute on notifications between 08:00 and 15:00 during school days.

Prompts noting when a teen has hit 15 minutes of continual use. Then notifications when cumulative use has hit 60 and 90 minutes.

The ability to choose a feed that is not driven by an algorithm.

The ability to turn off autoplay for videos and content.

Extreme make-up filters will no longer be accessible.

As for the new daily time limit for teen users, that will be reduced to one hour of total daily use should other social media platforms like TikTok, Snap and YouTube also agree to implement new restrictions for young users.

Bonta urged such platforms to do so, saying the settlement with Meta "is a good blueprint" for other companies to follow.

Should they not, he suggested on Wednesday that his office would now be "more focused" on bringing changes to the entire social media industry.

Meta also said TikTok and YouTube should implement the same safety features for their younger users.

"Our new Time Limit commitments, Night Mode features and usage limits during school hours set the right path forward for our whole industry, but this framework will only work if all our peers join us," Meta's Mahoney said.

YouTube and TikTok have been contacted for comment.

District of Columbia Attorney General Brian Schwalb called the Meta deal a "monumental public health victory".

He added: "The safety features Meta is required to install will fundamentally and immediately change how young people use Instagram and Facebook."

News.title: Woman who died in fire with niece, 7, was 'beautiful soul', mother tells BBC
News.content:
A woman killed in a house fire has been described by her mother as "a beautiful soul, who would have done anything for anybody".

Natalie McDonald, 34, died along with her seven-year-old niece, Valentina Foster, in the blaze in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of Wednesday.

Cleveland Police said the fire had also left a 48-year-old woman in a critical condition in hospital alongside another three people who suffered non-life threatening injuries.

Two men, aged 23 and 31, had been arrested on suspicion of murder and were in police custody, the force said.

Lisa Kirton, Natalie's mother, told the BBC her daughter was "lovely, bright and bubbly" and "everybody loved her".

She said Valentina, also known as Tina, had been spending the summer holidays with the family.

"She was a cute little kid," Kirton said. "I can't believe it, seven years old - it's just a disgrace."

She also said Natalie's 15-year-old daughter and a friend had managed to escape through an upstairs window.

The friend, she said, had "kicked out a window" and "had saved their lives".

News.title: Rocky Horror star Tim Curry dies at 80
News.content:
Born in Warrington in 1946, Curry's first acting job after university was in the original London production of groundbreaking rock musical Hair in 1968.

In 1973, a fellow cast member, Richard O'Brien, asked Curry to audition for his new musical, and cast him in the role of the flamboyant lingerie-clad "sweet transvestite" Dr Frank-N-Furter.

Curry first put his stamp on the character of the riotous scientist on stage in the upstairs theatre at London's Royal Court in 1973.

The show's popularity snowballed and resulted in a big-screen adaptation, which also starred Susan Sarandon, Barry Bostwick and O'Brien.

It was not an immediate hit at cinemas but became a fan favourite and holds the record for the longest-running theatrical release in film history.

Welsh actor Luke Evans, who played the role in a Broadway revival, called Curry "a force, a bright fierce flame, an exquisite charm".

In a letter he recently wrote to Curry, Evans thanked him for his fearlessness and for "creating something so enduring, and for inspiring generations of actors to be a little braver than they thought they could be".

"Being compared to you has been one of the greatest compliments I've ever received, even though it's a comparison no one could ever hope to live up to," he wrote in the letter.

The official Rocky Horror Picture Show on Broadway account similarly thanked the late actor for "giving the world a little more freedom, a little more fearlessness, and through the tears in our eyes, the courage to BE IT" - a nod to Curry's deliver of the famous line from the musical, "Don't dream it, be it".

News.title: World's first patient to undergo live AI-assisted brain surgery has tumour removed
News.content:
The world's first patient to have brain surgery with live artificial intelligence assistance has successfully had his tumour removed.

Rhys Hibbert, a father-of-two from Bedfordshire, could have lost his sight without the operation, said surgeons at University College London Hospital.

The AI tool analysed a video feed of the operation as it happened and advised surgeons on how to avoid crucial but hidden vessels and nerves in the brain. It allowed them to safely remove as much of the tumour as possible.

"From a patient safety perspective, I can see absolutely the benefit. There are no road signs inside our head," said Hibbert.

Until 18 months ago, 48-year-old Hibbert, a customer services manager, was fit and healthy, going on a two-mile walk every lunchtime.

It was on one of these walks that he fell unconscious and started fitting in the road.

A brain scan revealed he had an 11mm (0.433in) non-cancerous tumour growing on the pituitary gland - a marble-sized organ at the base of the skull.

The gland secretes vital hormones that help with processes like growth, metabolism and regulating blood pressure and temperature.

Crucially it sits very close to the carotid arteries which are vital vessels that supply blood to the brain, and the optic nerves that control vision.

As Hibbert's tumour began to press on his optic nerves, it narrowed his peripheral vision.

News.title: New thunderstorm warnings for parts of UK as rain set to continue
News.content:
The Met Office has issued fresh warnings for thunderstorms that will bring more wet weather to parts of the UK on Thursday.

The first warning is valid from 02:00 BST with thunder and heavy rain due to move across south-east England in the early hours of Thursday morning.

A second comes into force at 06:00 BST for a wider area of England and Wales. This will last through to 22:00 and may become slow moving in the afternoon and evening.

Downpours could bring localised flash flooding and travel disruption - with the wettest areas potentially seeing 75mm (3in) of rain. Large hail, lightning and gusty winds could accompany the showers and it will feel rather humid for many.

Spells of rain are set to continue over the weekend - a bank holiday for England, Wales and Northern Ireland - accompanied by windy conditions in the south.

News.title: Burnham calls summit of Welsh, Scottish and Northern Irish first ministers
News.content:
Burnham said: "I am in South Wales today because the answers to the UK's challenges will not come from an echo chamber. They will come from the places that know their own strengths, and from a government willing to listen and then act.

"Good jobs in every community, in every part of the UK. That is what I want every leader in this country signed up to."

He will meet the Welsh government's deputy first minister Sioned Williams at the visit.

Williams said the visit was "a positive example of governments working together to improve people's lives".

She will call for a "fair share of the UK government's steel fund", an "energy social tariff to support those facing fuel poverty and struggling with high energy bills", and high standing charges in Wales to be addressed.

She added: "Wales is an energy-rich nation. People should see that reflected in good jobs, stronger communities and lower bills."

The National Economic Council was created by the Gordon Brown administration in 2008, and has been revived by Burnham.

A previous meeting brought together government ministers and English local authority mayors.

Downing Street said the prime minister wanted to discuss "how we will drive good growth in every postcode across the UK" with the first ministers.

The Welsh government said: "We look forward to discussing shared challenges, including ensuring growth and investment in all the countries represented, and support for families facing the continuing cost-of-living crisis.

"This is alongside further discussions with the UK government to progress broader priorities in Wales, including fair funding and extending devolution."

Plaid Cymru has pressed the UK government for discussions over more powers and funding for the Senedd - Wales's parliament - and the Welsh government in Cardiff.

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth had his first meeting with the new prime minister on the sidelines of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games in July.

At the time, ap Iorwerth said it was "too early" to know whether the new Labour prime minister would agree to his calls.

Downing Street said then that the prime minister wanted an "open and ongoing dialogue" with the first minister.

News.title: At least one dead after car crashes into crowd in northern France
News.content:
At least one person has been killed and 10 people injured after a car crashed into a group of people near a train station in northern France, police say.

One person had been arrested and taken into custody after authorities launched a major emergency response in Caen, in the Normandy region, local officials told the BBC.

The incident took place near a bar, with local media reporting that a fight had broken out there before the incident took place.

Social media videos from the scene appear to show crowds gathering around police cars and ambulances, where a large area is cordoned off.

A spokesperson for the local administration of Calvados confirmed to the BBC that four people were receiving treatment in the emergency ward of a nearby hospital.

Six others were being treated for less serious injuries, the spokesperson said.

Detectives from Caen's Specialised Crime Division are leading the investigation.

Locals have been told to avoid the area around the Caen train station.

This breaking news story is being updated and more details will be published shortly. Please refresh the page for the fullest version.

You can receive Breaking News on a smartphone or tablet via the BBC News App. You can also follow @BBCBreaking on X, external to get the latest alerts.

News.title: Nepalese authorities say 33 UK nationals missing after flash floods
News.content:
Thirty-three people from the UK are among hundreds feared missing following a deadly flash flood near the Nepal-Tibet border.

Flooding and mud slides hit the Rasuaw region in the morning on Wednesday, killing at least 157 people in Nepal and three in Tibet, according to Chinese state media.

Nepal police said 579 tourists are missing - including 466 who are foreign nationals, from 28 different countries.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he is in touch with local authorities and "will do everything we can" to support British nationals affected, urging those in the region "to follow guidance from the local authorities and follow our travel advice".

The UK Foreign Office said it is working closely with Nepalese authorities "following concerning reports of British nationals who are missing" and has encouraged Brits to follow local guidance and "remain alert to the changing situation".

According to Nepal police, 113 of the missing tourists are Nepalese, and 54 are from the US.

Excursion company Alpine Eco Trek, which offers guided expeditions and tours in Nepal, confirmed to the BBC that it has not been able to establish contact with a group of 12 Britons who were booked on a tour to Mount Kailash, and were in the region when the flash floods struck.

The company said it had made attempts to charter a rescue helicopter but were unable to fly due to poor conditions, and will continue to help with ongoing rescue efforts on Thursday.

News.title: Murder arrests after fire kills two including child
News.content:
Two men have been arrested on suspicion of murder after two people died in a house fire including a child, police have confirmed.

The blaze in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, broke out just before 05:30 BST and also left a 48-year-old woman in hospital in a critical condition, alongside a further three people who suffered non-life threatening injuries.

Cleveland Police said the two victims were yet to be formally identified.

The men, aged 23 and 31, had been arrested on suspicion of murder and were in police custody, the force said.

Cleveland Police said it was "keeping an open mind and cannot rule out any links to wider organised crime at this time".

The fire happened about two miles from the A66 crash that killed five young men and two police officers on Saturday morning.

Redcar and Cleveland Local Policing Commander Supt Emily Harrison said the force was working to "establish the circumstances of exactly what has happened".

"We will have a high visibility presence in the Grangetown area and encourage anyone who has concerns, or who may have information, to approach our officers."

Patrols had been increased in the local area to "reassure the local community", the force said earlier.

News.title: Prince Harry and Meghan land in UK days after announcing move
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have arrived back in the UK, BBC News understands.

Prince Harry, Meghan and their children Archie and Lilibet are believed to have flown into the country privately from California, and landed in Birmingham shortly before midday.

A spokesman for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex said "this is not something we would comment on".

There did not appear to be a police presence as Harry and his family left the airport, a source told the BBC.

Last week, it was reported that the couple would be relocating to the UK in August. They will not return to official duties but will live in Britain as non-working royals.

It is thought the family will base themselves at a private property outside of London in the Cotswolds area.

Archie and Lilibet have been enrolled in school and the new term is due to start next week.

Though not confirming the family's arrival in the UK, a spokesman for the Sussexes did say their chickens were staying in California, but they were bringing their dogs Mia and Pula with them.

The chickens, which the couple rescued, have regularly featured on Meghan's Instagram account and also appeared in her Netflix programme.

News.title: Stourbridge fires that razed 19 homes accidental
News.content:
Two fires that destroyed 19 homes in Stourbridge were started accidentally in fields where farming machinery was in use, according to West Midlands Fire Service.

Investigators established agricultural equipment was being used in the vicinity of fields immediately before the fires were first reported. The service would not confirm the type of machinery.

The first fire started in a field near Racecourse Lane at about 13:27 BST on 13 August, while a second began shortly afterwards in a field near Quarry Park Road.

The day after the fires the government sent out an emergency alert to millions of people across England and Wales, warning them against "any activity that could start a fire".

News.title: King and Queen to visit the Caribbean in autumn tour
News.content:
King Charles III and Queen Camilla will travel to the Caribbean later this year, Buckingham Palace has announced.

The royal pair will travel to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting, with the King also visiting the Bahamas and Guyana as part of the eight-day trip.

The tour - planned for 27 October to 4 November - will "celebrate the communities, cultures and nature within the Commonwealth family," the palace said on Wednesday.

It marks the first time the King has visited the Caribbean since 2021, when he travelled to Barbados to see the country officially removed Queen Elizabeth II as its head of state and become the world's newest republic.

The monarch, who was the Prince of Wales at the time, acknowledged the "appalling atrocity of slavery" the Caribbean island suffered during a speech he made.

He also visited Antigua and Barbuda in 2017 following the widespread devastation caused by Hurricanes Irma and Maria, and made official visits to Guyana in 2000 and the Bahamas in 1973.

He travelled across the Atlantic Ocean earlier this year when he visited Bermuda in May, where he is also head of state.

The trip marked his first royal visit as monarch to a British overseas territory and came after a state visit to the US.

News.title: US designates Palestine Action a terrorist group
News.content:
The US has imposed sanctions on Palestine Action, designating it as a terrorist group.

The US Department of the Treasury said it had "taken action" against the UK-based group, which it accused of supporting "numerous acts of terrorism since July 2020".

Supporting Palestine Action became illegal in the UK in 2025 after the government banned it under anti-terror legislation.

The group's co-founder Huda Ammori responded in a social media post, saying: "As a Palestinian and Iraqi, the fact the country which destroyed both my homelands is calling me a terrorist, is beyond hypocritical."

In a statement to the BBC, Ammori said the group's actions had "always been about saving lives", adding the ban should be a "wake-up call to anyone who cares about free speech and democracy".

Announcing the move in a statement on Wednesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "Far-left extremists, their fronts, and their enablers should be on notice: We will bring the full weight of our economic tools to bear.

"Political terrorism has no place in our society, and we will continue to cut the financial lifelines of these groups until they are eliminated."

The sanctions imposed include freezing any assets belonging to the group that are either based in the US or in the control of US citizens.

The US ban on the group is part of a wave of sanctions announced by the Trump administration against what it says are far-left terror organisations around the world.

The Department of Treasury accused Palestine Action of having supported "numerous acts of terrorism since July 2020, including acts that have physically injured UK law enforcement personnel, as well as acts intended to intimidate lawful commercial enterprises and coerce the UK government".

Palestine Action, which used so-called direct action tactics against Israeli-linked arms companies in the UK, has been facing an ongoing legal battle to get its UK ban overturned.

In June, Court of Appeal judges ruled the UK government made a "justified and proportionate" interference on freedom of expression rights.

But Palestine Action has since been given permission to challenge the decision at the Supreme Court.

More than 2,000 people are facing potential trial after being arrested for protesting against the ban by allegedly declaring their support for a proscribed terrorism group during mass demonstrations.

Separately, four of its members were jailed in June for a break-in at a defence firm that caused more than Â£1m worth of damage, with one person sentenced for causing grievous bodily harm on a police officer who was hit with a sledgehammer.

News.title: Boy, 15, arrested over stabbing at Brent Council HQ
News.content:
On Wednesday, one man who works in the area told BBC London the stabbing "felt normal".

"These things happen every single day here, in London and in the area. It's not a big surprise," he said.

"You see things like this happen all the time. You read the news and every single day there's something going on. If it's in Harrow, or Wembley, or Neasden, or Willesden or wherever, it doesn't come as a surprise."

However, one woman who lives in the area said the stabbing "came as a shock".

"I've never felt unsafe around here and it's a bit concerning," she said.

Student Demi said he felt "uneasy" after the stabbing.

"It's not really an unsafe area," he said. "It's a bit out of the ordinary.

"These things happen, unfortunately, but it's a bit strange to have it happen here."

Kate, another local resident, said: "Usually we feel very safe. We're fortunate living in this area because there are lots of security patrols and there are always people around.

"Stabbings are terrible tragedies, but it could happen anywhere, and I know there are areas of London that have to deal with that every day.

"I still feel safe. We're fortunate to live here with so much security; I wish that everyone lived in such an area."

News.title: Call with couple in Iran prison 'enormous relief'
News.content:
The family of an East Sussex couple detained in Iran say they have spoken to them for the first time in three months.

Lindsay and Craig Foreman were sentenced to 10 years in jail over espionage charges, which they both deny, and are being held in Evin prison.

Lindsay's son, Joe Bennett, said hearing his mum's voice was "an enormous relief" and encouraged the government to visit the couple as the UK embassy in Iran reopened last week after closing due to ongoing security concerns in the region.

A Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) spokesperson confirmed staff had returned to the embassy and said the pair's health and welfare was a "top priority".

Bennett, who lives in Folkestone, said the 12-minute phone call was their first official conversation since the couple ended their hunger strikes.

He said his mother told him she and her husband were "slowly rebuilding their strength" after losing a substantial amount of weight.

"Just hearing mum's voice properly again was an enormous relief," he added.

"We only had 12 minutes, but after everything that has happened, those 12 minutes meant a great deal."

Bennett said his mother and her partner had remained "mentally resilient" and "determined to return home".

Bennett claimed the conversation was "monitored" and conducted with an interpreter present, limiting what could be discussed.

He is now calling for the UK Government to take "swift action" to arrange an urgent consular visit and ensure the couple receive appropriate medical care.

He also hopes to meet with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and for the government to use all available diplomatic and legal channels to secure their release.

He said the family was particularly concerned the couple did not receive a full medical assessment following their hunger strikes.

A federal judge on Wednesday declined to force Texas to extradite an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of shooting a man and lying about the incident during the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis.

U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. said in a written order that he could not stop the county sheriff from releasing Christian Castro or compel Texas Governor Greg Abbott to sign an extradition warrant.

The Cameron County sheriff said Castro would be released on Thursday morning.

open image in gallery Castro is charged in Minnesota with assault and falsely reporting a crime in the Jan. 14 shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis. ( Department of Homeland Security )

Castro is charged in Minnesota with assault and falsely reporting a crime in the Jan. 14 shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis.

Castro is accused of firing a gun through the front door of a Minneapolis home, shooting Sosa-Celis in the leg. Prosecutors say Castro also falsely accused Sosa-Celis and another man of attacking an ICE officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel.

After a Minnesota judge issued a nationwide warrant for Castro's arrest in May, authorities, including Minnesota’s Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, arrested Castro in Cameron County on May 29. Minnesota authorities have sought his extradition since his arrest, but he remains in custody in Brownsville, Texas, a city bordering Mexico.

Under Texas law and barring extradition, Castro must be released after 90 days of detention, which is Thursday.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison filed a request for a temporary restraining order last week seeking to block Castro's release or to order his return to Minnesota.

Texas attorneys on Tuesday argued the judge could not rule on a decision that's still pending. Abbott has not denied the extradition. Instead, he is waiting for the outcome of an internal state investigation considering whether Castro was legally a “fugitive” under the Extradition Clause, the lawyers said.

The judge wrote in Wednesday's order that the court can't yet step in.

open image in gallery Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison filed a request for a temporary restraining order last week seeking to block Castro's release or to order his return to Minnesota. ( AAP Photo/Mark Vancleave )

“The Court concludes that it lacks subject matter jurisdiction because the case is not ripe for adjudication,” the order read. “Minnesota cannot premise its causes of action on the allegation that Governor Abbott may violate those authorities in the future; it must prove that a violation has already occurred.”

The judge said in his order that the extradition laws do not outline how long the Texas governor can take to make that decision.

Ellison said in a statement that his office would keep litigating the case but didn't specify what it would do next.

“I respectfully but strongly disagree with the court’s order, which nonetheless acknowledges that Christian Castro is a flight risk, that Minnesota will be harmed if he is allowed to flee to Mexico, and that Governor Abbott’s consideration of Minnesota’s extradition request is of ‘an atypically long duration’ — to say the least,” Ellison said in a statement.

Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, whose office handles prosecutions in Minneapolis, said at a new conference that Abbott was unfairly harboring the former ICE agent.

"If Christian Castro walks out of the door of the jail tomorrow and disappears into Mexico, it will be the fault of one person: Governor Greg Abbott,” Moriarty said.

Abbott's press secretary, Andrew Mahaleris, welcomed the ruling and said it was the governor's duty to carefully consider the merits of extradition requests.

"Today’s order rebuffs Minnesota’s efforts to conscript federal courts into commandeering the authority of Governor Abbott’s office,” Mahaleris said in a statement.

Abbott said last week he would not respond to the extradition request, citing the ongoing investigation into fraud in government social service programs in Minnesota, which President Donald Trump used to justify his immigration crackdown there.

Minnesota officials say Castro could flee the country, citing calls he made from jail to a woman in Mexico, talking “about marrying her and buying a house in Mexico when he is released,” according to the lawsuit.

The judge conceded that Castro could flee the country but added that “the threat of injury by itself does not create an issue ripe for adjudication.”

President Trump has made a point of releasing UFO-related materials to the public, but if little green men ever visit Earth they’re unlikely to care much about our politics or who is in the White House, according to one of the president’s advisors on UFOs.

“If someone arrives from the vast expanses of interstellar space, recognizing how humans divided up territory on Earth is a very low priority for them,” Avi Loeb, who leads the administration’s Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) Science Advisory Council, told AlterNet this week. “They wouldn't care about the United States, and they wouldn't care who its president is.”

At the same time, Loeb said, if aliens were discovered or contacted during the Trump administration, that would define the president’s legacy forever.

“Obviously, for a president, it would be a great boon if, during his term, we discovered we're not alone — that we have a neighbor in our cosmic environment,” Loeb, a Harvard University physicist, told the outlet. “That kind of discovery would be remembered millions of years into the future. It's not like a dispute with another nation, which in a century will likely be forgotten. This would be a major discovery that shapes the future of humanity.”

The advisory council, announced in June, is part of the Trump administration’s larger effort to disclose more information about UAPs.

Aliens wouldn’t care who was in the White House, according to Trump’s UFO advisor, despite the president’s efforts to explore UFOs ( AP )

So far, the Pentagon has released five tranches of information to the public, though the materials have not revealed any new, definitive evidence of extraterrestrial life or technology. Instead, the releases consist of records tied to a mix of recent and decades-old mysterious encounters.

The administration is also working on a process to encourage government whistleblowers with information about UAPs to come forward without fear of violating non-disclosure agreements or other secrecy obligations.

Loeb’s selection as leader of the UAP advisory effort was somewhat controversial.

Despite his lengthy tenure as a top physicist, he has faced criticism from other scientists who have argued he has made premature claims about the possibility of alien life.

"I don't know what's going to come of this, but we're not going to get any closer to answering these questions with him in charge," Steve Desch, an Arizona State University astrophysicist, told The Associated Press in June.

Loeb, whose team has requested that the Pentagon declassify various UAP-related materials, has said he’s starting from the assumption that UAPs encountered around Earth are man-made phenomena until proven otherwise.

News.title: Tupac murder prosecutors rest case after playing Duane Davis’ own words
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Prosecutors rested their case Wednesday in the murder trial of Duane “Keffe D” Davis, calling 24 witnesses in the case over the 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur.

The prosecution’s final witness played jurors excerpts from Davis’ previous interviews and recorded jail calls. In one call following his 2023 arrest, Davis complained that authorities were using his own statements against him and said he should have stopped giving interviews.

“They’re trying to use my words against me,” Davis said in one of the calls played in court.

open image in gallery The defense is expected to begin presenting its case Thursday ( Caroline Brehman/via Reuters )

In a YouTube clip, Davis held up his book and encouraged viewers to buy it to “get the real truth.”

The defense is expected to begin presenting its case Thursday, with attorney Michael Sanft telling the judge he has a detective and two police officers lined up to testify. Davis is still deciding whether to testify in his own defense.

A former Compton gang detective testified Tuesday that Davis was a high-ranking “shot caller” whose authority meant younger gang members would not have opened fire on Shakur with Davis present unless he allowed it.

Robert Ladd, a former Compton police officer who spent years investigating gang homicides, described Davis as a leader of the South Side Compton Crips who could order younger members to act.

Prosecutors have not accused Davis of firing the shots that killed Shakur in Las Vegas nearly 30 years ago. Instead, they allege Davis orchestrated the shooting in retaliation for a casino brawl hours earlier involving Shakur and Davis’ nephew, Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson. Under Nevada law, someone who helps another person commit murder can be convicted of the crime.

Ladd testified that Shakur's shooting triggered a 10-day war in Compton between the South Side Crips and Mob Piru, resulting in three killings and 10 attempted murders.

open image in gallery Ladd testified that Shakur's shooting triggered a 10-day war in Compton between the South Side Crips and Mob Piru ( John Locher/Pool via Reuters )

Davis has said in past interviews that he was riding in a white Cadillac with Anderson and two other men when they pulled alongside Shakur and Death Row Records co-founder Marion “Suge” Knight in a black BMW. In a 2008 police interview played for jurors last week, Davis said he provided the gun and Anderson opened fire.

Asked Tuesday who would have been the leader among the four men in the Cadillac, Ladd answered, “Mr. Davis.”

Ladd said that Anderson, a younger-ranking gang member, could not have opened fire with Davis in the car without Davis' permission. If Davis had told the others to handle the dispute later, Ladd testified, “there wouldn’t have been a shooting.”

Sanft emphasized the lack of physical evidence supporting that theory. Ladd acknowledged that, aside from Davis’ own admissions, he had no physical evidence placing Davis in Las Vegas that night and no phone records showing Davis ordered the shooting.

Ladd said investigators collected bills and letters from Las Vegas hotels in Anderson’s and Davis’ residences, but they didn’t know when they were dated, or the current location of that evidence.

Prosecutors have argued that Davis’ own words are central to their case, while Sanft has characterized his client’s accounts as fabricated bravado and accused investigators of failing to corroborate them.

News.title: Tim Curry: Mischievous screen star with a grin worth a thousand words
News.content:

Last year, I was fortunate enough to spend some time with the veteran record and film producer Lou Adler. The 92-year-old has enjoyed a singular career that included producing Carole King and directing a Cheech & Chong movie, but there was one anecdote he shared that made his face light up more than any of the other major stars he could casually name-drop. In 1972, he recalled, he visited a tiny theatre in London and saw a madcap production that blended schlocky B-movie horror and Fifties rock’n’roll. “Can you imagine,” he asked me, still a little awestruck, “Seeing Tim Curry for the first time?”

The show, of course, was Rocky Horror, which Adler immediately optioned and brought to Hollywood, where it was adapted into The Rocky Horror Picture Show three years later. The film became a runaway hit, grossing over $170 million worldwide (having cost 1/100th of that) and going on to have the longest-running theatrical release in movie history.

It also launched Curry, who has died at the age of 80, to international fame. The success of Rocky Horror meant that many more people around the world got to experience the unfettered joy of laying eyes on the Cheshire-born actor with the Cheshire cat grin for the very first time.

Curry had graduated from the University of Birmingham with a degree in English and drama in 1968, at the age of 22, and landed his first West End role that same year as part of the original London cast of the hit musical Hair. It was there he met Rocky Horror creator Richard O’Brien, who wrote the role of the flamboyant, cross-dressing mad scientist Dr. Frank-N-Furter specifically for him.

Curry embraced the character immediately. “The motto ‘don’t dream it, be it’ is not necessarily limited to your sexuality,” he told Entertainment Weekly last year, referring to one of his character’s most famous lines. “I think it applies to whatever you dream to be, and that’s a good thing. If it gives people permission to behave in a sexual way that they secretly want to, that’s a good thing. As long as it doesn’t hurt them.”

open image in gallery Tim Curry as the flamboyant Dr Frank-N-Furter in 'The Rocky Horror Picture Show' ( Twentieth Century Fox )

After Rocky Horror became a hit, Curry found himself in demand both on Broadway and in Hollywood. On the stage, he was nominated for a Tony Award three times over the course of 24 years, for roles as varied as Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart in 1981’s Amadeus, swashbuckling movie star Alan Swann in 1992’s My Favorite Year and King Arthur in 2005’s Spamalot.

His film and television roles were just as eclectic. Where you remember seeing Tim Curry for the first time will likely depend on your age and tastes. Perhaps it was as the con artist Rooster Hannigan in the 1982 movie version of Annie, or as the supercilious butler Wadsworth in manic 1985 murder mystery comedy Clue. As Cardinal Richelieu in 1993’s The Three Musketeers or as Long John Silver in 1996’s Muppet Treasure Island. Maybe his clown Pennywise, from the 1990 ABC miniseries of Stephen King’s It, has been ruining your sleep for years.

open image in gallery Curry as Pennywise the clown in Stephen King’s ‘It’ (1990) ( ABC )

Personally, I know exactly where I first saw Tim Curry: playing the smug, scheming concierge who becomes Kevin’s nemesis in Home Alone 2. The shot that dissolves from the smirking cartoon Grinch to Curry pulling off the exact same evil grin is indelibly burned into my memory. I’m not alone. On social media today, fans have been admiringly comparing it to Stanley Kubrick’s famous match cut from the prehistoric bone to the orbiting satellite in 2001: A Space Odyssey.

open image in gallery Curry as the concierge who becomes Kevin’s nemesis in 1992’s ‘Home Alone 2’ ( 20th Century Fox )

The scene also seems to have left an impression on his co-star Rob Schneider, who was among the many paying tribute to him. “I have never known another actor who could say more with a knowing grin or a raised eyebrow than the splendid Tim Curry,” remarked Schneider in a social media post, before offering some insight into Curry’s acting process. “I was astonished as a young actor to witness Tim do a scene 7 completely different ways and ALL OF THEM FANTASTIC!” remembered Schneider. “Tim said, ‘I want to give the director different choices! It’s not my job to decide which one. It’s up to him!’”

A major stroke in 2012 left Curry partially paralyzed and unable to walk, but he continued to work and make public appearances. Last year, he published his wildly entertaining memoir, Vagabond, in which he reflected on the impish delight that he managed to inject into every character he played.

“My own way was to sprinkle a bit of mischief onto even my most villainous roles, just as I brought a little mischief into my encounters with my mother,” he wrote. “Doing whatever I could to make the darkness sparkle.”

Wherever and however you first saw Tim Curry, you never forgot watching him sparkle.

Since becoming Defence Secretary in July, Wes Streeting has been targeted by more online homophobia than at any other point in his life.

Appearing on LBC’s All Talk podcast, he said he faced an "unbelievable volume" of abuse "because people cannot cope with the idea that a gay person might lead the armed forces of the United Kingdom".

He became the first openly gay Defence Secretary under Andy Burnham’s leadership.

Streeting became the first openly gay Defence Secretary under Andy Burnham’s leadership ( Aaron Chown/PA Wire )

Between 1967 and 2000, gay people were banned from the army, navy, and air force.

Those in the armed forces suspected of being gay were subjected to brutal interrogation and bullying, and forced out of service, often with long-term impacts on their life and careers.

LGBT+ ex-servicemen and women who suffered historical mistreatment have until December 12 to apply for a financial redress scheme and have been urged to come forward.

Mr Streeting told the podcast hosted by Iain Dale: “I have experienced more online homophobia in the last three weeks than I have in my entire life.

“Unbelievable volume – because people cannot cope with the idea that a gay person might lead the armed forces of the United Kingdom.”

He added “I’m proud of the fact that in my lifetime we’ve gone from gay people not being allowed to serve in the military to a gay Defence Secretary.

“And in my first week, someone in the MoD said to me, ‘you know, as a gay man, I’m really proud that we have our first gay defence secretary, and it means a lot to many of us who remember the bad old days’. So I was quite touched by that.”

Speaking at the Edinburgh Fringe earlier this month, Mr Streeting noted that while his appointment “almost entirely unremarked upon in the media”, the online reaction has been starkly different.

Despite the negativity, he views the position as a chance to demonstrate “strength” and “challenge this sort of stereotype that clearly persists in dark corners of the internet”.

Mr Streeting served as health secretary under Sir Keir Starmer, before resigning in May this year, telling the then-prime minister he had “lost confidence” in him.

News.title: Large parts of UK under thunderstorm and flood warnings today – full list of regions
News.content:

Thunderstorm warnings have come into place across parts of the country as the Met Office warns of flooding and disruption.

Yellow warnings for storms are in place across the West and East Midlands, as well as the North West, South East, London, South West and east of England, and all of Wales.

The alerts came into force in England and Wales at 3am and will last until 10pm on Wednesday. Another thunderstorm warning will kick in at 2am on Thursday until 8am, while a third will start at 5am on Thursday until 10pm.

open image in gallery A thunderstorm warning is in place across England and Wales today ( Met Office )

The Met Office warned there is a “small risk of flooding and disruption from thunderstorms” with the potential for power cuts after a summer of record-breaking dry conditions.

Twenty-two flood alerts have been put in place by the Environment Agency, where flooding is possible, while a flood warning has been issued for Perry Brook at Perry Barr, which means flooding is expected.

A band of heavy showers and thunderstorms is expected to move northwards this morning, with the possibility an intense downpour of 20 to 30mm of rain could fall in less than an hour.

Some spots could see 40 to 50mm in two to three hours, leading to some surface water flooding, with the possibility of large hail and frequent lightning.

These showers and thunderstorms are expected to drift northwards and ease during the evening.

open image in gallery Two thunderstorm warnings are in place on Thursday ( Met Office )

On Thursday, another band of thunderstorms and heavy rain is expected to move slowly across England and Wales. The Met Office said that 20 to 30mm of rainfall is expected to accumulate in three hours across the affected areas, and up to 50mm in 12 hours can be expected in places.

There is a small chance that some places may see more than 50mm in three hours and more than 75mm through 12 hours, especially over east-facing high ground. Lightning and hail of 1 to 2cm will also be hazardous, the forecaster warned, with some strong gusts presenting a hazard across the south of England early on Thursday morning.

open image in gallery Heavy rain is expected across parts of the country ( Met Office )

The Met Office warned of a slight chance that power cuts could occur, impacting homes and businesses which could be flooded quickly. Buildings could face damage from floodwater, lightning strikes or hail. Flooding and lightning could cause delays and cancellations to train and bus services.

The risk of spray and sudden flooding could also lead to road closures and difficult driving conditions.

Met Office chief forecaster Steve Willington attributed the unsettled weather to warmer and more humid air moving north across the UK.

open image in gallery People under an umbrella in the rain on Sunny Sands Beach in Folkestone last week ( Getty )

He said: “As we move into Wednesday there is a growing risk of heavy rain and thunderstorms, with warm and humid air helping to trigger heavy showers and thunderstorms. Some places could see significant amounts of rain falling in a short period of time, bringing the potential for localised flooding, travel disruption and frequent lightning.

“On Thursday, slow-moving heavy and thundery rain may bring prolonged rainfall to some areas, increasing the risk of localised impacts. There remains some uncertainty around where the heaviest rain will fall, so it is important to keep up to date with the latest forecast and warnings."

The incoming downpour comes as England and Wales are expected to record one of the driest summers on record. Almost three-quarters of England is designated as under drought, as is the entirety of Wales.

Scientists previously warned that a heavy downpour could cause more harm than good following the dry and hot summer, as it could lead to flash flooding in parts of the country.

News.content:

Forty people who disappeared as children from UK asylum seeker hotels have still not been located, prompting parliamentarians to demand the Government outline its efforts to trace them.

While the majority of those who vanished have since turned 18, two remain children, the Joint Committee on Human Rights (JCHR) said as it highlighted its anxiety over the missing young people.

It was revealed in 2023 that more than 400 unaccompanied asylum-seeking children had gone missing from Home Office hotel sites, with some reported to be as young as 12.

That same year, the High Court ruled that the Home Office’s routine practice of placing lone child asylum seekers in hotels was unlawful.

At the time, the Conservative administration stated that "due to the unsustainable rise in illegal Channel crossings, the Government has had no option but to accommodate young people in hotels on a temporary basis while placements with local authorities are urgently found".

open image in gallery The government has been urged to do more to find the missing people ( AFP/Getty )

The JCHR report confirmed that, as of June this year, 40 people who went missing during their childhood had still not been found.

A director of children’s social care at the Department for Education, told the committee: "Guidance was issued to police from the Home Office, to be shared with local networks, to ensure that we continue to look for those children and that we can surface whether they have been found, and information can be updated to provide more reassurance."

In a letter sent to the committee last year in her then-role as border security and asylum minister, Dame Angela Eagle noted that some of those who were traced were "located in exploitative situations and may have been trafficked or victims of other forms of exploitation".

The committee, which published a wider report on children’s social care on Thursday, said: "We welcome the fact that the majority of missing children have now been found.

"However, we continue to be extremely concerned about the fact that some children who went missing from asylum hotels in previous years remain missing."

Parliamentarians called on the Home Office to "make clear what specific action is being taken to locate these children, to investigate the causes for them going missing, and to avoid unaccompanied asylum-seeking children going missing in the future".

They further requested that the Home Office provide updates every three months "with details of efforts to locate the children who remain missing".

Dame Rachel de Souza, England’s Children’s Commissioner, said she shared the report’s "serious concern" regarding the missing youngsters.

She added: "Every child arriving in this country has the right to safely apply for asylum and to be provided with shelter and support while they do so.

open image in gallery Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood speaks to the media ( PA )

"The disappearance of these children represents an unacceptable failure, and the Government must set out the action it is taking to locate those still missing and prevent this happening again."

A Government spokesperson said: "The safety and wellbeing of children is paramount, and we take any child going missing extremely seriously.

"The Home Office-operated accommodation for unaccompanied asylum-seeking children closed in January 2024. Since then, the vast majority of children reported missing from those settings have subsequently been located.

"Police forces are responsible for investigating missing children cases and we continue to review our records, share relevant information with them and work closely with local authorities and safeguarding partners to support those investigations."

The findings come after it was announced earlier this month that an additional 13 hotels housing asylum seekers had closed, following Labour’s commitment to end the use of asylum hotels entirely prior to the next election.

Ministers are expanding the use of more "basic" locations, such as former military barracks. The latest closures are expected to save taxpayers £51 million, reducing the total number of sites below 160, down from a peak of around 400 under the Conservatives.

News.title: Savio scores on debut as Spurs cruise past Charlton in Carabao Cup
News.content:
It looked like this was going to be a night for “one of their own”, but Tottenham Hotspur’s latest big-money arrival, Sávio, stole the headlines to crank up the excitement at his new club.

Mikey Moore had set Spurs on their way to what proved a comfortable Carabao Cup success over Championship club Charlton Athletic and heard his name sung by the home fans.

But Sávio stepped off the substitutes’ bench to take the limelight with a late goal just a few days after completing his expensive switch from Manchester City, and head coach Roberto De Zerbi is demanding many more to come.

“A perfect day for him,” said De Zerbi. “His biggest improvement is to increase the number of goals. He is one of the best wingers, but the best wingers score many goals and I spoke with him two days ago, and we put the goal at 10-12 goals.

“We need 10-12 goals from the wingers. Last season, we suffered too much because the number of goals were not enough.”

News.title: German airport worker dies of malaria after mosquito imported on plane
News.content:
Five airport workers in Frankfurt have been infected with malaria and one has died after being bitten by a stowaway mosquito, health officials have said.

The employees are thought to have been infected in early July, but their diagnosis was delayed due to a lack of travel history to malaria-endemic regions, according to the Robert Koch Institute, Germany’s federal agency responsible for disease control.

It is believed that they were bitten by mosquitoes which arrived at the airport on a plane, most likely from Africa, where 95 per cent of global malaria cases are found.

The five surviving airport workers – who are all male and are said to work in different parts of the facility and in different jobs – are undergoing medical care.

Traps have now been installed across the airport in an attempt to catch any remaining mosquitoes and analyse their origin, according to an airport spokesperson.

It is not the first time that Frankfurt Airport, Germany’s busiest travel hub, has recorded a case of malaria, according to the Robert Koch Institute, which added that there was another incidence in 2023.

More than 610,000 people die of malaria every year, the overwhelming majority children under five in Africa who are unable to quickly access treatment.

The disease, which is caused by a parasite carried by infected mosquitoes, is largely curable if treated early with antimalarials.

In Britain and Europe, there are thousands of imported cases of malaria every year reported in returning travellers from Africa and Asia – but local transmission is exceedingly rare.

Of the 5,000 or so cases recorded in Europe every year, typically just five are caught locally – either from an airport or from a non-infected European mosquito picking up the disease from a sickened person and spreading it to others.

Early symptoms include fever, headaches, and chills, which can quickly develop into multi-organ failure.

Vaccines were made available for the first time in 2024 and are licenced for use in young children in Africa, although they are thought to be only between 30 and 50 per cent effective at preventing the disease.
