News.title: Livestock bacterial disease spreading among humans in Europe
News.content:
In Barcelona, researchers found further evidence that the bacterium was spreading between people.

Nine cases identified between December 2025 and March 2026 were caused by strains that differed by just zero to four genetic mutations, suggesting the infections were part of a recent transmission chain rather than separate cases acquired from animals.

The bacterium can survive in crusted areas on the skin for up to 42 months, according to Dr McHale, raising questions about the role of contaminated surfaces, equipment and shared spaces.

People should not be alarmed by the infection, which is treatable with a course of antibiotics, he added.

This could make hygiene particularly important in places such as saunas, where people may have prolonged skin contact with others and with shared surfaces.

Saunas have historically been a destination for gay and bisexual men seeking social and sexual contact.

Dating apps such as Grindr have since made casual encounters in these environments far easier to arrange, experts say.

“What we’re seeing is the kind of in-person venues like saunas being combined with apps,” said Rusi Jaspal, a Professor of Psychology at the University of Brighton and expert on wellbeing among gay men.

“Someone might, for example, be in a sauna but also have their app on, and that might be a way of getting people to come to the sauna. So they’re not only attracting people who are already in the sauna, but who might be outside of that environment and coming in.”

Progress and complacency

Professor Jaspal believes the success of Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP), which protects against HIV, has also played a role.

“I think that is a really big contributor,” he said. “On the one hand, obviously it’s fantastic that PrEP is there. It prevents HIV; it’s extremely effective against HIV. But it’s not effective against other infections.”

He argued that because PrEP has removed the fear of HIV that shaped gay men’s sexual behaviour for decades, some men are now having condomless sex with more partners, in the belief that other infections are treatable in a way HIV once was not.

“Because they think, well, everything else is treatable – gonorrhoea, syphilis, it’s all treatable – they’re going to just not use condoms,” he said. “That is not only creating more of a risk of infection, but I think people are having more partners as well.”

Sexual contact is not the only route by which the bacterium appears to be spreading.

In Norway, ten cases have been linked to martial arts, with some infections occurring during training in Norway and others during trips to Thailand.

One case report described a 34-year-old Muay Thai fighter who developed recurrent pustular lesions after returning from a training trip, later confirmed as D. congolensis through whole-genome sequencing.

Dr McHale said the bacterium tends to take hold where the skin has already been compromised in some way.

“Predisposing factors for infection include cutaneous microtrauma, for example, from ultraviolet radiation, tick exposure and insect bites, and maceration of the skin,” he said.

Dermatophilus congolensis is notoriously difficult to grow in culture, meaning infections can easily go undiagnosed or be mistaken for more common skin conditions.

Researchers in Barcelona have warned that cases could be going unrecognised because sexual health clinics do not routinely test for the bacterium.

But Professor Jaspal believes the legacy of the HIV/Aids epidemic explains why this cluster was identified so quickly.

He said the crisis of the 1980s, when confusion and stigma allowed the virus to spread largely undetected, forced public health bodies to build far stronger surveillance and communication systems for outbreaks among gay and bisexual men.

That same infrastructure, he argued, has since been used to manage subsequent threats such as mpox – and now this obscure bacterium – far more effectively.

“I think we are quite rightly identifying cases early on, so that we can then communicate that risk to people and encourage precautions to protect themselves,” Professor Jaspal said. “That is really, really important.”

News.title: The five best coastal places to retire in the UK
News.content:
How equity release can help you purchase a seaside property

UK homeowners aged 55 or over may be able to use equity release in two main ways: either to help fund the purchase of a second home, or to buy a new home and release equity from that property as part of the same legal transaction. Seeking professional advice is key to understanding which option may be right for you.



The most popular equity release product is a lifetime mortgage. A lifetime mortgage is a loan secured against your home. It will reduce the value of your estate and could affect your entitlement to means-tested benefits. There is no obligation to make monthly repayments with a lifetime mortgage, although you can choose to make some if you wish. Instead, the full amount plus interest is only repaid when the last homeowner dies or enters permanent long-term care, and this is usually done with the sale of the home.



You must always seek professional help when considering equity release. Make sure your adviser is looking at products from lenders that are members of the Equity Release Council. The Equity Release Council, the industry trade body, requires its members to offer plans that comply with its product standards.

News.title: Households warned of ‘worse to come’ as energy bills rise
News.content:
Households have been warned there is “worse to come” on energy bills after Ofgem raised its price cap to a three-year high.

On Wednesday, the regulator announced typical annual household gas and electricity prices will rise by £60 from October.

The 4pc rise follows a 13pc jump in July as the Iran war pushed up global oil and gas prices.

Analysts at Cornwall Insight, the energy consultancy, said there was no relief in sight for households in January if the conflict in the Middle East continues.

It said a further 9pc rise should be expected in the new year, putting an average January bill up to £1,872 a year, £149 higher than the prices coming into effect from October.

The forecast underlines the challenges faced by Andy Burnham as he stakes his reputation on lowering the cost of living.

Mr Burnham on Wednesday said he recognised rising energy bills were “difficult” for people, adding the government had decided to remove VAT from electricity bills to “give people that little bit of help”.

Speaking to reporters from a supermarket in London, the Prime Minister said: “We know the price cap will have an impact, but it is what we can do right now.

“We’ll continue to look as we go forward at how we get energy prices down in the long term, and that’s what we need to do too.”

However, the latest increase to the price cap effectively wipes out the £45 reduction from Mr Burnham’s VAT cut.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, hinted on Wednesday there could be more action from ministers “to protect families from unaffordable bills”, with the Budget due to be held on October 28.

Commenting on the price cap, Craig Lowrey, of Cornwall Insight, said there was a risk of “more hardship” by January.

“Where January bills land will depend on whether the situation in the Middle East calms down in the next couple of months.”

He added that low European gas stocks heading into the winter meant bills were unlikely to fall.

Elsewhere Ms Fahnbulleh appeared to suggest that investment in net zero projects was contributing to higher household bills.

Asked on LBC if the rise in bills could not solely be blamed on the Middle East conflict, but also on political choices to pay for renewable subsidies, she replied: “Well, no, so it is both.”

However, she later insisted it was “simply not true” that net zero was adding to bills, when questioned by Sky News.

News.title: China clamped down on exotic wildlife farms – now they’ve moved to Southeast Asia
News.content:
We hear the bamboo rats before we see them. At the bottom of almost 200 concrete containers are hundreds of chunky rodents – some squealing as they scurry in circles, others loudly gnawing corn, sugar cane and bamboo with their sharp protruding teeth.

“They’re very easy to keep,” says Suriyan Wanpakwaen, as he peers into one of the pits at the DIY breeding facility beside his home in Nakhon Ratchasima, a province roughly 150 miles northeast of Bangkok. “My favourite thing is how clean they are, there are no bad smells.”

For almost seven years, Mr Suriyan has been farming bamboo rats – and now, the business is booming. A single rodent can sell for as much as 4,000 baht (roughly £90), and there’s so much demand that Mr Suriyan and his wife can’t keep up.

They’re not the only ones cashing in. Since the coronavirus pandemic, backyard wildlife farms like this have proliferated across Southeast Asia.

While this industry long existed in the region, the mounting new additions are filling a vacuum created when, in the wake of Covid-19, China closed thousands of similar farms over bio-security concerns.

“There was obviously a void and therefore an opportunity,” said Dr Ross McEwing, a project officer focused on the illegal wildlife trade and emerging zoonotic diseases at the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) in Bangkok.

“There was a coordinated effort to set up these wildlife farms, led by people who could consolidate stock and move that stock illegally across multiple international borders,” he added.

News.title: Ten years after Brazil’s Zika epidemic, its children are still paying the price
News.content:
In the heated pool, ten-year-old Stephany Vitória Silva Costa is weightless. The water soothes her convulsing muscles, providing brief respite from constant pain, and she coos with delight, igniting smiles among everyone in the room.

Stephany is a “Zika baby”; one of more than 3,080 children born with Congenital Zika Syndrome (CZS) following a devastating outbreak of the mosquito borne virus that swept Brazil in 2015-16. At least 444 of those children have died, mainly from respiratory and infectious diseases.

Like most of the surviving children from the cohort, she has suffered from an array of symptoms including microcephaly, severe cognitive and motor impairment, vision and hearing loss and seizures – which can occur up to ten times a day.

But a decade after the outbreak, a second wave of complications are emerging in children like Stephany.

Stephany’s exposed back, showing the pronounced 120-degree curvature caused by rapid, severe scoliosis Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

As her therapist gently turns her in the pool, a pronounced bulge shows through the back of her pink and blue swim top. Over the last two years, her growing spine has been pulled 120-degrees into an S-shaped curve that is now crushing her lungs.

While many of the children born with microcephaly after the outbreak died in early infancy, a much-loved group including Stephany lived on. Now, however, mortality rates are again climbing as the children near adolescence.

An x-ray image showing a severe s-shaped spinal deformity threatening to compress a young patient’s lungs Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“It weighs heavily on my heart. After so many years of following these children, it is inevitable to form bonds – not only with them, but with their families,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti, one of just 11 paediatric neurologists in the state.

“Every loss affects me deeply. It is very hard to say goodbye to them”.

At the Altino Ventura Foundation’s (FAV) hydrotherapy centre, steam clings to murals depicting ocean scenes – a smiling pink octopus swims around a silver painted shipwreck.

As Stephany coos, another girl in a brown swimsuit and rainbow coloured shorts smiles as her mother fills a cup with water and pours it over her black curls.

Originally an ophthalmology institute, FAV expanded into neuro-rehabilitation as the Zika crisis unfolded. It provides free therapy to children with CZS twice a week, with treatment plans reassessed every six months.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation and 84 are currently being treated. Its clinicians are tracking the cohort's long-term development.

Physiotherapist Gustav Wagner assists a young patient in the hydrotherapy pool Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

None of the Zika children present can walk or hold themselves up, and the majority have already had at least one major surgery.

Nevertheless, Gustav Wagner, a physiotherapist, says installing the hydrotherapy pool – which increases blood flow and loosens muscles – was a major breakthrough.

The children can’t express pain verbally. Mr Wagner and his team instead use a visual scale from one to ten, based on reading their posture and expressions. The mothers, above all, learn to spot the smallest changes and the pool, they say, makes a huge difference.

“It’s a very peculiar disease,” says Amanda Rodrigues, a physiotherapist. “We have to learn with them how to get better – we have never treated something like this before”.

A silent invasion

First discovered in 1947 in Uganda’s Zika forest, the Zika virus is thought to have quietly reached Brazil in 2014.

Experts attribute its arrival to increased air travel; either carried by visitors landing for the 2014 FIFA World Cup or brought from active outbreaks in the South Pacific islands.

Either way, the virus spread unnoticed and unchecked in Brazil for over a year.

Most Zika infections are asymptomatic or easily mistaken for dengue, both cause a similar red rash and flu-like symptoms.

The alarm was finally raised in August 2015 when neuropaediatrician Dr Vanessa van der Linden identified an unprecedented surge in infants born with microcephaly across Pernambuco state.

“It was very chaotic at the beginning,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti. She added that doctors frantically coordinated emergency responses over WhatsApp as the crisis unfolded.

“The physical toll on the children was devastating,” she said.

Paediatric neurologist Dr Milena Cavalcanti Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Infections early in pregnancy inflicted the worst damage. And in one of the side rooms of the hydrotherapy centre, it's evident that the disabilities are profound.

Five children sit motionless in their wheelchairs with blankets pulled up to their necks. One of them, Emily Sophia dos Santos Luna, weighed just six kilograms at age two before being given a feeding tube to enable her to survive.

The children are unable to swallow, causing mucus to pool in the back of their throats. To prevent choking, their wheelchairs are permanently tilted at a 45 degree angle.

Maria José da Silva wheels her granddaughter to specialist transport Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“In the beginning, we thought they would discover a treatment,” says Emily’s grandmother, Maria José da Silva, 43. “But now we understand she will always be this way”.

She added: “It’s a very difficult life, but God gave us the power to keep going. I will take care of her until the day God wants”.

In the therapeutic gym, a large room filled with foam mats, standing frames and slings hung from the ceiling, Allana Kauane perches on a large silver balance ball.

She wears a green skirt, shin-high pink socks, and a white T-shirt that has “be happy” printed in shimmery lettering.

Ms Rodrigues, her physiotherapist, supports her torso and bounces her gently to build core strength. With every movement, she patiently lifts Allana’s head back up as it falls onto her chest.

Thailene Maria uses a bright gold pompom to draw her daughter’s focus Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Thailene Maria, the child’s 28-year-old mother, waves a bright gold pompom in front of her eyes in an effort to draw her focus.

Down the corridor in a consultation room, Dr Cavalcanti examines another patient.

It’s a girl who has not had a seizure in six years, but her last one lasted thirty minutes – six times the length that defines a medical emergency in Brazil.

Manuelle does not like to be touched, her grandmother says. She used to bite herself, now she pulls at her own hair instead.

As Dr Cavalcanti taps gently at her knee with a reflex hammer, the girl tenses and struggles to lie flat. Fine dark hair has started to grow along the girl’s shins – a side effect, says Dr Cavalcanti, of the anticonvulsant medication she relies on to control her seizures.

It is one of several changes the clinic still cannot fully explain. Many patients entered puberty years earlier than expected, one as young as three. Most are treated with hormone-blocking injections.

Dr Cavalcanti gently tests the reflexes of a young patient’s knee Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“We don’t know,” says Dr Cavalcanti, when asked about the cause. “We are just following the cases”.

On the ground floor, past the therapy rooms, sits the Capela Santissima Trinidade, a small wood-pannelled chapel. Inside, there are rows of pews, and in the centre is a large stained glass window.

It’s a small reminder that the building was designed to cater for the spiritual needs of its patients alongside their medical care.

While infants with CZS initially received only basic motor stimulation, severe musculoskeletal issues are emerging as they reach adolescence.

Dr Epitácio Rolim, the top orthopaedic surgeon in the state, has tracked a cohort of 152 children since the outbreak.

By age 10, 98 per cent developed orthopaedic deformities – 70 per cent suffer hip deformities, and 64 per cent from spinal curvature.

Previously, the public health system did not offer corrective surgeries or have a structured waiting list.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation Credit : Lucas Landau

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco state, told The Telegraph: “We know we have a lot to do yet. The needs are giant and the funds are not”.

The root problem is neurological, says Dr Rolim. Damaged brain pathways create severe muscle imbalances around major joints. Unable to reposition themselves, the children’s relentless muscle tightness pulls their hips out of their socket and twists their spines.

Delaying intervention drastically restricts surgical options, Dr Rolim warns.

In the worst cases, repairing the hip is no longer possible. Surgeons must instead remove the top of the thigh bone simply to stop it from grinding against the socket.

“I am not talking about surgery to make most of these children walk,” says Dr Rolim. “The realistic goal is quality of life… hope does not mean promising a cure that we do not have… it means living with as little pain as possible”.

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco State Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Only five to seven per cent of pregnant women exposed to Zika had babies with visible symptoms like microcephaly. For the rest, timing of the infection in pregnancy determined how destructive the virus was.

“The children you saw with microcephaly were at the extreme end of the spectrum,” says Dr Ernesto Marques, a senior researcher at Fiocruz in Recife. “As the others become teens, developmental delays are showing up more clearly”.

Dr Patricia Garcez, a neuroscientist at King’s College London who helped establish the link between Zika and brain defects in 2016, said that many of the “milder” CZS cases are now displaying severe autism and neurodevelopmental delay, or motor deficits caused by prenatal Zika exposure without severe microcephaly.

The perfect breeding ground

The night we arrive in Recife, known as the “Brazilian Venice”, heavy rains transform the city’s roads into rivers. Gesturing to the rising water outside, our taxi driver chuckles: “Here we say: When someone sneezes, the whole city floods”.

Centuries ago, the city was a low-lying landscape of tidal sandbanks, estuaries and mangroves. When Dutch colonisers arrived in the 1600s, they engineered canals, bridges and dikes to prevent flooding and make the swamplands habitable.

It is this geography that made Recife, the capital of Pernambuco, the epicentre of the 2015-16 Zika outbreak, its pools of still water proving the perfect breeding ground for mosquitoes.

The state recorded around 742 confirmed CZS cases – 24 per cent of cases nationwide, and 39 per cent of cases in the northeast.

In Recife’s hillside favelas – densely populated, self-built communities largely lacking basic public services – residents were forced to store tap water in open buckets and barrels due to intermittent water flow making the mosquito problem worse.

Joane da Silva Sena pushes her son Heytor up a steep hill to their home in Favela do Monte Credit : Lucas Landau

Halfway up a steep hill in Favela do Monte, Joane da Silva Sena lives in deep poverty, caring alone for her 10-year-son, Heytor, who was born with microcephaly in November 2015.

Ms Sena, 36, a thin, weary-looking woman with a kind face, is entirely on her own.

The father abandoned them at birth, and the neighbours refuse to even watch Heytor while she goes to the shop, instead watching her struggle up the hill from their homes.

Ms Sena rarely receives any help with her son Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“My family doesn’t help me, nobody cares,” she says. “People are afraid of Heytor, they say he’s ‘special’.”

Inside the house, only secured with metal bars on gaping door and window frames, Ms Sena frequently skips meals so Heytor can eat. There’s a shadow on the wall of the pink-painted kitchen where the fridge should be. She had to throw it out because it kept giving her electric shocks and was too expensive to repair.

Heytor’s specialised wheelchair broke months ago, leaving him only with an ill-fitting wicker chair that he constantly slumps on.

Ms Sena lifts her son roughly 10 times a day Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Ms Sena lifts his 54 kg frame roughly 10 times a day between the chair and the bed to soothe him when he gets agitated. She also carries him up the steep hill twice a week to reach physiotherapy classes.

“I will not abandon him,” Ms Sena says through tears. “I just ask God for health, because if I get sick, no one will look after him”.

In August 2025, Brazil’s Congress passed a bill – first floated in 2015 – to compensate the families of children born with microcephaly and other disabilities caused by Zika.

The package includes a one-off payment of 50,000 BRL (£7,150), and a tax-free monthly support payment of 8,150 BRL (£1,165), five times the previous allowance.

But despite the national law, Ms Sena receives very little support.

The hospital Heytor was born in did not provide official documentation linking Heytor’s condition to Zika, even though multiple experts say that it is the cause.

Ms Sena said she dreams about having access to the funds, adding that she would love to “buy a beautiful armchair that will be so comfortable for him”.

Ms Sena prays for her own robust health so that her son is not without a carer Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

After The Telegraph raised her case with the Pernambuco Health Department, state officials launched an investigation into Heytor’s birth records and admitted him to the hospital for a complete evaluation.

They also dropped off medication and nappies at the house and have arranged for a vehicle to transport them to therapy classes.

Acknowledging that Ms Sena’s struggles span housing, transportation, social support and caregiver mental health, the state told The Telegraph it would assemble a multi-agency task force to assist her.

Across Brazil, the mothers of children with Zika are renowned for their resilience.

Many were young and living in poverty when the outbreak hit. Fuelled by deep rooted stigma, most were then abandoned by their partners after their children were born with disabilities.

It took a decade of campaigning for these women – a movement known as the Mothers of Angels – to finally secure the social security breakthrough last year.

They proved that the state failed families twice over: by not containing the virus, and by under-compensating the children for years.

It remains unclear whether Brazil is vulnerable to another Zika outbreak.

In 2016, amid the original epidemic, the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern.

However, that immunity is unlikely to last forever.

Originally focused on eye care, the Altino Ventura Foundation expanded its operations during the 2015 outbreak Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A new generation has grown up without having been exposed to the virus, creating a growing population vulnerable to infection, he says.

The root cause of poor water infrastructure and mosquito infestation also hasn’t been resolved.

“Almost everybody born after 2016 has not been exposed to Zika at all... they are naive, and that piles up with the older people who did not get infected,” he told The Telegraph.

“Once the population vulnerable to Zika reaches a critical threshold, the risk of another outbreak grows”.

The research that could prepare Brazil for that eventuality has stalled.

There is still no approved Zika vaccine or antibody treatment. The most advanced candidate has only just completed early-stage safety trials, and experts say a larger trial is nearly impossible without an active outbreak to test it.

Basic diagnostic tools also have major limitations. Standard antibody tests still cannot reliably distinguish Zika from dengue, and PCR testing – the only definitive testing method – is only effective for around five days at the peak of infections.

Ms Costa contracted Zika five months into her pregnancy. When doctors recommended that she terminate, she refused.

Erika Silva Costa, Stephany’s mother and full-time caregiver, is also a fierce campaigner Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A former MRI technician, Ms Costa is now a full-time caregiver and a prominent campaigner for Zika children.

“My dedication to her is total, 24 hours a day… my brain is always awake,” she says, adding that she sleeps in the same bed facing Stephany in case she chokes during the night. “I feel like the umbilical cord was never cut”.

Despite the urgent need, Stephany’s position remains perilous.

Her doctors say she needs an operation costing 150,000 BRL (£21,400) on her spine but so far she has been refused coverage by medical insurers. Ms Costa is now mounting a legal battle to fight the decision in court.

“The authorities together with the health services aren’t tackling this properly,” said Dr Rolim.

“It’s so frustrating. The professionals know what needs to be done, but can’t do it because the system doesn’t provide the right conditions”.

With the public health system crippled by long waiting lists and a lack of specialised equipment, families like Ms Costa are waiting in limbo.

“Sometimes one of the children dies and we all fall apart,” she says. “We have to believe in God to wake up the next day and be strong”.

News.title: Ten years after Brazil’s Zika epidemic, its children are still paying the price
News.content:
In the heated pool, ten-year-old Stephany Vitória Silva Costa is weightless. The water soothes her convulsing muscles, providing brief respite from constant pain, and she coos with delight, igniting smiles among everyone in the room.

Stephany is a “Zika baby”; one of more than 3,080 children born with Congenital Zika Syndrome (CZS) following a devastating outbreak of the mosquito borne virus that swept Brazil in 2015-16. At least 444 of those children have died, mainly from respiratory and infectious diseases.

Like most of the surviving children from the cohort, she has suffered from an array of symptoms including microcephaly, severe cognitive and motor impairment, vision and hearing loss and seizures – which can occur up to ten times a day.

But a decade after the outbreak, a second wave of complications are emerging in children like Stephany.

Stephany’s exposed back, showing the pronounced 120-degree curvature caused by rapid, severe scoliosis Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

As her therapist gently turns her in the pool, a pronounced bulge shows through the back of her pink and blue swim top. Over the last two years, her growing spine has been pulled 120-degrees into an S-shaped curve that is now crushing her lungs.

While many of the children born with microcephaly after the outbreak died in early infancy, a much-loved group including Stephany lived on. Now, however, mortality rates are again climbing as the children near adolescence.

An x-ray image showing a severe s-shaped spinal deformity threatening to compress a young patient’s lungs Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“It weighs heavily on my heart. After so many years of following these children, it is inevitable to form bonds – not only with them, but with their families,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti, one of just 11 paediatric neurologists in the state.

“Every loss affects me deeply. It is very hard to say goodbye to them”.

At the Altino Ventura Foundation’s (FAV) hydrotherapy centre, steam clings to murals depicting ocean scenes – a smiling pink octopus swims around a silver painted shipwreck.

As Stephany coos, another girl in a brown swimsuit and rainbow coloured shorts smiles as her mother fills a cup with water and pours it over her black curls.

Originally an ophthalmology institute, FAV expanded into neuro-rehabilitation as the Zika crisis unfolded. It provides free therapy to children with CZS twice a week, with treatment plans reassessed every six months.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation and 84 are currently being treated. Its clinicians are tracking the cohort's long-term development.

Physiotherapist Gustav Wagner assists a young patient in the hydrotherapy pool Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

None of the Zika children present can walk or hold themselves up, and the majority have already had at least one major surgery.

Nevertheless, Gustav Wagner, a physiotherapist, says installing the hydrotherapy pool – which increases blood flow and loosens muscles – was a major breakthrough.

The children can’t express pain verbally. Mr Wagner and his team instead use a visual scale from one to ten, based on reading their posture and expressions. The mothers, above all, learn to spot the smallest changes and the pool, they say, makes a huge difference.

“It’s a very peculiar disease,” says Amanda Rodrigues, a physiotherapist. “We have to learn with them how to get better – we have never treated something like this before”.

A silent invasion

First discovered in 1947 in Uganda’s Zika forest, the Zika virus is thought to have quietly reached Brazil in 2014.

Experts attribute its arrival to increased air travel; either carried by visitors landing for the 2014 FIFA World Cup or brought from active outbreaks in the South Pacific islands.

Either way, the virus spread unnoticed and unchecked in Brazil for over a year.

Most Zika infections are asymptomatic or easily mistaken for dengue, both cause a similar red rash and flu-like symptoms.

The alarm was finally raised in August 2015 when neuropaediatrician Dr Vanessa van der Linden identified an unprecedented surge in infants born with microcephaly across Pernambuco state.

“It was very chaotic at the beginning,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti. She added that doctors frantically coordinated emergency responses over WhatsApp as the crisis unfolded.

“The physical toll on the children was devastating,” she said.

Paediatric neurologist Dr Milena Cavalcanti Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Infections early in pregnancy inflicted the worst damage. And in one of the side rooms of the hydrotherapy centre, it's evident that the disabilities are profound.

Five children sit motionless in their wheelchairs with blankets pulled up to their necks. One of them, Emily Sophia dos Santos Luna, weighed just six kilograms at age two before being given a feeding tube to enable her to survive.

The children are unable to swallow, causing mucus to pool in the back of their throats. To prevent choking, their wheelchairs are permanently tilted at a 45 degree angle.

Maria José da Silva wheels her granddaughter to specialist transport Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“In the beginning, we thought they would discover a treatment,” says Emily’s grandmother, Maria José da Silva, 43. “But now we understand she will always be this way”.

She added: “It’s a very difficult life, but God gave us the power to keep going. I will take care of her until the day God wants”.

In the therapeutic gym, a large room filled with foam mats, standing frames and slings hung from the ceiling, Allana Kauane perches on a large silver balance ball.

She wears a green skirt, shin-high pink socks, and a white T-shirt that has “be happy” printed in shimmery lettering.

Ms Rodrigues, her physiotherapist, supports her torso and bounces her gently to build core strength. With every movement, she patiently lifts Allana’s head back up as it falls onto her chest.

Thailene Maria uses a bright gold pompom to draw her daughter’s focus Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Thailene Maria, the child’s 28-year-old mother, waves a bright gold pompom in front of her eyes in an effort to draw her focus.

Down the corridor in a consultation room, Dr Cavalcanti examines another patient.

It’s a girl who has not had a seizure in six years, but her last one lasted thirty minutes – six times the length that defines a medical emergency in Brazil.

Manuelle does not like to be touched, her grandmother says. She used to bite herself, now she pulls at her own hair instead.

As Dr Cavalcanti taps gently at her knee with a reflex hammer, the girl tenses and struggles to lie flat. Fine dark hair has started to grow along the girl’s shins – a side effect, says Dr Cavalcanti, of the anticonvulsant medication she relies on to control her seizures.

It is one of several changes the clinic still cannot fully explain. Many patients entered puberty years earlier than expected, one as young as three. Most are treated with hormone-blocking injections.

Dr Cavalcanti gently tests the reflexes of a young patient’s knee Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“We don’t know,” says Dr Cavalcanti, when asked about the cause. “We are just following the cases”.

On the ground floor, past the therapy rooms, sits the Capela Santissima Trinidade, a small wood-pannelled chapel. Inside, there are rows of pews, and in the centre is a large stained glass window.

It’s a small reminder that the building was designed to cater for the spiritual needs of its patients alongside their medical care.

While infants with CZS initially received only basic motor stimulation, severe musculoskeletal issues are emerging as they reach adolescence.

Dr Epitácio Rolim, the top orthopaedic surgeon in the state, has tracked a cohort of 152 children since the outbreak.

By age 10, 98 per cent developed orthopaedic deformities – 70 per cent suffer hip deformities, and 64 per cent from spinal curvature.

Previously, the public health system did not offer corrective surgeries or have a structured waiting list.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation Credit : Lucas Landau

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco state, told The Telegraph: “We know we have a lot to do yet. The needs are giant and the funds are not”.

The root problem is neurological, says Dr Rolim. Damaged brain pathways create severe muscle imbalances around major joints. Unable to reposition themselves, the children’s relentless muscle tightness pulls their hips out of their socket and twists their spines.

Delaying intervention drastically restricts surgical options, Dr Rolim warns.

In the worst cases, repairing the hip is no longer possible. Surgeons must instead remove the top of the thigh bone simply to stop it from grinding against the socket.

“I am not talking about surgery to make most of these children walk,” says Dr Rolim. “The realistic goal is quality of life… hope does not mean promising a cure that we do not have… it means living with as little pain as possible”.

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco State Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Only five to seven per cent of pregnant women exposed to Zika had babies with visible symptoms like microcephaly. For the rest, timing of the infection in pregnancy determined how destructive the virus was.

“The children you saw with microcephaly were at the extreme end of the spectrum,” says Dr Ernesto Marques, a senior researcher at Fiocruz in Recife. “As the others become teens, developmental delays are showing up more clearly”.

Dr Patricia Garcez, a neuroscientist at King’s College London who helped establish the link between Zika and brain defects in 2016, said that many of the “milder” CZS cases are now displaying severe autism and neurodevelopmental delay, or motor deficits caused by prenatal Zika exposure without severe microcephaly.

The perfect breeding ground

The night we arrive in Recife, known as the “Brazilian Venice”, heavy rains transform the city’s roads into rivers. Gesturing to the rising water outside, our taxi driver chuckles: “Here we say: When someone sneezes, the whole city floods”.

Centuries ago, the city was a low-lying landscape of tidal sandbanks, estuaries and mangroves. When Dutch colonisers arrived in the 1600s, they engineered canals, bridges and dikes to prevent flooding and make the swamplands habitable.

It is this geography that made Recife, the capital of Pernambuco, the epicentre of the 2015-16 Zika outbreak, its pools of still water proving the perfect breeding ground for mosquitoes.

The state recorded around 742 confirmed CZS cases – 24 per cent of cases nationwide, and 39 per cent of cases in the northeast.

In Recife’s hillside favelas – densely populated, self-built communities largely lacking basic public services – residents were forced to store tap water in open buckets and barrels due to intermittent water flow making the mosquito problem worse.

Sports.title: Liverpool close in on £115million Bradley Barcola transfer with Premier League clubs to spend £1BILLION before deadline
Sports.content:
LIVERPOOL are closing in on an agreement for Paris Saint-Germain star Bradley Barcola.

The Reds are in the hunt for a new star on the wing following the departure of Mohamed Salah at the end of last season.



The French champions originally quoted suitors for the 23-year-old with a price tag of £145million.

But the Times claim that a deal could now be struck for something in the region of £115m.



That fee would provisionally make him the club’s second most expensive signing ever, just less than the £125million paid for Alexander Isak last summer.

The monster sum could be part of a late Premier League transfer rush reaching sums of over £1 BILLION.

Several deals have neared or broken the £100m mark so far this summer, including Elliot Anderson‘s move to Manchester City and Morgan Rogers‘ switch to Chelsea.

While other deals in that region are still under negotiation, with Enzo Fernandez linked to a City move, while Arsenal battle for Julian Alvarez‘s signature.

Nicolas Jackson‘s £65million agreement to move to Aston Villa looks like a reasonable fee in comparison, but still constitutes a record for the side.

If those deals go through, among other, it could amount to £1bn spent in the final fortnight of the window alone, per the Telegraph.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

Barcola has been the subject of strong interest to Andoni Iraola and Co since the start of the window.

And it wasn’t just the Anfield club sniffing around him, with Mikel Arteta‘s title-winning Arsenal also weighing up a move to upgrade their wide attack with the star.

The France international impressed at the World Cup, scoring three times at the tournament despite often being used as an impact substitute.

He also played a significant role in his club’s back to back Champions League triumphs.

Sports.title: Tottenham and Man Utd fans blast Carabao Cup draw as ‘rigged’ with two brutal ties while Man City get ‘easy’ opponents
Sports.content:
TOTTENHAM and Manchester United fans have slammed the Carabao Cup draw as “rigged”.

The two Premier League sides were handed tricky ties for the third round of the competition.



Spurs progressed to the third round with a romping 5-1 win over Charlton in North London on Tuesday evening.

Savio shined on his debut with a goal and an assist off the bench following his £85million switch from Manchester City.



United enter the League Cup in the next round thanks to qualifying for the Champions League last term.

Fans had already called it the “most rigged draw ever” before the main draw had even started.

That’s with EIGHT teams competing in the Champions League and Europa League being kept apart.

They, United included, were assigned either a home or away fixture in an earlier draw.

But Red Devils fans were still left far from happy after still being drawn against a team in Europe this season, Brighton.

The Seagulls were the exception as they are competing in the Conference League – and were therefore the toughest fixture on paper for United.

West Ham v Fulham or AFC Wimbledon

And they have become a bogey team for United in recent seasons, dumping them out of the FA Cup last term.

Spurs, on the other hand, were not protected in the draw after their 17th-place finish last season.

And they were handed a nightmare tie as they travel to Anfield to take on Liverpool.

Salt was then rubbed into the wounds when Man City were paired with Norwich at the Etihad.

One fan posted: “They have to be rigged, when did City last have a hard early round? And we’ve had five in the past two seasons.”



A second commented: “How have we been drawn with Brighton proper rigged, whilst City gets Norwich.”

Another wrote: “Arsenal and Man City yet again draw the easiest teams. It’s rigged for pair of them just like last season.”

A fourth added: “SO RIGGED.”

While a fifth sarcastically joked: “Brilliant lads! Not rigged at all.”

Another added: “City always getting easy fixtures.”

Other notable ties in the third round include Newcastle travelling south to take on Millwall at The Den.

Sports.title: Ex-Arsenal hothead Matteo Guendouzi sparks enormous brawl and attacked by fan after heated Champions League tie
Sports.content:
MATTEO GUENDOUZI was attacked by furious Lyon players, fans and staff after sparking a mass brawl with his taunting celebrations.

The former Arsenal midfielder, 27, went wild after his Fenerbahce side sealed their place in this season’s Champions League.





After a 1-1 draw in Turkey last week, the Super Lig side went 2-0 up in the fiery play-off second leg in France.

Despite Malick Fofana pulling one back on the hour mark for Lyon, they could not find the all-important equaliser.



And Guendouzi – who previously played for Lyon’s rivals Marseille – revelled in the victory.

It was reported he flashed a middle finger at the Lyon fans during the warm-up and was accused of shouting “we’re f***ing you” when his side went 2-0 up.



Then video footage from full-time showed him holding his arms out in smug celebration.

That prompted an angry reaction from the Lyon players, who shoved the smirking midfielder.

And plenty of his Fenerbahce team-mates – including Romelu Lukaku and ex-Manchester City keeper Ederson – rushed over to protect their man.

Then a full-on mass brawl broke out between players and backroom staff in dramatic scenes.

Guendouzi refused to calm down and had to be pulled away by team-mates, before he shouted at the TV camera.



But things then got even more violent when Guendouzi headed down the tunnel.

Despite his team-mates trying to curb his exuberant celebrations, he continued skipping and waving his arms.

Home supporters launched missiles at the big-haired Frenchman – just as they did during the game.

He then shouted towards the raging fans in the stand before a man in a white jacket – thought to be a member of Lyon staff in the club tracksuit – approached him and tried to assault him.



Guendouzi and other Fenerbahce players went mad and angrily pinned him against the wall, with Ederson in the thick of the fight and security holding players back to stop punches being thrown.



More video footage from inside the tunnel showed further Lyon staff members needing to be calmed down amid the vitriolic anger.

Guendouzi was hailed by various Marseille fans on social media for his antics and wrecking Lyon’s Champions League dreams.

Sports.title: Man City legend and TNT Sports pundit’s son, 17, makes Carabao Cup debut in stunning 3-2 win
Sports.content:
THE son of a Manchester City legend and TNT Sports pundit made his senior debut in a stunning Carabao Cup win.

Barnsley came from behind to beat Crewe Alexandra 3-2 on an eventful night at Oakwell.



And as well as the League One side progressing to round three, it was a special evening for a certain 17-year-old.

Midfielder Tayo Dunne came on for the final five minutes to make his Barnsley bow.



He completed all three of his attempted passes and – despite Crewe pulling one back in the 89th minute – helped his side hold on to advance.

Tayo is the son of ex-City, Everton, Aston Villa and QPR defender Richard Dunne.

Dunne Sr, 46, made 431 Premier League appearances – infamously scoring a record ten own goals – and earned 80 caps for Ireland.

His son has already represented the country too, featuring for the Republic of Ireland at Under-15 level.

And Dunne Jr gave an insight into what it has been like trying to follow in his father’s footsteps.

MANCHESTER UNITED were handed their hardest possible draw as they host Brighton in the Carabao Cup third round.

The draw was already mired in baseless fan controversy before the main event rolled round.



There was a pre-draw as a result of new rules meaning teams in the Champions League and Europa League cannot be allowed to draw each other.

All eight teams in those competitions were put in a separate pot and drawn home or away before the conclusion of Wednesday’s games, with fans claiming even the pre-draw was ‘rigged.’

Sports.title: Tottenham 5 Charlton 1: £85million Savio shines on debut as Spurs get over woeful Brentford loss in style
Sports.content:
SAVIO sparkled on his debut as he scored and assisted from the bench as Tottenham thrashed Charlton.

The Brazilian, who arrived from Manchester City for £85million this week, showed off his dancing feet as he masterminded two goals in quick succession.



Manager Roberto De Zerbi has splashed over £320m on new signings this summer already, with Omar Marmoush expected to walk through the door from City in the coming days too.

But who can blame the Italian when his big-money arrivals are having this kind of impact.



Tottenham are on the back of two dismal domestic campaigns and something has had to change in North London.

Turns out breaking the bank to bring in a host of new star players could be the answer.

New £85m midfielder Mateus Fernandes also made his full debut, while there wasn’t even space in the matchday squad for £100m man Sandro Tonali and fellow new arrival Marcos Senesi.

But it was Savio, who failed to impress often at City, was the star of the show following his 70th-minute introduction.

His contribution helped Spurs win just their second domestic game at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in over EIGHT MONTHS.

Nathan Jones’ visiting Charlton side paled in comparison, not least because the Addicks boss had made ten changes to his side that beat West Ham at the weekend.

Jones has 19-year-old striker Micah Mbick leading the line, while his goalkeeper, Tiernan Brooks, has never played a game in England’s top four leagues and joined from National League Gateshead in the summer.

Former Southampton chief Jones was hoping to rest most of his stars for their Championship clash with Preston this weekend, but was forced to introduce Danny McNamara and skipper Lloyd Jones after just 15 minutes.

Centre-back partnership Collins Sichenje and Billy Koumetio were both forced off with injuries.

Koumetio hobbled off holding his hamstring after treatment from a Charlton physio, while Sichenje was seemingly inconsolable as he was taken off on a stretcher following an innocuous knock in the box.

Despite Tottenham’s squad being laden with newly-acquired firepower, it was academy ace Mikey Moore that got things kicking.



The wideman, who spent last season on loan with Rangers, cut in from the right flank and unleashed a venomous strike that left Brooks helpless.

Moore is expected to join German side Cologne before the window closes next week, especially following the signings of Savio and Marmoush.

Moore’s goal kicked Spurs into life, and the hosts had doubled their lead through Dominic Solanke just four minutes later.



Solanke lashed home a loose ball in the area after a deflected effort from Lucas Bergvall.

It meant Spurs were cruising 2-0 up at half-time and if Charlton’s attention wasn’t already on Saturday’s game against Preston, it was now.

Any hope of a dramatic comeback was killed by substitute Kevin Danso, who rose up to nod home a floated free-kick with his first touch of the game.



Even with three goals flying in, perhaps the loudest cheer of the night came when Savio was introduced for a 20-minute debut cameo.

And those cheers only got louder when he got a goal of his own minutes later.

Savio, who no longer wants to be referred to as Savinho, wriggled his way into space off the right wing and fired into the bottom corner.



The fifth goal was all of his own making too, the winger twisted and turned in the box before his shot bounced off Ben Davies and went in the back of the net.

Charlton hit back with a consolation goal through Lloyd Jones, but Savio had already put the Addicks to bed.

The new arrival has certainly got Spurs fans excited about what could come in the next few month and helped them forget all about their woeful defeat to Brentford at the weekend.

Sports.title: When is the Champions League 2026/27 draw? Start time, FREE stream and pots as Arsenal and Man Utd learn fate
Sports.content:
EUROPE’S footballing elite will attempt to dethrone back-to-back supremos PSG as the Champions League gears up for its next electrifying instalment.

Last season’s final saw the Parisian powerhouse sneak past Arsenal after an agonising penalty shoot-out in Budapest crushed the Gunners’ bid to bag North London’s first Champions League crown.



Luis Enrique and his glittering array of attacking talent are strongly tipped to extend their continental dominance and secure a three-peat, having also thumped Inter Milan 5-0 in the 2024/25 curtain-closer.

Hot on their heels will be vengeful Premier League champions Arsenal, alongside German giants Bayern Munich and a Barcelona side bursting with eight top talents from Spain’s World Cup-winning squad.



Five Premier League sides will do battle with Europe’s big boys, with Manchester City, Manchester United, Aston Villa and Liverpool all in the draw for the league phase along with Mikel Arteta‘s runners-up.

A staggering six English clubs reached the last 16 in a record-breaking 2025/26 competition, but the initial euphoria quickly fell flat after four failed to progress further and Liverpool were outclassed by PSG in the quarter-finals.

The fight for the most coveted prize in European club football will kick off with a league phase once more, and SunSport has all the crucial details for the draw.

When is the Champions League draw?

The draw for the league phase of the 2026/27 Champions League will take place on Thursday, August 27.

Proceedings are scheduled to begin at 5pm BST.

Uefa’s headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland, will host the event.

How to watch the Champions League draw FREE

The Champions League draw will be broadcast live and will be available to watch FREE on Uefa.com, Uefa.tv and the Uefa app.

TNT Sports 1 will also air the draw on regular TV, and subscribers will be able to stream it via HBO Max.

Alternatively, you can follow all the ties as they get confirmed on the night through SunSport’s live blog of the draw.

How does the Champions League league phase draw work?

Europe’s premier club competition will once again follow a Swiss System, commencing with a 36-team league phase in which each side plays eight times, evenly split between matches at home and on the road.

SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

The continent’s top 36 teams are seeded into four pots containing nine similarly-matched teams, as determined by their five-year Uefa club coefficient.



Beginning with the top pot, a ball will be physically drawn before the automated software randomly draws two opponents from each pot, in an attempt to ensure every club faces an equally balanced set of rivals.

As stipulated by Uefa’s country protection rule, sides in the same league cannot play each other, and clubs cannot play more than two opponents from any one country.

The top eight teams in the final league standings automatically qualify for the last 16, while those who finish ninth to 24th are whittled down by two-legged play-off ties.

Sports.title: Southampton exploring emotional return for James Ward-Prowse just three years after selling ex-England ace for £30m
Sports.content:
SOUTHAMPTON are exploring a move to bring James Ward-Prowse back to the club.

The ex-Saints skipper, 31, left St Mary’s following relegation in 2023 to join West Ham in a £30million deal.



Ward-Prowse made 410 appearances for the club having come through the academy at the age of eight, spending 20 years at the club before his exit.

The midfielder has just one year left on his deal at the London Stadium and would be allowed to leave for a nominal fee.



Ward-Prowse is still thought to earn around £50,000-a-week in the Championship, which could prove a stumbling block for his former club.

However, the former England man is thought to be open to returning to the south coast club.



Ward-Prowse was not part of the West Ham squad for their 4-1 Carabao Cup win at Southampton on Tuesday night.

Meanwhile, Southampton have have agreed a deal to sign German defender Keven Schlotterbeck.

Saints will pay around £4million to Bundesliga side Augsburg amid interest in Taylor Harwood-Bellis.

Harwood-Bellis has been left out of Southampton’s last two matchday squads after the club rejected bids from Benfica and, more recently, Aston Villa.

Sports.title: Savio steals show on debut as Spurs thrash Charlton
Sports.content:
Savio grabbed a goal and assist on a dream debut as Tottenham thrashed Charlton to progress into the third round of the Carabao Cup.

The Brazilian, signed from Man City for £85m on Tuesday, was introduced as a second-half substitute and took just 11 minutes to open his account, adding to the hype surrounding his arrival in north London.

Roberto De Zerbi named a strong side to face the Championship opposition, with many senior names included in the starting XI after Spurs' dreadfully disappointing defeat to Brentford in their Premier League opener.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mikey Moore fires Spurs ahead in their Carabao Cup clash with Charlton.

It was youngster Mikey Moore who finally broke down a stubborn Charlton defence though, smashing the ball through the hands of Tiernan Brooks to score his first Tottenham goal. That lead was quickly doubled just five minutes later, with Dominic Solanke smartly finishing after the visitors failed to clear their lines.

Several other high profile names were introduced after an hour, including Kevin Danso who headed home from a Mateus Fernandes free-kick with his first touch. However, Spurs fans will only thinking about the magic of Savio after he came on in the 71st minute.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Savio scores 11 minutes into his Spurs debut against Charlton.

The forward cut inside from the right and fired smartly into the bottom corner to add Spurs' fourth, before his scrappy effort deflected off veteran Ben Davies for a fifth just three minutes later.

There was still time for Charlton to find a consolation courtesy of the head of Lloyd Jones, but it meant little as Spurs cruised into third round, where they will meet Liverpool at Anfield.

'He lit the place up' - All the reaction from Savio's electric Spurs start

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jamie Redknapp looks back at Savio's debut for Tottenham against Charlton.

Sky Sports' Jamie Redknapp:

"He lit the place up. This is what Tottenham want. Players like that who can get you off your seat. Who can cut inside and hit a ferocious left footed shot. He was excellent."

Sky Sports' Jermaine Beckford:

"When players are full of confidence, especially attacking players, they like to attack at you. He's no different. The confidence is there to be seen."

Tottenham striker Dominic Solanke:

"He did great when he came on. He's going to be a joy for all of us to watch. I'm sure he will be a fan favourite. He showed what a player he is tonight. To get one goal and an assist on his debut is great."

Image: Savio celebrates opening his account for Tottenham

Sky Sports' Callum Bishop:

"A lot can happen in just one minute of football. Even more can happen in 20. As we have just seen, that's enough time to make yourself a cult hero.

"Savio's arrival at Tottenham was shrouded in question marks. Why were Spurs willing to part with so much money for a player who managed just three goal contributions in the Premier League last season?

"Yet, the moment he stepped out onto the pitch in a white shirt, he was a livewire. Spurs fans value entertainment, and they were off their feet any time he got on the ball.

"The fact there was some end product that came with the excitement is even more important, especially for a Spurs side that have often been lacklustre in attack.

"The opponents will get tougher, and Savio will need to rise to that. However, as first outings go, having joined barely 24 hours ago, you can't ask for much more."

Bradford extended Burnley's uncomfortable start to the season with a 4-2 penalty shoot-out win after their second-round Carabao Cup tie had finished goalless at Valley Parade.

Jon McCracken saved from Jacob Bruun Larsen after Zeki Amdouni had hit the post with the first spot-kick.

Bradford, who had not conceded a goal in their first three games, defended solidly against the Championship club's pressure and Reece Welch denied Zeki Amdouni from close range.

Former Burnley midfielder Adam Phillips had Bradford's first chance but lifted Jake Beesley's cross over the bar.

McCracken denied Laurent and Ugo Raghouber volleyed over as the game became more open.

The 'keeper saved again from Laurent before the League One side won the penalty decider.

Jaissle was full of praise for Championship side West Brom, revealing he spoke to opposite number James Morrison after the game.

"Relieved, it's always the most important thing in a Cup run that you take the result, that's what we did against a strong opponent.

Sports.title: Police investigating alleged assault in connection with Carse nightclub incident
Sports.content:
Derbyshire Police said on Wednesday it was investigating allegations of an assault in the city centre, but no arrests have yet been made

Brydon Carse has been dropped from the England squad for the second Test against Pakistan

Derbyshire Police are looking into "allegations of assault" following the incident that saw England bowler Brydon Carse handcuffed outside a nightspot over the weekend.

Carse was removed from the squad for the second Test against Pakistan, which begins at Lord's on Thursday morning, after the Cricket Regulator initiated a probe into an episode that saw the Durham player briefly arrested outside a late bar in Derby - then de-arrested after agreeing to depart.

In an updated statement issued on Wednesday evening, Derbyshire Police said: "We are investigating allegations of assault in Derby city centre. No arrests have yet been made and the investigation is ongoing."

Further details are unknown, with no clarity over what part - if any - Carse had in the alleged assault.

The England and Wales Cricket Board declined to comment when contacted by the Press Association.

An initial statement from the force, released after a video clip of Carse apparently being detained by officers in the street, had said: "A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly in Derby city centre on Saturday night. However the man was de-arrested shortly afterwards having agreed to leave the area."

Former England captain Ben Stokes and centrally contracted seamer Matthew Potts both appeared in the footage, captured in the aftermath of their Durham's side's County Championship victory over Derbyshire, though there is no suggestion that either was involved in anything untoward.

Reacting to the incident, Stokes' replacement as Test skipper Joe Root spoke angrily about the latest in a growing line of alcohol-related issues which have swamped the team.

Root, who made a point of abolishing the midnight curfew which played a partial role in Stokes' exit following another controversial night out earlier this summer, said: "If I'm being brutally honest I'm really hacked off.

"I've spoken to Brydon and when I first found out my first concern was him as a person. I don't think I'm speaking out of turn in saying he's very upset, very apologetic and understands his actions. I'm sure when he gets his chance, he will say that himself.

"But it's not the isolated incident itself, it's the fact we continuously keep making stupid mistakes away from the game and it's detracting from what we are doing on the field."

Sports.title: 'He's the one we wanted': Newcastle sign Gonzalez from Man City
Sports.content:
Newcastle have signed Nico Gonzalez from Man City.

The deal for the 24-year-old midfielder is set to reach £50m after add-ons. He will wear the No 6 shirt at St James' Park.

The midfielder said his goodbyes to his City team-mates on Tuesday morning before travelling to Newcastle and completed a medical on Wednesday, before he was presented to the club's fans ahead of their Carabao Cup clash with West Brom.

The Spaniard has become Matthias Jaissle's second signing as Magpies head coach after Amar Dedic joined last week.

Former Spain U21 international Gonzalez joined City from Porto in February 2025 and played 59 times for the club, scoring four goals.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Nico Gonzalez was spotted in Newcastle ahead of his medical on Wednesday

'He's the one we wanted'

Newcastle sporting director Ross Wilson said Gonzalez had been the Magpies' primary target, in a summer where they have lost Bruno Guimaraes and Sandro Tonali to Arsenal and Tottenham, given his experience already with Barcelona, Porto and in the Premier League with Manchester City.

He said: "We've worked patiently on this transfer for a number of weeks. This was the one we wanted, and we're delighted to welcome Nico to Newcastle United this evening. He was an ambitious target but following our discussions, he was so keen to join this club.

"He fits the exact criteria we set for this position and we weren't prepared to compromise on that. He's 24 years old, with an abundance of elite experience across Manchester City, FC Porto and Barcelona. He's already already shown his quality in the Premier League and we're sure there is more to come here in a black and white shirt."

Sports.title: Sávio savours debut goal as Spurs coast to emphatic Carabao Cup win over Charlton
Sports.content:
A new season at the snazziest modern stadium in England and something extremely welcome for Tottenham. A home win over domestic opposition. There were only four of them last time out; three in the Premier League with the final one – over Everton on the last day – helping them to avoid relegation. Had they lost that, this Carabao Cup fixture against Charlton would also have been played in the Championship.

Spurs needed this tonic for another reason – to begin the clean-up operation after Saturday’s awful 3-0 defeat at Brentford.

The season could not have started any worse. With no European football, a decent cup run or runs are imperative and Spurs got themselves up and running in this competition on a night when everything came together perfectly.

For a good while, it looked as though Mikey Moore was going to be the story.

The homegrown 19-year-old broke the deadlock with a vicious drive from the edge of the area; it was the purity of the strike that made it. But then came Sávio.

Spurs were 3-0 up with further goals from Dominic Solanke and the substitute, Kevin Danso, when Roberto De Zerbi sent on his £75m signing from Manchester City for his debut. It was a devastating cameo from Sávio, something to wet the whistle for the bigger challenges ahead. “A perfect day for him,” De Zerbi said.

It took Sávio just 11 minutes to score and it was a lovely goal – a glide inside from the right, his markers close and yet nowhere near, his control of the situation total before the fizzing low finish into the near corner. De Zerbi has said he wants end product from Sávio, especially goals and he challenged him afterwards to score 10-12 before the end of the season. This was a good start. There was more.

Once again, it was Sávio on the right, cutting back, closer to goal this time. He put one would-be challenger down and skated around another. It was all about the composure. The shot hit his teammate, Ben Davies, and went in. The goal was credited to Davies, who was pretty unapologetic about it.

The Charlton manager, Nathan Jones, made wholesale changes to his preferred lineup – 10 in total from Saturday’s win at West Ham – and it was a difficult evening for his team. “Absolutely disastrous,” as he put it. “This was a game we didn’t need.” Charlton did enjoy the last word when another substitute, Lloyd Jones, headed home from a corner.

View image in fullscreen Mikey Moore of Tottenham Hotspur scored their first goal. Photograph: Elli Birch/IPS/Shutterstock

The major take-away was the sense of possibility brought by Sávio, with De Zerbi insisting he was not daunted by being drawn to face Liverpool at Anfield in the next round. “It’s a great game,” he said. “If we want to win the competition, we have to win these games.”

It was a night when there was a focus on De Zerbi’s selection. There was a sense of the calvary returning. The manager started Destiny Udogie, Rodrigo Bentancur, Mateus Fernandes and Solanke, players that were fit enough only for the bench at Brentford. Pedro Porro and Micky van de Ven, who did not kick a ball in pre-season and were not available for Brentford, were among the substitutes. They got on. There was no Marcos Senesi or Sandro Tonali in the squad. They will be ready for Newcastle here on Saturday.

Bantams keeper Jon McCracken [pictured] saved from Jacob Bruun Larsen after Zeki Amdouni had hit the post with Burnley's first spot-kick. Both teams missed chances to win the game inside 90 minutes as it ended goalless. The Burnley head coach, Nicky Hayen, made nine changes from Sunday's defeat to West Brom, but the visitors could not break down the Bradford defence, which has now kept four clean sheets in a row. Thank you for your feedback.

Spurs were always going to dominate the ball. The question concerned what they could create with it. The answer at the outset was very little. Spurs did not threaten until the 30th minute when Solanke had a shot blocked and Archie Gray extended the goalkeeper, Tiernan Brooks, with a low prod on the rebound. Charlton might have been in front by then. Greg Docherty exploded a drive through a crowd that Antonin Kinsky did well to save while Nathan Asiimwe headed narrowly off target.

Spurs upped the tempo after the Brooks save from Gray. Fernandes impressed. There was a flicker from Moore, even if the end product was not there. Then it was. Gloriously. When Moore moved inside from the right, the Charlton player close to him – Millenic Alli – slipped. Moore knew what he had to do and the sweetness of the left-footed connection took the breath. The shot ripped through the hands of Brooks.

View image in fullscreen Dominic Solanke displays textbook technique to double Tottenham’s advantage. Photograph: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty Images

What Charlton did not need shortly afterwards was hesitant defending inside their box on a bouncing ball. Lucas Bergvall saw a shot blocked and Timothy Ouma seemed to freeze. When it broke for Solanke, he swept a clinical finish into the bottom corner.

Moore’s only other goal for Spurs was against Elfsborg in the Europa League in January 2025. After that game, his teammate, James Maddison, compared him to Neymar. Moore’s career trajectory has not been as steep as once envisaged but he remains young. He wanted to do more in the second half and there was a swagger about him on the ball; some lovely skills and darting runs. The home crowd saluted him. He remains a loan target for FC Köln before the transfer window shuts. As De Zerbi acknowledged, he needs regular football.

De Zerbi introduced Porro, van de Ven and Danso after Gray had once again worked Brooks. It was some entrance from Danso, his first touch a header past Brooks from Fernandes’ free-kick. He was bloodied into the bargain, caught in the aerial challenge by the Charlton substitute, Danny McNamara. Sávio stood and watched. He was stripped and ready while Danso had treatment. He had to wait. When he got on, he more than made his mark.

Sports.title: Barnes settles stormer to hand Jaissle first Newcastle win against West Brom
Sports.content:
Around this time last week Matthias Jaissle wore a sorrowful look as he spoke of his “disappointment” at the “negativity” surrounding a transitional young Newcastle side.

Fast forward seven days and a team slightly unlucky to have been held to a draw at home by Liverpool last Sunday have now provided Jaissle with his first competitive win since replacing Eddie Howe as head coach. It is safe to say the doubters are being confounded.

Granted Newcastle’s passage to the third round of the Carabao Cup and an impending visit to Millwall was not exactly seamless against a very decent West Brom but it appears that Jaissle’s faith is far from groundless.

It helps that he has been able to sign the £30m right-back Amar Dedic from Benfica. Dedic, who played for the German at RB Salzburg, shone here with his stellar crosses creating one of Harvey Barnes’s two goals and another for Bazoumana Touré.

“West Brom were a strong opponent, they’re brave and I will follow them now but I’m happy,” said Jaissle, who delighted home supporters by engaging in an animated stoppage-time debate with match officials over a disputed free-kick. “Amar joined us late but it’s like he’s been here for years.”

Ten minutes before kick-off Nico González, Newcastle’s £52m signing from Manchester City, was introduced to the crowd. As the stadium echoed to chants of “Nico, Nico,” the Spanish holding midfielder beamed broadly.

View image in fullscreen Harvey Barnes sweeps the ball home to score Newcastle’s third goal. Photograph: Richard Lee/Shutterstock

When González’s new head coach first talked to Newcastle executives about succeeding Howe at the end of July, part of their pitch involved a spot of modern Geordie history. Jaissle was shown a video of 300,000 fans packing the city centre as Howe’s team brought the 2025 Carabao Cup back to Tyneside. “They tried to convince me with that footage,” he said. “But it was not needed.”

The German’s hopes of lifting the trophy himself next spring were initially dented as West Brom took a 19th-minute lead.

With the visiting Ousmane Diakité establishing himself as a key central midfield combatant, the Championship side grew increasingly confident. When they won a free-kick, Isaac Price curled that 25-yard dead ball around the wall and beat Ewen Jaouen at his near post.

Jaissle’s second-choice goalkeeper, a 20-year-old Frenchman signed from Ligue 2 Reims, got a hand to the ball and arguably should have saved it. Not that the 2,000 travelling fans perched high in the Leazes End were complaining.

James Morrison’s team impressed while winning their first two second-tier games this season and, for a while at least, his fluid version of 4-4-2 confused Newcastle and subdued Nick Woltemade in equal measure.

Then the 18-year-old Sean Steur – culpable for conceding the foul for the preceding free-kick – began re-asserting himself in the home anchoring role. The former Ajax midfielder’s fine run and pass permitted Dedic to whip in a brilliant cross that Touré lashed in from close range under considerable pressure from Chris Mepham.

View image in fullscreen Ewen Jaouen is beaten at his near post by Isaac Price’s free-kick on his Newcastle debut. Photograph: Adam Cook/IPS/Shutterstock

As Jaissle raised a celebratory fist he could reflect that three exciting recent arrivals – Steur, Dedic and Touré – had combined seamlessly for that equaliser. As Touré, a Côte d’Ivoire left winger signed from Hoffenheim to replace Anthony Gordon, celebrated his first goal for Newcastle it appeared that there really might be life at St James’ Park after Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães after all.

Touré was replaced by Barnes at the interval and the substitute wasted no time in reminding Jaissle that he is far from a shabby left winger either. Three minutes into the second half Barnes gave Newcastle the lead after pouncing on the fallout from a corner and firing the ball home from close range at the second attempt after his initial shot was blocked.

West Brom’s legs turned a little heavy but they revived when Lewis Hall handled in the area and Price registered his second goal of the night after beating Jaouen from the penalty spot.

Extra time beckoned but Barnes was not about to be eclipsed and duly swept another splendid, low Dedic cross beyond Matt Ingram.

“We were in the game, pushing Newcastle right to the end,” said Morrison. “We gave them some problems. I had a nice chat with Matthias afterwards; he was very complimentary.”

Sports.title: Thierno Barry fires hat-trick as ruthless Everton sweep Preston aside
Sports.content:
Thierno Barry resembled a striker reborn, and the goalscorer David Moyes desperately needs, as the first hat-trick of his Everton career plus an assist for new signing Brennan Johnson delivered a resounding win for the Scot on his competitive return to Preston.

The France under-21 international scored eight times in a difficult debut season in England but has half that amount two games into this fledgling campaign. Barry followed up his header against Crystal Palace with a poacher’s hat-trick to give Moyes a convincing victory back at the club where he made his name before leaving for Everton in 2002.

“Thierno worked with somebody back home in the summer who tried to change his mindset a bit,” said the Everton manager of the 23-year-old’s early season improvement. “He found it difficult last year, as a lot of boys coming in from overseas do, and it can be even worse if you’re a centre forward. Generally, he has been much better since he came back but I would still like more. A couple of his goals were laid on a plate and I want him to score some of the other opportunities he had as well.”

Before the tie Moyes attracted accusations of a lack of ambition – the kind that has contributed to the longest trophy drought in Everton’s history at 31 years – with a spiky response to being asked how important cup competitions are this season. “I’ll ask you the question,” he had replied. “Is winning a cup more important than staying in the Premier League? What would your answer be?” But a club of Everton’s stature should not have to choose between league survival and cup success. Perhaps Moyes’s question was directed towards Everton’s owners, The Friedkin Group, who have so far shown little ambition themselves in this summer’s transfer market. The Scot maintains Everton are short on numbers and quality ahead of Tuesday’s deadline.

The Everton manager could not be accused of treating the Carabao Cup lightly on the evidence of his team selection at Deepdale, where only Jarrad Branthwaite and Tyrique George were missing from the side that started on the opening day. Paul Heckingbottom, by contrast, made seven changes from the Preston team beaten by Wolves on Saturday.

View image in fullscreen Thierno Barry fires Everton into a first-half lead from Vitalii Mykolenko’s square pass. Photograph: James Harrison/Focus Images Ltd/Shutterstock

Everton’s approach mirrored Moyes’s intent. The visitors dominated from the start with Preston struggling to establish a foothold. Harrison Armstrong received a warm reception on his return to the club where he spent a fruitful spell on loan last season and, as against Palace, produced another accomplished display. The 19-year-old’s sharp touches and movement, alongside that of Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, stretched the Championship defence repeatedly.

Dewsbury-Hall engineered the breakthrough with a beautifully weighted pass over the Preston defence to Vitalii Mykolenko. The Everton left-back’s neat control gave him time to assess his options and he squared for Barry to convert with ease.
