The fire broke out inside the maternity ward at the government-run Pakistan Institute for Medical Sciences (PIMS), the largest hospital in Pakistan’s capital Islamabad, around seven am local time.

The blaze appears to have been triggered by an air conditioning compressor explosion inside the nursery where the newborn babies were being cared for, rescue sources told CNN.

Hospital workers were able to rescue one child, the sources said.

Outside the hospital, a grieving father told reporters his three-day-old baby had been killed in the fire.

“No one can understand the pain I’m going through,” he said.

A woman named Muneeba who was visiting family in the hospital described narrowly escaping with her nephew and sister-in-law as the fire began to spread.

“Thank God our baby is safe,” she told CNN.

Multiple people reported encountering locked doors in the ward.

Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said he is “deeply saddened by this tragic incident” and ordered an immediate investigation into the fire, according to statement from his office.

He promised “strict action against anyone found responsible.”

A worker removes broken pieces of a glass window after a fire broke out at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital in Islamabad, Pakistan, August 26, 2026. Akhtar Soomro/Reuters

Health care in Pakistan is delivered through both private and public providers. Government-run facilities are chronically underfunded and short-staffed, and have faced criticism for aging infrastructure and lack of emergency preparedness.

Sharmila Sahibah Faruqui, a member of Pakistan’s national assembly, called the tragedy “shameful and unforgivable” in a post to X.

“Heads must roll. Please do not hide behind another inquiry committee,” she wrote. “Those responsible must be taken to task.”

Islamabad is home to Pakistan’s political and military elite and its facilities are generally of a higher standard than those found in other towns and cities in the country.

A woman carrying an infant moves past police officers as she leaves a ward following the deadly hospital fire in Islamabad, Pakistan, August 26, 2026. Akhtar Soomro/Reuters

The PIMS facility is located on a sprawling site in the capital.

According to its website, its mission is “to be a premier research-intensive medical university that will educate medical students, paramedics, and postdoctoral fellows in accordance with international professional standards.”

Pakistan has experienced several major fires in recent years, including in hospitals, which often run on outdated electrical systems.

Earlier this year, a massive blaze at a shopping center in Karachi killed at least 67 people.

In June 2022, a fire broke out at a children’s hospital in Lahore and destroyed thousands of dollars worth of medicine, local media reported.

World.title: Electricity minister discusses Dabaa plant, SMRs with Rosatom in Russia
World.content:
Minister of Electricity and Renewable Energy Mahmoud Esmat on Tuesday, August 25, 2026, met with Rosatom Director General Alexei Likhachev in Nizhny Novgorod, Russia, to review progress on the al-Dabaa Nuclear Power Plant and explore cooperation on Small Modular Reactors (SMRs).

During the meeting, both sides assessed ongoing construction timelines and target schedules, emphasizing coordination between Egyptian and Russian teams to maintain safety and quality standards. Esmat highlighted the strategic importance of the al-Dabaa project in diversifying Egypt’s energy mix, noting steady progress on-site.

Likhachev reaffirmed Rosatom’s commitment to delivering the plant on schedule while emphasizing broader cooperation in technology transfer and training Egyptian personnel to operate nuclear facilities.

Esmat also met with executives from a Rosatom subsidiary specializing in SMR technology to evaluate its application for industrial sectors, remote areas, and future power grids. He underscored Egypt’s interest in integrating SMRs into its long-term energy strategy subject to economic and safety evaluations.

World.title: Egypt, Italian firms discuss $278M bioethanol production project
World.content:
Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade Mohamed Farid held talks with representatives of Italian companies Proger and Draxil on the latest developments in an investment project to produce second-generation bioethanol using bagasse generated from sugarcane processing, with targeted investments of around $278 million.

The meeting reviewed the latest technical and implementation developments of the project, which aims to utilize agricultural and industrial waste and convert it into a value-added, exportable product, supporting Egypt’s drive toward a green economy, sustainable industries and deeper local manufacturing.

Farid affirmed that the ministry is working to facilitate procedures for investors and improve the efficiency of services needed to attract further investment, noting that priority is given to projects that contribute to increasing Egypt’s production and export capacities, supporting economic growth and creating jobs.

He said green economy and biofuel projects represent promising areas for attracting investment and opening new export markets, stressing that the project combines the utilization of local resources, deeper manufacturing, value creation and export opportunities.

The minister said the ministry would provide the necessary support to expedite the completion of the project’s requirements, enabling it to move from the study phase to implementation, production, operation and export, while benefiting from the availability of raw materials and other prerequisites for establishing the project in Egypt.

The two sides also discussed opportunities to export a substantial portion of the project’s output to European markets, enhancing its access to foreign markets and generating sustainable export revenues.

Representatives of the Italian companies outlined their vision for implementing the project, stressing that the availability of sugarcane bagasse in Egypt presents an opportunity to establish an integrated industrial project for producing second-generation biofuel, with the potential to direct a significant share of production to European markets.

The meeting also reviewed the results of technical tests conducted on bagasse samples and studies related to bioethanol production, as well as efforts to update the feasibility study ahead of completing the final study and determining the project’s investment and financing structure.

The meeting followed talks between representatives of the two companies and Minister of Supply and Internal Trade Sherif Farouk on the project’s technical and implementation developments, completed tests and studies, proposed partnership structures and steps toward implementation.

World.title: Egyptian Red Crescent receives 79th group of injured, sick Palestinians at Rafah crossing
World.content:
Teams from the Egyptian Red Crescent received the 79th group of injured and sick Palestinians arriving in Egypt through the Rafah crossing to receive medical treatment.

The teams also accompanied recovered patients as they left after completing their treatment, in coordination with the ministries of health and population and social solidarity.

The response included psychological support, particularly for children, as well as family-reunification services and the distribution of meals, drinks, clothing and personal-care supplies to meet the needs of injured and sick Palestinians during the crossing process.

The Egyptian Red Crescent continues its humanitarian work at the Rafah crossing around the clock, providing humanitarian and relief assistance to Palestinians and supporting Egyptian efforts to ease their suffering amid difficult humanitarian conditions.

World.title: FM affirms Egypt’s pride in historical ties with Chad
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty emphasized Egypt’s pride in historical, fraternal ties with Chad, stressing Cairo’s keenness to advance cooperation across various fields under directives from President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and Chadian President Field Marshal Mahamat Idriss Déby to serve both nations’ mutual interests.

The remarks came during a phone call on Tuesday, August 25, 2026, between Abdelatty and Chadian Minister of Foreign Affairs Abdoulaye Saber Fadoul to discuss bilateral relations, cooperation tracks, and regional issues of mutual concern.

The ministers followed up on implementing the outcomes of the fourth session of the Egypt-Chad Joint Committee, including agreed cooperation projects, agreements and memoranda of understanding.

Both sides exchanged views on Sudan, with Abdelatty reaffirming Egypt’s steadfast support for Sudan’s unity, sovereignty, territorial integrity and national institutions while rejecting parallel entities. He underscored the need for a Sudanese-owned, comprehensive political settlement that restores security, stability and development.

The two top diplomats also reviewed Libyan developments, as Abdelatty reiterated Egypt’s firm support for Libya’s unity, sovereignty and state institutions, emphasizing the necessity of a Libyan-Libyan political solution leading to simultaneous presidential and parliamentary elections as soon as possible.

World.title: Liberia: No Sacred Cows,” But Some Cows Are More Equal Than Others
World.content:
President Joseph Boakai told the nation Wednesday that his drug war spares no one. The record so far tells a more complicated story — and the former First Lady’s rough road from hospital bed to prison cell is only the latest chapter.

SUMMARY: In his national address, President Boakai insisted his anti-narcotics campaign follows the law “without fear or favor” and targets conduct, not politics. But eight months into Liberia’s biggest drug scandal, the pattern on the ground looks uneven: junior airport clerks and mid-level officers have faced swift punishment, while questions about who financed and protected the trade at the top remain largely unanswered. Jewel Howard-Taylor’s fall — from VIP passenger to prison inmate within a week — has become the flashpoint for a question opposition leaders, civil society, and now even a member of the president’s own political family are asking out loud: is this justice, or is it selective?

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

MONROVIA — President Boakai told the nation this week that his government would enforce the law “without fear or favor,” that no one is too powerful to face it, and that his crackdown on narcotics is not a hunt for political enemies. It is a line he has repeated since the scandal broke: no sacred cows.

Liberians have heard that promise before. What they are watching now is whether it holds.

A tale of two treatments

The clearest test case sits in a cell at Monrovia Central Prison. Jewel Howard-Taylor — Liberia’s First Lady during Charles Taylor’s presidency and, decades later, Vice President under George Weah — was stopped at Roberts International Airport on August 19 as she tried to board a flight out of the country. Within a week she had been charged on a seven-count indictment alleging she took more than $135,000 from figures tied to a cocaine cartel, hospitalized under guard for asthma and high blood pressure, denied compassionate release by a judge who said only the Justice Ministry could grant it, and moved into general population at South Beach.

Her party, the Coalition for Democratic Change, has called the process degrading and accused the government of weaponizing the justice system against a political rival. The opposition Alternative National Congress went further, telling the administration directly that it appears eager to “cast a wider net” that catches CDC-aligned figures while leaving others untouched.

Compare that trajectory to the pace of accountability elsewhere in the same investigation. When Boakai purged security officials over the record $317 million cocaine seizure in July, the dismissals fell on an airport security director, a deputy police commissioner, NSA deputies, and Drug Enforcement Agency officers — the operational layer of the scandal. An earlier allAfrica analysis of the case put the concern plainly: charges have concentrated on lower-level figures in the cargo and screening chain, while whoever financed and protected the operation at a more senior level has not been touched. If the investigation stops there, the analysis warned, it would confirm the very pattern of selective accountability that Boakai was elected to end.

He was elected on exactly that promise. That is what makes the gap between rhetoric and result politically dangerous for him.

The president is not the only one asking the question

What makes this moment different from ordinary opposition griping is who else is asking it. Dr. Clarence Moniba of the Liberian National Union — not a CDC figure — this week publicly challenged Boakai to prove the drug probe is free of political favoritism, calling for an independent three-member panel to review whether cases are being pursued consistently. His test for the president was direct: does the campaign actually show that no one, regardless of office or connections, sits beyond the law’s reach?

Even a party sympathetic to the administration’s anti-corruption push, the RNC, coupled its praise for the $317 million probe with an explicit warning against selective justice and a call to fight corruption equally across the political spectrum.

That is a notable chorus. It is not just Howard-Taylor’s allies complaining about her treatment — it is a broader, cross-partisan unease about whether the people closest to power, or with the right friends inside it, are being handled more gently than a former official from a rival camp.

What “no sacred cows” would actually require

Boakai’s own government has, to be fair, produced real numbers: a dozen officials sacked in a single sweep, NSA and airport personnel referred for prosecution, U.S. and Rwandan investigators brought in to internationalize the probe. That is more institutional accountability than Liberia saw during the previous administration’s own cocaine scandal, which collapsed in court amid accusations of a cover-up.

But numbers of dismissals are not the same as evenness of consequence. The unresolved question — the one Moniba is asking, the one the ANC is asking, the one hanging over Howard-Taylor’s prison cell — is whether the people with the money and the protection at the top of the network will face the same swiftness the mid-level operators already have. Until an indictment reaches that level, “no sacred cows” remains a promise made in a speech rather than a fact on the ground.

For a president who staked his legitimacy on breaking Liberia’s old habit of selective justice, that is the standard his own words have set. His government does not get to grade its own homework on it.

World.title: Let our Flag Unite Is, Let Education Transform Is’ — Atty. Sayeh Urges Nimba Communities to Reject Violence
World.content:
Lawyer leads Nyor Butuo residents in peace, education and unity pledge during 2026 National Flag Day celebration

By Franklin Doloquee

NYOR BUTUO, Nimba County — Lawyer and community advocate Atty. Elijah M. Sayeh has challenged residents of Zoe-Geh Statutory District to make peace, education, respect and unity the foundation of community development, warning that violence, political division, drug abuse and disorderly conduct threaten the future of Liberia’s young people.

Sayeh delivered the keynote address at the 2026 National Flag Day celebration in Nyor Butuo, where residents, traditional leaders, religious leaders, educators, students and members of the Friends of Atty. Elijah M. Sayeh (FOE) gathered under the theme, “United Under One Flag: Promoting Peace, Education, Respect, and Hope for a Better Liberia.”

The celebration was held under the slogan: “Let Our Flag Unite Us, Let Education Transform Us.”

Sayeh said Liberia’s national flag should serve as more than a national symbol, arguing that it represents the country’s history, sacrifices, freedom, democracy and collective responsibility to future generations.

“Every time we salute our flag, we are making a promise—not merely to our country, but to ourselves and to generations yet unborn,” Sayeh said.

He said that promise must include building peace, protecting justice, educating children, respecting others and placing Liberia’s national interest above personal interests.

From Village Boy to Lawyer

Reflecting on his personal journey, Sayeh told students that his rise from a village boy in Wentuo, Buutuo, to a practicing lawyer demonstrates what determination and education can achieve.

He recalled walking long distances to school and studying in environments where educational materials and qualified teachers were sometimes scarce.

But, he said, difficult circumstances did not prevent him from pursuing his ambitions.

“Today I practice law. Not because my journey was easy, but because I refused to let my circumstances determine my destiny,” Sayeh said.

He encouraged young people in Buutuo and surrounding communities to believe that they, too, can rise to the highest levels of professional and national leadership.

He pointed to the possibility that a future Chief Justice, medical doctor, engineer, professor, scientist, Minister of Education or even President of Liberia could emerge from the region.

“Never underestimate yourselves,” he told the students.

‘Our Challenges Do Not Define Us’

Sayeh acknowledged that Zoe-Geh and surrounding communities face significant social challenges, including political divisions, violence, disorderly conduct, school dropouts, drug abuse among some young people, low school enrollment and shortages of qualified teachers.

But he insisted that the problems should not become the community’s identity.

“These challenges do not define us. They challenge us,” he said.

According to Sayeh, the critical question is whether residents possess the courage and determination to confront those problems.

“I believe we do,” he declared.

Education as a Community Culture

The lawyer called on parents, teachers, community leaders and successful sons and daughters of Zoe-Geh to make education a central priority.

“Every child should be in school. Every parent should value education. Every teacher should teach with dedication. Every leader should support education,” he said.

He urged successful people from the district to consider helping at least one child obtain an education, stressing that knowledge remains valuable even when money and political positions disappear.

“Money can disappear. Political power can change. Positions come and go. But knowledge remains. Nobody can steal your education,” Sayeh said.

Addressing students directly, he warned them against allowing social media, violence, alcohol and drugs to derail their future.

He instead urged them to embrace reading, discipline, integrity, respect and perseverance.

Appeal to Parents and Teachers

Sayeh also appealed to parents to prioritize their children’s education and instill values of honesty, responsibility, hard work and respect at home.

“Education is expensive. Ignorance is even more expensive,” he said.

Teachers, he added, should see themselves as nation builders whose influence could extend beyond their own lifetimes.

He urged educators to teach not only academic subjects but also honesty, discipline, patriotism and leadership.

‘Respect Must Return’

The keynote speaker further called for the restoration of respect within families and communities, particularly respect for parents, elders, traditional leaders, teachers and lawful institutions.

He argued that respect is essential to maintaining peace and creating an environment where communities can develop.

“Without respect there can be no lasting peace. Without peace there can be no development,” he said.

FOE Urged to Focus on Impact

Sayeh also recognized the Friends of Atty. Elijah M. Sayeh, saying the organization was established in 2024 by sons and daughters of Zoe-Geh who shared a commitment to community service.

He urged members to continue supporting students and families while promoting peace and hope.

“Organizations become great not because of their names. They become great because of their impact,” he said.

A Vision for Zoe-Geh

Sayeh outlined a vision of a community where every child attends school, young people are protected from violence, neighboring towns live peacefully, teachers are respected, traditional leaders are honored and women participate fully in development.

He also envisioned a community where young people establish businesses, roads improve, agriculture flourishes and educated sons and daughters return home to contribute to local development.

He cautioned, however, that such transformation cannot be achieved by government alone.

“Development is everybody’s responsibility,” he said.

‘One Star, One Nation’

Using the Liberian flag as a symbol of national unity, Sayeh urged residents not to allow political differences to destroy relationships.

“When we look at the Liberian flag, we see one star. Not two stars. That single star reminds us that Liberia is one nation,” he said.

He appealed to residents to ensure that politics, elections, religious differences, family disagreements and competing interests do not permanently divide communities.

“Our children deserve better,” he said.

Nyor Butuo Declaration

The celebration concluded with a community declaration and pledge led by Sayeh, with residents responding collectively, “We so pledge.”

The five-part pledge committed residents to peace, education, respect, unity and service.

Under the peace pledge, residents committed to rejecting violence, hatred, revenge and disorderly conduct while resolving disagreements peacefully.

The education pledge called on students to study diligently, parents to ensure children attend school, and teachers to perform their duties with dedication, integrity and professionalism.

The respect pledge committed residents to respecting parents, teachers, elders, traditional and religious leaders, as well as lawful institutions.

Under the unity pledge, residents vowed not to allow politics, tribe, religion, family disputes or personal interests to destroy community peace.

The final pledge called on citizens to contribute their time, knowledge, skills and resources to national and community development.

The declaration culminated in a collective affirmation:

“We are one people.

We are one community.

We are one nation.

We believe in peace.

We believe in education.

We believe in respect.

We believe in unity.

We believe in hope.

We pledge to build a better Liberia.”

Sayeh closed the celebration by calling on residents to transform the Flag Day observance into a sustained community movement reaching schools, homes, religious institutions and towns throughout the region.

“Let this Flag Day become the beginning of a movement,” he said.

“Let Our Flag Unite Us. Let Education Transform Us.”

World.title: Boakai Assures Due Process for Former Vice President Taylor
World.content:
Monrovia— President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has assured Liberians and the international community that former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor is being treated in full compliance with Liberia’s Constitution and laws following her arrest and detention.

By J.H. Webster Clayeh [email protected]

In a special national address on Wednesday, August 26, 2026, President Boakai said his administration remains committed to enforcing the law “without fear or favor” while protecting the constitutional rights of every person.

Addressing the arrest and detention of former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor, President Boakai acknowledged the national and international attention generated by the case.

“I assure every Liberian, our regional neighbors, and our international partners that former Vice President Taylor is being treated in full compliance with the Constitution and laws of Liberia,” he said.

The President stressed that Taylor is presumed innocent, has access to legal counsel, and is entitled to due process.

“She is presumed innocent, has access to legal counsel, and is entitled to due process, which will be upheld,” Boakai added.

He said the former Vice President was arrested and charged in accordance with established legal procedures, while making clear that determining her guilt or innocence is not the responsibility of the President.

“It is not the President’s role to determine guilt or innocence. That responsibility belongs to our independent justice system,” Boakai stated.

The President’s address comes amid growing public discussion and concern over recent developments surrounding the government’s intensified campaign against illicit drug trafficking, organized crime, and money laundering.

Boakai said it was his responsibility to speak directly to the Liberian people and assure them that justice would be pursued “firmly, fairly, and independently.”

He emphasized that upholding the rule of law remains fundamental to his administration, noting that progress in the economy, education, infrastructure, and public institutions cannot be sustained without strong respect for constitutional principles.

Drugs a National Security Threat

President Boakai described illicit drugs and organized crime as among the greatest threats facing Liberia, warning that narcotics are destroying young lives, weakening families, fueling violence, and threatening the country’s future.

“This is not simply a law enforcement issue; it is a national security and moral issue,” Boakai declared.

He said his administration has intensified the fight against narcotics trafficking, money laundering, and organized crime, with security institutions directed to operate professionally, independently, and without fear or favor.

According to the President, Liberian security agencies are working with national and international partners to prevent the country from becoming a transit point for illegal drugs or a safe haven for criminal networks.

“Let me be clear: this campaign is deliberate, coordinated, and unrelenting,” he said, adding that the campaign is intended to defend the Liberian people and safeguard the nation’s future.

He urged citizens to allow the courts to determine the outcome of the case rather than relying on political considerations, rumors, conjecture, or public pressure.

‘Law Must Apply Equally’

President Boakai further pledged that his administration would neither persecute nor shield anyone based on political affiliation, public office, social status, or influence.

“Whether one has held high office, served in government, led a business, or lived as an ordinary citizen, the law must apply equally to all,” he said.

He also commended members of the Joint Security for their professionalism, courage, and commitment to duty, while urging them to remain steadfast, impartial, and respectful of the rights and dignity of all citizens.

Boakai warned against attempts to intimidate security personnel or undermine the anti-drug campaign through misinformation.

Boakai Calls for Public Responsibility

The President acknowledged that the fight against drugs and organized crime cannot be won by government alone.

He called on parents, communities, schools, religious institutions, traditional leaders, and young people to support prevention efforts, reject misinformation, report criminal activity through lawful channels, and allow due process to take its course.

Boakai also urged political and religious leaders, civil society organizations, and public commentators to exercise responsibility in their statements and actions.

“Differences of opinion are healthy in a democracy, but we must reject words and actions that incite violence, undermine institutions, or seek to intimidate those enforcing our laws,” he said.

The President warned that Liberia must not return to a culture where justice is influenced by fear, power, or political pressure, noting the country’s history of conflict, hardship, and division.

“Let us preserve that peace by upholding the Constitution and strengthening the institutions that safeguard our democracy,” he urged.

Boakai concluded by reaffirming his administration’s commitment to justice, fairness, accountability, and peace.

“We will govern without fear or favor, protect every citizen’s rights, and build a Liberia where peace is preserved, justice is impartial, and accountability applies equally to all,” the President said.

World.title: Liberia: Writ In Six Days for Jewel Howard Taylor. Still Nothing for Others – The Speed of Justice Selectively Applied
World.content:
Jewel Howard-Taylor’s arrest reads like a spy thriller and moved like one too. Mark Egon Kuiah, Leroy Harris, Jonathan Momolu and others have been named in the same investigation for months — one cooperating, one merely questioned — and neither has been charged with anything a judge could rule on.

By Rodney D. Sieh | [email protected]

MONROVIA — For the second time in a decade, Liberia has hauled a household political name into a cocaine investigation. This time it’s Jewel Howard-Taylor — Vice President from 2018 to 2024, and before that, the wife of a president who ended up at The Hague. Her writ of arrest, dated August 25, reads more like a spy thriller synopsis than a court filing: hotel meetings in Dubai, forty-five thousand dollars in cash handed over for “shopping,” a foundation named Jewel Star Fish quietly receiving cartel money while she kept her office. She was picked up six days earlier, on August 19, stopped at Roberts International Airport on her way out of the country.

It’s a remarkable document. It’s also, so far, a lonely one.

The Charges Against Howard-Taylor

The writ and the Ministry of Justice’s own charging documents lay out a formal case that spans three separate Liberian statutes. Under the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act of 2023, she faces unlicensed importation of a controlled drug or substance; unlicensed sale, trading, administration, dispensation, delivery, distribution, dispatch in transit and transportation of a controlled drug or substance; and illicit trafficking of a controlled drug or substance. Under Chapter 10 of the Penal Law, she faces criminal solicitation, criminal facilitation and criminal conspiracy. And under the Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Law, she faces a money laundering charge tied specifically to the Jewel Star Fish foundation — the vehicle prosecutors say received cartel funds while she held public office. Taken together, it is one of the most detailed charge sheets brought against any Liberian official in this scandal, naming specific cash amounts, specific meeting locations and a specific financial instrument rather than the vaguer language of “linked to” or “connected with” that has characterized most of this year’s other cases. That specificity is precisely why the six-day turnaround between her arrest and the formal writ stands out — and why the comparative silence around Kuiah and Momolu reads as more than a scheduling quirk.

The Men Named Months Ago

Because sitting a few paragraphs down in the same broader investigation are men whose names have been circulating for weeks — sometimes months — without a single charge attached, and without the country ever really stopping to notice how long that silence has run. Mark Egon Kuiah ran operations at RIA, the same airport that has become this case’s center of gravity, the place every road in this scandal seems to lead back to eventually. His name turned up on a writ of arrest back in June — not a rumor, not a leak, an actual writ, with his name on it, in black and white. He signed off on a letter vouching for a “distressed” ship that Liberian troops are now chasing down off Rivercess, suspected of ferrying more product. He was fired from his job in late July. And then, nothing. He has not been arrested. By most accounts, he is currently helping investigators — a cooperation that only started, notably, after his name was already public, after the firing, after the writ, once staying quiet had stopped being an option.

Jonathan Momolu tells a similar story from a different angle, and his is, if anything, the more uncomfortable of the two. A security officer at the airport, he is tied not just to this year’s case but to an older one that should have been a warning sign years ago — a 2023 shipment labeled as tea leaves that turned out to be methamphetamine, waved through an unauthorized gate while he was the senior inspector on duty that day. In between, he spent months moonlighting as a driver for the head of the Drug Enforcement Agency, a detail that sits uneasily in a country trying hard to convince itself, and everyone else, that its own drug agency isn’t compromised from the inside. Momolu was questioned briefly. He went home the same day. He is free.

So the uncomfortable question writes itself, the way these questions always do once you lay the timeline out side by side: why did it take six days from arrest to a formal, detailed writ for the former Vice President, while men named in writs since June are still walking around, still going home at night, still, as far as anyone can tell, living exactly the lives they were living before their names became part of Liberia’s biggest drug story in years?

The Optics Problem

Government officials would say the comparison isn’t fair, and they would say it with real conviction — that a case against a former Vice President requires a different evidentiary bar, more coordination, more care, precisely because it will be picked apart by defense lawyers and international observers alike, in a way a mid-level airport officer’s case never will be. There’s something to that. Overcharging a former head of the executive branch and watching it collapse in court would be its own kind of disaster for a government trying hard to prove it isn’t simply performing accountability for an audience.

But Liberians have heard this argument before, and it hasn’t aged well in their memory. The country’s last nine-figure cocaine case, back in 2022, ended with everyone accused walking free — no convictions, no accountability, just a case that quietly evaporated once the cameras moved on. That memory is doing a lot of work right now, sitting underneath every headline this summer like a low hum nobody can quite tune out. It’s why the sheer volume of activity this season — dismissals across five agencies, cocaine burned in a public ceremony with officials standing solemnly around the flames, a president promising “we will find you” — hasn’t actually translated into public confidence. Motion is not the same as justice, and Liberians, this time, seem to know the difference. Of the people swept into this scandal since June, only a couple have actually been charged and sent toward trial: an LDEA officer and a Paynesville bar owner. Everyone else, including Kuiah, is still suspended in a kind of legal limbo — fired, named, talked about, but not formally accused of anything a judge could actually rule on.

That gap between “named” and “charged” is where public trust usually goes to die, quietly, without anyone ever announcing it happened. Opposition voices have already tried to use it, with the CDC framing the Taylor charges as a distraction from other people — unnamed in their statement, but the implication isn’t subtle — whose conduct deserves equal scrutiny. That’s a self-serving argument coming from a party defending one of its own, and it shouldn’t be taken at face value simply because it was said loudly. But the underlying observation underneath it, that a mid-level airport official can sit named-but-uncharged for two months while a former Vice President goes from questioning to a formal writ in under a week, is not something the government has really answered. Not denied, not explained. Just left sitting there.

What Would Actually Settle It

The honest answer is probably not conspiracy. It’s leverage, and evidence quality, and the unglamorous mechanics of how real prosecutions get built. Kuiah, unlike Taylor, appears to be cooperating, and prosecutors sometimes let cooperating witnesses stay uncharged longer while they build a bigger case around them — using the very silence that looks so suspicious from the outside as a tool to reach higher up the chain. That’s a normal, defensible prosecutorial strategy, the kind taught in any competent law school. It is also, and this is the uncomfortable part, indistinguishable from the outside from protecting someone with the right connections — which is exactly why the president’s own son found himself having to publicly clarify that his friendship with Kuiah wasn’t a shield. When a president’s family has to say that out loud, the appearance problem has already done its damage, whatever the underlying facts turn out to be.

What would change this story isn’t another dismissal, and it isn’t another press conference with cameras and confident language. It is a charge sheet with Kuiah’s or Momolu’s name on it, in the same black-and-white detail that now sits beside Jewel Howard-Taylor’s — the Dubai meetings, the cash, the foundation, spelled out for a judge to weigh. Or, absent that, it is a plain public explanation for why there isn’t one yet. Liberia has shown this year that it can move fast when the target is politically convenient, when a name is already a headline. The real test of this investigation, the one that will decide whether Liberians believe any of it meant anything, is whether it can move at that same speed for the people nobody is watching quite as closely.

World.title: Liberia: Justice Ministry Moves to Dismiss Vehicle Allegations Against AG Tweh
World.content:
A social media advocate says the Justice Minister’s official vehicle traces back to drug cartel money. The Ministry says it traces back to a formal request, a government fleet, and a supplier called Dutch Health BV — and that nobody has shown the evidence connecting the two.

By Rodney D. Sieh | [email protected]

MONROVIA — There is a particular kind of controversy that does not begin with a scandal at all, but with a vehicle — a white SUV parked outside a ministry, a license plate somebody photographed, a question that starts on social media and ends, a few days later, in front of a Senate committee.

That is roughly the shape of the week Attorney General N. Oswald Tweh has had. He “voluntarily” appeared before the Senate Committee on Defense, Security, Intelligence and Veterans Affairs Tuesday amid daunting questions surrounding a vehicle given to him by Gregory Coleman, Inspector General of the Liberia National Police. What was said behind those closed doors has not been made public. Senator Momo Cyrus, the Chairman of the Senate Committee on Defense and Intelligence, declined to speak to reporters about the meeting, saying what was discussed in the meeting was not meant to be made public.

What has been made public, in increasingly forceful terms, is the Ministry’s own attempt to get ahead of a rumor it says has already outrun the facts: that the Minister was riding around Monrovia in a vehicle traceable to the same drug cartel network under investigation in both the US$19 million and the US$317 million cases.

The Ministry’s response stems from a single, persistent voice — social media advocate Martin Kollie, whose posts on the vehicle have circulated widely enough that the Ministry felt compelled to answer them point by point rather than let them sit. The Ministry’s framing of the dispute is itself telling: it describes Kollie’s criticism as crossing a dangerous but real line between exposing a criminal network and manufacturing suspicion around public institutions — the kind of language a government reaches for when it believes it is fighting not just an allegation, but a narrative that has already started to take on a life of its own.

The Ministry’s Position: Missing the “Evidentiary Bridge”

Strip away the back-and-forth, and the Ministry’s argument comes down to one image, repeated in different forms throughout its response: a bridge that was never built. According to the Ministry, the weakness in Kollie’s allegation is not that it has been denied. It is that, on the face of the materials he has presented, the conclusion drawn against the Ministry and the Minister arrives without the factual link connecting either of them to drug proceeds, a drug trafficker, or an unlawful transaction. Kollie has repeatedly asserted, in a series of public posts, that the Minister is “compromised,” that he must “step aside,” and that his official vehicle is somehow connected to cartel activity. The Ministry’s position is that an accusation of this gravity cannot rest on placing several suspicious-sounding facts beside one another and inviting the public to draw its own conclusion about what they add up to.

As the Ministry frames it, the relevant question is not whether the Minister uses a Toyota Land Cruiser, whether Coleman was involved in assigning it, or whether separate allegations exist concerning other vehicles connected to the police force. The question the Ministry says matters is narrower: what credible evidence connects this specific vehicle, or the Minister himself, to drug proceeds, a trafficker, or an unlawful transaction? Kollie’s write-up and photographs, the Ministry argues, do not show that connection. His narrative moves from allegations about three “cash-gifted cars” associated with Coleman to a separate assertion that the Minister requested and received an official vehicle — two claims the Ministry says are not automatically the same thing. A vehicle allegedly tied to one transaction, in the Ministry’s telling, cannot without evidence be transformed into proof that every vehicle assigned through the Liberia National Police shares the same origin.

The Ministry’s Account of the Vehicle

Where Kollie alleges a cartel connection, the Ministry answers with paperwork — dates, a letter, a license plate, a supplier’s name, the specific texture of a bureaucracy trying to prove it has nothing to hide. It says the Ministry formally wrote Inspector General Coleman on November 10, 2025, requesting a suitable vehicle, the kind of routine administrative letter that exists in a filing cabinet somewhere and, in ordinary times, would never be read by anyone outside the two institutions involved. The LNP, in response, assigned a white Toyota Land Cruiser Prado carrying LNP identification GSA-LNP-03-14. The Ministry states the vehicle came from a government-procured fleet acquired from a supplier identified as Dutch Health BV, and that it remains government property, used for official duties rather than personally owned. Whatever further verification the public may reasonably want, the Ministry argues, that account at least identifies a traceable chain addressing the specific vehicle in dispute — a formal request, a marked vehicle, a stated procurement source, and a government ownership record, laid end to end for anyone willing to check it.

“Assignment Is Not Confession”

A central plank of the Ministry’s rebuttal is a distinction it says Kollie has collapsed: the difference between the LNP assigning a government vehicle for official use, and the Inspector General personally gifting the Minister a vehicle. Kollie has described the episode as a “confession” — that Tweh acknowledged Coleman gave him a car. The Ministry says that characterization misstates its own position. Its actual account, the Ministry says, is that an official vehicle was assigned by the LNP following a formal request, while expressly denying that the vehicle was a personal gift, a cartel gift, or a vehicle purchased with drug proceeds for the Minister’s benefit. Acknowledging that an institution assigned a vehicle, the Ministry argues, is not the same as admitting the vehicle was privately gifted by an individual or a criminal organization — and treating those as identical, in the Ministry’s view, changes the factual and legal character of what happened.

The Ministry also pushed back on the idea that its own swift response was itself suspicious. The speed of a rebuttal, it argues, does not establish the falsity of the rebuttal — a prompt clarification is, if anything, an ordinary response when a public allegation directly concerns the integrity of the Attorney General and the Ministry of Justice. A statement does not become dishonest because it was issued quickly, the Ministry says, and an allegation does not become true because it was made first.

“Evidence Is Coming” Versus Evidence in Hand

The Ministry’s sharpest criticism of Kollie’s campaign concerns timing and certainty. Kollie has described his own reporting as evidence-based, using phrases like “100% fact” and “hard facts” while demanding immediate resignations — even as he has also indicated that additional documentation, photographs, audio and video would follow later. The Ministry argues those two postures are in tension: if presently available evidence is already sufficient to publicly pronounce the Minister compromised and demand his resignation, it asks, why is connective evidence still being promised for later? And if the crucial evidence has not yet been produced, the Ministry argues the responsible course is to verify and present it before converting suspicion into a public verdict. Under Liberian legal principle, the Ministry notes, the burden of proof does not shift simply because an accusation is dramatic — the person making a positive allegation must establish its factual basis, and a public official is not required to disprove a claim merely because an accuser has promised more evidence may eventually appear.

A Second Objection: Guilt by Association

The Ministry also objects to what it describes as an attempt to treat unresolved questions about Coleman as automatic proof against Tweh. Even assuming, for argument’s sake, that questions exist regarding other vehicles or other transactions involving other people, the Ministry argues that does not establish that the Minister participated in, knew of, benefited from, or was connected to those alleged transactions. Because the Ministry has identified the Minister’s vehicle as a specific government vehicle from a stated fleet, it argues the allegation against him requires more than institutional proximity or hierarchy — it requires a demonstrated link showing the particular vehicle was unlawfully acquired, that the Minister knew of an unlawful source, that he solicited an improper benefit, or that he entered into an arrangement with alleged cartel actors. The Ministry says none of those links have been shown.

Nor, the Ministry argues, is it improper on its face for the Justice Ministry to request a vehicle from the LNP. The Ministry says it lacked a budgetary allotment at the relevant time for a new ministerial vehicle, and that ordinary administrative communication between the Ministry and the police force it supervises is not, by itself, evidence of wrongdoing — supervision, it argues, does not eliminate the need for institutional coordination.

The Ministry’s Broader Charge: A “Fishing Expedition”

The Ministry characterized Kollie’s overall pattern as casting an unusually wide net — vehicles, police officers, past dismissals, institutional relationships, alleged conversations, housing projects, historical allegations and the wider drug crisis — and then presenting the accumulation of suspicion as though volume itself amounted to proof against the Minister. The number of allegations, the Ministry argues, does not cure the absence of proof connecting a specific person to a specific unlawful act; ten unproven insinuations, in its framing, do not become one proven fact simply because they are repeated together. The Ministry draws a distinction between saying “this matter should be investigated” and declaring “this official is compromised” or demanding resignation as though guilt were already established — the first, it says, is a call for inquiry; the second is a public verdict issued without the evidentiary chain to support it.

The Ministry went further, framing Kollie’s campaign as a potential distraction from the underlying investigation rather than a contribution to it. Because the fight against drug trafficking depends on investigators following financial trails, communications and verifiable relationships, the Ministry argued that a national conversation pulled toward defending or debating unproven allegations can divert attention from the evidentiary work needed to identify and prosecute traffickers. The Ministry stopped short of accusing Kollie of intentionally helping the network under investigation, but argued that irresponsible, unsubstantiated allegations can have that practical effect regardless of intent — and suggested, in unusually pointed language for an official government response, that the matter could rise to the level of criminal interference with an active investigation, a characterization Kollie has not publicly responded to and which this newspaper has not independently assessed.

What the Ministry Is Asking For

The Ministry’s closing position is that the burden now rests on Kollie to move from accusation to substantiation. If the underlying claim is that the vehicle came from drug money, the Ministry argues the evidence must connect the money, the purchase, the vehicle and the Minister specifically — not merely gesture at proximity between the Ministry and a broader scandal. If Kollie disputes the Ministry’s stated procurement trail, the Ministry says the proper response is documentary evidence identifying the specific discrepancy, not repetition of the original claim. “We call on the Ministry of Justice to remain focused on the lawful dismantling of criminal drug networks,” the Ministry said of its own mandate, adding that those who make grave public allegations should be held to the same evidentiary standard they demand of public officials.

What This Doesn’t Resolve

This is not the first time a vehicle has become a flashpoint inside Liberia’s drug investigation. LDEA Officer-in-Charge Fitzgerald Biago recused himself earlier this year over a separate, unresolved allegation involving vehicles accepted from a figure tied to the case. That precedent is part of why a vehicle allegation involving the country’s chief law enforcement officer has drawn this much attention so quickly — Liberians have already watched one senior official’s position become entangled with exactly this kind of claim once this year. The Ministry’s rebuttal is detailed and specific about the Minister’s own vehicle. It does not, however, address the broader question raised by Kollie’s original allegations concerning Coleman and the three “cash-gifted cars” — a claim the Ministry treats as a separate matter rather than one it is defending. Tuesday’s closed-door Senate session, called specifically because of the vehicle questions, remains undisclosed. Until its substance becomes public, or until either side produces the documentary evidence each is demanding of the other, this remains what the Ministry itself says it should not become: a contest of accusations rather than a settled account of the facts.

World.title: Liberia: Gongloe Urges Government to Match Humanitarian Generosity With Capacity as Liberia Receives U.S. Deportees
World.content:
Monrovia — Renowned Liberian human rights and constitutional lawyer Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe has called on the Liberian government to carefully balance its longstanding tradition of humanitarianism with the country’s limited capacity as it begins receiving third-country nationals deported from the United States.

Gongloe’s comments come as Liberia has agreed to receive up to 1,200 foreign nationals transferred from the United States over a one-year period. The first group of 20 deportees arrived in Liberia last week, triggering public debate over the government’s decision and its potential implications for the country.

In a commentary on the policy, Gongloe said Liberia has a “long and honorable tradition” of welcoming people fleeing difficult circumstances in their home countries.

He recalled that during the Biafran Civil War in Nigeria in the 1960s, Liberia received thousands of Nigerians. He also pointed to Liberia’s role in providing refuge to Sudanese during conflicts in Sudan and welcoming Africans fleeing colonialism and liberation struggles across the continent.

“Liberia was also a home for Africans during the struggle for independence across the continent and during the liberation struggles in Southern Africa,” Gongloe said.

He recalled seeing students from countries including Angola, South Africa, Namibia, Zimbabwe and Uganda at the University of Liberia, Cuttington University and various high schools.

According to Gongloe, Liberia’s history of hospitality extends beyond Africa and is deeply connected to the country’s founding as a refuge for formerly enslaved Africans and free-born Black people of African descent seeking freedom and security.

He also noted that Liberians themselves have benefited from the generosity of other nations.

“Since 1980, military rule, political persecution and civil conflict forced many Liberians to seek safety abroad,” he said, citing the United States, Canada, Europe, Australia and African countries that opened their doors to Liberians during periods of crisis.

“We therefore cannot reasonably become a country that rejects people simply because they are facing difficult circumstances elsewhere,” Gongloe argued.

However, he stressed that Liberia’s humanitarian tradition must be weighed against its present-day socioeconomic realities.

“The concern is not whether Liberia should remain welcoming. It should be whether Liberia has the capacity,” he said.

Gongloe said Liberia today faces serious challenges, including unemployment, food insecurity, inadequate healthcare and education, poor housing, limited electricity and insufficient access to clean water.

He said those challenges raise legitimate questions about whether the country can responsibly accommodate a large number of additional people without placing further pressure on already strained public services.

The human rights lawyer said the issue deserves even greater consideration because many of the individuals being transferred to Liberia are coming from a socioeconomic environment significantly better than what they are likely to encounter upon arrival.

“The question, therefore, is not whether Liberia should close its doors,” Gongloe said. “It is whether we can responsibly provide decent living conditions, healthcare, housing, security and opportunities for those we receive without worsening the hardship already faced by ordinary Liberians.”

Gongloe ultimately urged the government to preserve Liberia’s reputation as a welcoming nation while ensuring that humanitarian commitments are supported by adequate resources and planning.

“Liberia should remain a welcoming country. But humanitarian generosity must be matched by humanitarian capacity,” he concluded.

World.title: Liberia: How a Gbarnga Tailor Built a School That Trains Hundreds and Offers a Model for Small Businesses in Rural Areas
World.content:
ACD Vocational Training Institute’s main building in Gbarnga, Bong County, houses its vocational training, school uniform production and literacy programs, with a business center operating on the ground floor. Credit: Nukanah Kollie/New Narratives

Summary:

ACD Vocational Training Institute in Gbarnga has trained hundreds of young people, especially women, over 25 years after starting with one borrowed sewing machine, creating pathways to employment and self-reliance without government or donor funding.

Despite its success, ACD faces challenges including high training costs, limited equipment and unpaid student fees, mirroring broader struggles in Liberia’s vocational training and small business sectors.

Experts say ACD’s self-sustaining model offers a blueprint for workforce development throughout the country, showing how local ownership and market partnerships can succeed without donor dependency.

By Nukanah Kollie with New Narratives

GBARNGA, Bong County —A bright blue two-story building stands in central Gbarnga, overlooking Broad Street. Red railings surround the balcony, where freshly sewn school uniforms hang beneath a sign reading, “ACD Vocational Training, School Uniform Production, Literacy Program.”

Inside, shelves hold colorful fabrics as sewing machines hum across the center. Founder Joseph M. Kamara, 66, sits on a wooden bench behind a black sewing machine, a measuring tape around his neck, turning cloth into uniforms while leading the self-financed vocational campus he has built over 25 years.

“I think the best thing to do for our people is impact knowledge in them,” said Kamara as he inspected a uniform completed by one of his employees. “When we talk about empowerment, I think the best empowerment is what gives them skills.”

Kamara has grown Accelerated Career Development Incorporated, known as ACD, which from a single borrowed sewing machine in 2001 into a two-campus institution that produces school uniforms sold across the region and creates opportunities for hundreds of women and young people.

Today, the school trains students in professional tailoring, driving, satellite installation, catering, hairdressing and weaving. It has grown at a time when experts say practical skills training is increasingly important in Liberia. The 2022 Liberia Population and Housing Census found that more than half of rural Liberians have no formal education, while rural literacy stands at 44 percent.

Nationally, Liberia’s vocational training sector has grown through international partnerships. A mid-term evaluation of the €25 million ($29 million) Youth Rising Project which ran from 2018 – 2024 rated the program as “satisfactory” but flagged heavy reliance on outside funding and gaps in graduate support.

Liberia’s private sector is dominated by small businesses. The World Bank’s 2024 Liberia National Establishment Census counted more than 40,000 businesses nationwide, 86 percent of them micro-enterprises. Development experts say their growth is a key factor in job creation and economic stimulation. But the World Bank has found that entrepreneurs continue to face limited access to finance, high interest rates and unreliable electricity.

Abraham Tumbey, a staff member at the UN Development Program, said vocational training is critical to addressing Liberia’s youth and female unemployment in a post-conflict economy where formal education cannot scale fast enough to absorb the labor force.

Joseph M.Kamara, founder of ACD Vocational Training Institute, works at a sewing machine in the school’s uniform store in Gbarnga, Bong County. Credit: Nukanah Kollie/New Narratives.

A School Built Almost Entirely By Women, For Women

Roughly 90 percent of ACD’s students are women, many of them single mothers. Kamara said the imbalance is intentional. The last Demographic and Health Survey in 2020 found that women head about one in three Liberian households, carrying the burden of supporting their families alone. Of the 107 students who have completed ACD’s full three-year tailoring program since 2001, about 96 percent have been women.

“Many of the men, they born by women, they leave the children with them, they go by their business, and the women struggle,” Kamara said.

For many women, the training was less about learning a trade than reclaiming independence. Patience Kollie, 40, a mother of three, completed ACD’s tailoring course before becoming an instructor in 2019 after the father of her children left the family.

“I want to tell all women out there who may be facing hard times,” she said. “Whether ACD can help you or people can help you, if you are serious, you can even pay your school fees yourself.”Martha Paye, 26, a mother of two and eight months pregnant, became an instructor in 2022 after her partner abandoned the family.

Former graduate and instructor Martha Paye, eight months pregnant, works alongside her colleagues at ACD’s new space known as “Annex Two”. Credit: Nukanah Kollie/ New Narratives.

“I decided to come to ACD to learn something, at least to help myself, because there was no support,” she said. “If I say I won’t go to school, we shall not have anybody to send me to school, and it will be suffering for myself.”

Korpo Boakai, another graduate turned instructor, said the training transformed her life.

“I able to support my home,” she said. “I’m trying to do something good for my children, and I change my life. I able to support my three children.”

Beyond tailoring: uniforms, employment and a growing footprint

The institution has relied on commercial bank loans seven times over the years to sustain and expand operations rather than turning to donor funding. He said the key to his success has been being careful with money.

“When you are doing business, you don’t play with the business money. We have always been very careful with it, not to tamper with it. We also go around looking for contracts, and the people we are training are our manpower.”

Kamara said professional tailoring is the course ACD can guarantee leads to work because graduates are absorbed into the school’s own production operations, including a uniform business that has grown into a storefront on Broad Street.

Tumbey said connecting graduates directly to production contracts turns capability into capital.

“Training alone does not put food on the table, market access does,” he said.

The scale is significant. Kamara said ACD partnered with the American Institutes for Research on a contract to produce 17,500 sets of school uniforms distributed across Bong, Lofa, Margibi and Grand Bassa counties. The school has also trained students in Bong, Margibi, Montserrado and parts of Lofa County.

It manufactures graduation gowns annually for Cuttington University. Workers, paid every two weeks based on output, earned a combined US$4,320 producing gowns and hats for Cuttington in June 2025 alone.

Aaron G.V. Juahkollie, Executive Director of the Foundation for International Dignity, said ACD has achieved what many vocational institutions struggle to do: survive without unreliable and unpredictable donor funding.

“The sustainability of any organization is what matters,” he said. “With the fact that they are sustaining themselves up to now, I think they are to be emulated, and government needs to look at them too, especially for the skills they are providing to women in the community.”

He pointed to ACD’s uniforms, tax compliance and 25 years of operation as proof of its credibility.

Persistent struggles faced by all small businesses

Without support from government or donors building the business has been challenging.

“Every day we beg, we go online, we look for people to help this program,” Kamara said.

He listed recurring challenges: high material costs, difficulty paying instructors and students struggling to complete tuition. Students unable to pay can work off fees once advanced enough to contribute to production.

Students echoed those concerns, describing a lack of personal sewing machines and difficulty accessing water.

“We don’t have, money and water around here,” Paye said. Like everyone here. She is hoping some benefactor will step up. “If they can help us with a water pump… that can help us to carry our school far, we’ll be happy.”

Tumbey has recommended that government make available low-interest micro-loans for small businesses like ACD, along with government investment in rural infrastructure – roads, electricity, water access – and tax incentives for businesses that hire and train young people.

One of the newly constructed buildings at ACD vocational training institute’s Annex Two in Gbarnga, Bong County. Credit: Nukanah Kollie

A school uniform for the future

Kamara said ACD’s ambition is to expand uniform production into a full factory capable of supplying government schools nationwide.

“Our first target is government schools,” he said. “We want to target government schools so that any government school in the republic… everything about school uniform, we’re going to produce.”

Tumbey called ACD an example other Liberian entrepreneurs could replicate, proving a movement does not require a massive grant; it can begin with a single borrowed machine.

ACD’s growth continues largely through word of mouth and Kamara’s outreach on local radio, where he encourages young people, particularly women, to enroll.

“If you don’t have any skill in your head, you have no hope,” he said. “But if you get skill in your head as you’re moving, you have hope that you will get something to do.”

Twenty-five years after beginning with one borrowed sewing machine, Kamara’s experiment has become far more than a tailoring school. It is a business, a training center and a source of opportunity for women and young people who might otherwise struggle to find a livelihood.

“You live by what you learn,” Kamara said.

This story is a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the “Investigating Liberia” Reporting Project. Funding was provided by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency. The donor had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Weah Consoles Guinea After Conakry Landfill Landslide Kills 30
World.content:
Paynesville — Former Liberian President George Manneh Weah has extended condolences to Guinea’s President Mamady Doumbouya and the people of Guinea following a devastating landslide at a major landfill in the capital, Conakry, that killed at least 30 people and critically injured six others.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The disaster occurred early Sunday, August 24, when heavy rains triggered a landslide at the Dar es Salaam landfill, a massive open-air waste dump in Conakry. The collapse buried nearby makeshift structures and destroyed several homes.

In a statement issued Tuesday, August 25, the Office of Former President Weah said he conveyed his “profound condolences” to President Doumbouya, the Guinean government and, particularly, families affected by the tragedy.

Weah also wished those injured a speedy recovery, saying he shared in the grief of the Guinean people during what he described as a difficult national moment.

“It is my fervent prayer and hope that you, your Government and the people of the Republic of Guinea, including, but not limited to the bereaved and affected families, in your usual resilience, will take solace in God The Almighty, as you go through this challenging national period of your existence,” Weah said in his message.

Disaster Strikes Before Landfill Closure

The landslide reportedly occurred shortly after 2 a.m. GMT on Sunday following heavy rainfall. Authorities said the rains washed over the enormous heap of refuse at Dar es Salaam, causing the unstable waste pile to collapse onto nearby dwellings.

Authorities launched a search-and-rescue operation to locate possible survivors. Six people were reported seriously injured, while several homes were destroyed.

The landfill had reportedly been designated for closure on Sunday, according to Lt. Col. Baldé Mamadou Bailo, a sanitation official with Guinea’s military engineering battalion.

The disaster has drawn renewed attention to the dangers posed by informal settlements around large waste dumps, particularly during Guinea’s rainy season.

Weah Praises Guinean Resilience

In his condolence message, Weah expressed confidence that President Doumbouya, his government and the Guinean people would overcome the tragedy with renewed strength and hope.

He said Guinea’s resilience would help the country navigate the aftermath of the disaster and urged the affected families to find comfort in their faith.

The former Liberian leader’s message comes as rescue workers and authorities continue efforts to respond to the deadly landslide and assess the full extent of the destruction in Conakry.

Weah concluded by assuring President Doumbouya and the Guinean people of his solidarity as they mourn those who lost their lives.

World.title: Mo Ibrahim Warns Hichilema Against Wasting Zambia’s Democratic Legacy
World.content:
Mo Ibrahim, the Sudanese-British telecoms billionaire and founder of the Mo Ibrahim Foundation, has issued a public statement expressing deep concern over developments in Zambia following the general election, warning President Hakainde Hichilema against squandering the progress made during his first term in office. The statement, dated 26 August, was published on the foundation’s website.

“Mr President, your first mandate was defined by progress. Do not waste what you have achieved,” it reads.

Ibrahim said his foundation was watching post-election developments in Zambia closely, arguing that elections test democracy well beyond what happens at the ballot box. He pointed to the arbitrary arrest of opposition members, the killing of a former minister, and the suspension of vote counting as developments he said should never occur in a genuine democracy.

“The arbitrary arrest of opposition members; the killing of a former minister; and the suspension of vote counting: these should never happen in a true democracy,” he said.

He also raised the closure of Zambia’s top courts, including the Constitutional Court, ahead of the deadline for challenging the election result, describing it as adding to the country’s difficulties. Ibrahim said Zambia had built a reputation over decades for competitive elections, peaceful transfers of power and respect for constitutional processes, a legacy he said had been held up internationally as a model for other nations to follow.

“Mr President: Your own legacy could be just as strong,” he said, adding that no legacy could be taken for granted and must be protected and strengthened from one mandate to the next.

Ibrahim closed with a direct warning to the Head of State.

“It would be a waste and a shame for it all to crumble now,” he said.

There was no immediate response from State House or the Zambian government to the foundation’s remarks. Ibrahim’s organisation is known across the continent for its annual index measuring governance quality in African states and for a leadership prize awarded to democratically elected leaders who transfer power at the end of their term, giving the intervention added diplomatic weight.

The statement adds an international voice to the domestic dispute over the vote, which has centred on the constitutional petition window, the closure of the courts, and the death of former MP Mutotwe Kafwaya. Civil society groups in Zambia have separately raised concerns over the handling of the vote count and the timing of the court closures relative to the petition deadline, and Ibrahim’s statement is among the most prominent international responses to the post-election dispute to date.

World.title: Sampa says Tonse Alliance’s AU letter will only damage Zambia’s image
World.content:
Former Matero MP and Patriotic Front faction president Miles Sampa, who worked with the African Union for five years, has dismissed a letter written by the Tonse Alliance to the AU asking the continental body to halt President-elect Hakainde Hichilema’s swearing-in, describing the move as a waste of time that will only damage Zambia’s international standing.

Sampa, who says he served as a senior member of the Pan African Parliament during his time with the AU, said the organisation only engages with member states and not political parties, alliances or individuals, making a response to the Tonse letter unlikely.

“Asking them by ba Tonse to halt HH’s swearing-in is a waste of the white paper the letter was put on,” he said.

He argued the AU has a track record of endorsing disputed elections elsewhere on the continent. He cited Tanzania, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Equatorial Guinea, where he served as an accredited AU election observer, saying thousands died in those polls and opposition leaders were detained weeks before voting.

Sampa singled out AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf of Djibouti, the official the Tonse Alliance addressed its complaint to, accusing him of declaring Tanzania’s election free and fair before vote counting had even finished.

“We were in Dar and he was in Addis but before we could even compile our report, uyo,” he said, adding that he had publicly challenged the Djiboutian diplomat’s conduct at the time.

He recalled that the AU observer mission to Tanzania was led by former Botswana president Mokgweetsi Masisi, who also headed the SADC observer mission that monitored Zambia’s own election. Sampa said a fellow Zambian delegate on that Tanzania trip, opposition figure Patrick Mucheleka, experienced the same restrictions he did.

Both men were confined to their hotel rooms in Dar es Salaam from 9am on polling day, with internet and phone lines cut for five days until they left the country, he said.

Sampa argued that experience should give Masisi grounds to question opposition complaints about Zambia’s own vote, which he said fell far short of what he witnessed in Tanzania.

He described a similar pattern in Equatorial Guinea, where the AU also certified the election as free and fair. Sampa said one polling station there had been relocated to the backyard of a ruling party ward chairman’s home, while others closed two hours ahead of schedule.

He said he would not detail his experience observing elections in the Democratic Republic of Congo, but noted the AU had again rushed to call that vote free and fair.

Turning to Zambia’s own polls, Sampa said no opposition leader was detained ahead of the vote despite what he called arguable grounds to do so, no internet access was cut, no voters were intimidated, and no international journalists or observers were refused visas or accreditation.

He said these were core indicators tracked on AU and SADC election observation checklists, and called on SADC, the AU and the European Union to apply consistent standards across the continent.

Sampa also addressed the death of former Minister and MP Mutotwe Kafwaya, calling it devastating and saying he initially assumed reports of it were political spin until they were confirmed true. He said the matter had been linked to national security concerns and should now be left to law enforcement agencies.

He extended the same sentiment to Tanzania and Equatorial Guinea, saying the loss of life recorded during those elections should never occur during a democratic process.

Sampa questioned the Tonse Alliance’s timing, asking where its members stood in 2016 when the Constitutional Court failed to hear a petition filed by Hichilema and his then running mate, Geoffrey Bwalya Mwamba.

He noted that when Michael Sata and Hichilema lost previous elections, neither approached the United Nations or the African Union to challenge the outcome internationally.

Sampa called the Tonse Alliance’s approach to the AU unprecedented and unpatriotic, arguing it risked damaging Zambia’s reputation abroad rather than advancing the alliance’s case at home. There was no immediate response from the alliance to his remarks.

World.title: IMF, Egypt congratulate President Hichilema on re-election
World.content:
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Egyptian President, Abdel Fattah Al-Sisi have congratulated President Hakainde Hichilema on his re-election as Republican President in the 2026 general elections.

In separate statements availed to the media, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva and President Abdel Fattah Al-Sisi pledged continued cooperation with Zambia, with the IMF reaffirming its commitment to supporting the country’s development agenda.

Ms Georgieva said the IMF looks forward to working closely with President Hichilema and his administration to deepen its engagement with Zambia.

“The IMF’s unequivocal commitment to supporting Zambia’s ambitious developmental agenda remains firm, and we look forward to working closely with you and your administration to advance our common objective of building a prosperous Zambia,” she said.

Meanwhile, President Abdel Fattah Al-Sisi expressed Egypt’s keenness to further strengthen Zambia-Egypt relations, building on the solid foundation of bilateral cooperation between the two countries.

He also pledged to enhance cooperation at all levels and strengthen coordination between Zambia and Egypt on regional and international matters.

World.title: FRA buys 165,684 bags of maize in Mpongwe
World.content:
The Food Reserve Agency (FRA) has purchased 165,684 bags by 50 kilograms of maize from farmers in Mpongwe District.

Mpongwe District Commissioner, Mwambashi Mwitwa, says the maize was bought from 19 satellite depots across the district.

Speaking during the launch of the 2026/2027 input redemption exercise, Mr Mwitwa disclosed that the maize was cultivated on 98,283.59 hectares and yielded 280,365.38 metric tonnes.

Mr Mwitwa said the district recorded an average productivity of about 2.85 metric tonnes per hectare.

“This is the first time in the history of Zambia that farmers are redeeming inputs in August. It shows our commitment to ensuring farmers access inputs early for the next farming season,” Mr Mwitwa said.

He further revealed that 500 farmers in Mpongwe have already received codes to enable them to redeem farming inputs under the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP).

And Luanshya Agro Suppliers Director, Dinah Kabonso, urged farmers to only access inputs through approved channels.

Ms Kabonso warned that buying inputs from the streets compromises quality and can lead to poor yields.

“Farmers should avoid shortcuts. Genuine inputs accessed through the proper system will guarantee better production,” she said.

The early start of input redemption is expected to give farmers in Mpongwe and across the Copperbelt adequate time to prepare their fields ahead of the 2026/2027 farming season.

World.title: Lavushimanda residents urged to venture in fish farming
World.content:
The Department of Fisheries in Lavushimanda District in Muchinga Province has harvested three thousand tilapia fish from local fish ponds situated in Mabonga area.

Assistant Aquaculture Officer at the Department of Fisheries, Ashes Mulenga, has disclosed that this is an initiative from a local farmer who stocked 6, 000 tilapia fingerlings in two out of ten fish ponds some eight months ago.

Mr Mulenga said the fish has matured and have so far harvested from one fish pond.

“We have assisted this farmer in harvesting the fish, which has all been sold and the farmer has realised about K10, 000 from the sale of the fish”, he said.

Mr Mulenga has called on the local community to consider venturing into fish farming as another source of income.

He stated that the market for fish is readily available in Lavushimanda owing to the non-availability of relish as most of it is imported to the area.

Mr Mulenga however, said the presence of a wild animal, locally known as ‘akababo’ is posing threat to fish farmers as the animal feeds on fish.

He has appealed to well-wishers such as Non-Governmental Organisations to support fish farmers by providing perimeter fences on the fish ponds in order to protect their business from the predators
