World.title: States try new tactics to bring down high hospital prices
World.content:
States try new tactics to bring down high hospital prices

toggle caption utah778/Getty Images

For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

Every year Jim Evans faces the challenge of keeping health care costs reasonable for the more than 400 teachers, custodians and bus drivers at Concord Community Schools. Evans, the chief financial officer for the Northern Indiana school district is trying something new this year — negotiating directly with a local hospital.

"We think that it could be significant savings," said Evans.

This is possible because of a new state law that goes into full effect on Sept. 1, requiring 75 hospitals to offer employers deals below a new price threshold. Instead of a specific number, it's a multiple of Medicare rates. The federal health insurance program for Americans 65 and older publishes standardized prices, and that has become a benchmark for Indiana and other states trying to control health costs.

Sponsor Message

"What the law did was it kind of changed the conversation in terms of how we look at pricing," Evans said. "Now it's up to us to take advantage of that."

Hospital prices are one of the main reasons why health care is so expensive. In fact one out of every two dollars of commercial health insurance goes to hospital care.

But most employers don't negotiate their own rates. Usually they hire an insurer who negotiates prices, but rarely have insight into how those prices compare to Medicare rates. For years employers have absorbed the increases — KFF, a nonpartisan health research organization, found prices hospitals charged private insurers went up 30 percent over the last seven years.

Indiana and other states including Vermont and Delaware have passed laws over the last few years to place upper limits on hospital prices for people with private health insurance.

Indiana puts employers at the center

"This is impacting wage growth," Randa Deaton, CEO of the Employers Forum of Indiana, said about employers struggling to absorb high hospital prices. "It impacts businesses, it's impacting our workers."

The Forum commissioned a study by the policy research organization RAND back in 2017 that found some large hospitals in Indiana were charging three to four times Medicare prices. Since then the Forum has pushed for a slate of reforms to increase transparency and limit prices.

"People have exhausted a lot of the low-hanging fruit for improving care and driving affordability," Deaton said. "We're moving to the next set of levers."

In 2025, Indiana lawmakers enacted two major price reforms. The first requires hospitals to offer direct employer deals no more expensive than 2.6 times Medicare prices. These direct deals have grown in popularity nationwide because in exchange for more patients and faster payment, hospitals offer employers lower prices.

Sponsor Message

Parkview Health, one of the largest health systems in Indiana, has offered these kinds of arrangements for 30 years. Parkview's chief of commercial partnerships, Lainie Dean, expects the law to make them more popular.

"We're getting a lot of reach-outs in all areas of direct-to-employer product offerings," Dean said. "We actually see this growing significantly."

These deals will likely add up slowly, hospital by hospital as employers start to choose the option. The 2017 RAND study found Parkview Health was among the hospital systems charging the highest prices in the state.

A 2026 state report shows Parkview and the other hospitals are already complying with the law, offering deals below this threshold.

Before Indiana, other states tested price caps on a smaller scale — starting with their own state employee health plans. Montana, North Carolina and Oregon were among the first.

Evidence on price caps

Researchers found that after two years under the price limit, Oregon saved over $107 million and outpatient prices per procedure fell by 25%. However, some hospitals that had been charging below the cap raised prices up to it.

Tony Lo Sasso, a health economist at the University of Wisconsin, worries this side effect could spread. He warns caps don't fix the underlying problems driving high prices — a lack of competition.

"You'll get that sugar high of price relief," Lo Sasso said, "But it's not going to be sustainable."

Focus on the nonprofits

The second provision of Indiana's price reform law kicks in by 2029 and has more teeth. If large nonprofit hospitals don't bring prices below a separate statewide average by then, they risk losing their nonprofit status — and they would be required to start paying taxes.

Indiana Hospital Association President Scott Tittle points to reports showing hospitals have voluntarily cut prices over the last three years.

But he warns these price reforms are hitting as hospitals are being squeezed by deep Medicaid cuts and increased labor costs.

Sponsor Message

"The increased cost of goods and services, the threat and then actual imposition of tariffs. And these are costs that our members have no control over," Tittle said. "Our members are certainly struggling on the ground."

Tittle adds, it's up to insurers to pass those savings on to patients. Patients will see immediate changes in the form of lower out-of-pocket costs for specific bills. But when it comes to monthly premium reductions the picture is more complicated, said John Sadtler, CEO of SIHO insurance Services, a small, hospital-owned insurer in Indiana.

"That's a part of the equation, but that's not the whole equation," Sadtler pointed to expensive medications and people seeking more care as other factors that are contributing to high premiums.

Indiana's law doesn't require insurers to reduce premiums commensurate with hospital price reductions. Vermont's price cap law, also passed in 2025, does. It gives the state's insurance regulator the authority to ensure that lower hospital prices actually reach patients.

World.title: Judge clears the way for Postal Service work on Trump's mail-in voting order for now
World.content:
Judge clears the way for Postal Service work on Trump's mail-in voting order for now

toggle caption Joe Raedle/Getty Images

A federal judge in Boston has handed the Trump administration another temporary win in the legal fight over the president's executive order to restrict mail-in voting for the midterm election.

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani on Wednesday canceled a nationwide ruling she had issued that blocked the U.S. Postal Service from working on Trump's directives.

The decision sets the stage for another possible consideration of the executive order by the Supreme Court. So far, the high court has ruled on a procedural issue, but not weighed in on whether Trump's order is legal.

Sponsor Message

In that earlier procedural ruling, the Supreme Court halted a similar June ruling from Talwani that applied only to the 23 mainly Democratic-led states, plus Washington, D.C., that sued over the order. The high court concluded Talwani weighed in too early, before USPS issued a finalized plan for carrying out Trump's directives.

In Wednesday's order, the judge cited that reasoning by the Supreme Court for granting the administration's request to cancel her nationwide ruling, which was also issued before USPS' Aug. 21 release of a final rule for federal ballot mail.

That rule's most controversial provision lays out a plan for delivering mail-in ballots only to people on lists of absentee voters that states would have to turn over to the mailing agency, as called for by Trump's order.

Trump, who himself has voted by mail in Florida, has said he signed this executive order in March to stop illegal voting by non-U.S. citizens, a problem that many studies and audits find is extremely rare.

The order's challengers argue that it oversteps a president's authority under the Constitution, which gives the power of setting federal election rules to the states and Congress. They also claim that USPS has no authority to control mail-in voting.

It remains unclear if and how Trump's directives would ultimately affect voting by mail for the midterms, which is set to start in a matter of weeks.

Sponsor Message

Trump's order is expected to face more legal hurdles as this lawsuit and other related cases filed by Democrats, voting rights groups and two dozen mainly Democratic-led states proceed.

Those challengers are asking Talwani, as well as another federal judge in Washington, D.C., to issue new rulings that would block USPS from carrying out its finalized plan and likely be appealed to the Supreme Court.

Editor's note: USPS is a financial supporter of NPR.

Edited by Benjamin Swasey

World.title: Will Trump's latest beef plan make your hamburger cheaper? Not much, experts say
World.content:
Will Trump's latest beef plan make your hamburger cheaper? Not much, experts say

toggle caption Tony Gutierrez/AP

On Friday, President Trump announced a plan to temporarily lower tariff rates on some imported ground beef in hopes of reducing the price of the American dietary standby.

Trump said in a post on social media that the U.S. would "allow up to 300,000 metric tons of product for ground beef to be imported with no out of quota tariff. We have a commitment that this beef will be sold at 25 percent below current market prices."

The announcement, which rankled some U.S. ranchers and Republican lawmakers, comes just weeks ahead of the November midterm elections, when the economy and cost of living are expected to be among the top issues on voters' minds.

Sponsor Message

As inflation has risen, ground beef has often been a bellwether of surging consumer prices. According to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics , the average cost of a pound of ground beef jumped nearly 57% over the last five years.

Yet agricultural industry experts say they don't expect Trump's plan to lead to a major decline in prices at the meat counter.

"I don't think it's going to be $1.50 [less]" under Trump's plan, said Andrew Griffith, a University of Tennessee professor who studies livestock economics. "Now, we might see a quarter to 35 cents [less]."

U.S. consumers who bought ground beef last month paid an average of $6.89 per pound, federal data showed.

A major price decrease is unlikely

One reason the proposal may have little impact on ground beef prices is that the amount of ground beef subject to the lower tariff rate is relatively small compared to America's strong appetite for red meat.

Jaime Luke, an assistant professor and livestock economist at Michigan State University, said an additional 300,000 metric tons of ground beef would represent about a 2% increase in the domestic beef supply. "So when we look big picture, it maybe isn't as big of a number as you might think when you first see it outright," she said.

Sponsor Message

Luke added that it was unclear from Trump's announcement if the imported ground beef would be on top of what was already destined for the American market — or product that was coming to the U.S. anyway and would simply benefit from a lower tariff rate.

If consumers do see any cost savings, Griffith said, they'll likely be temporary.

Trump announced that the lower tariff rate would apply for the next 90 days, but it may not take the U.S. that long to import 300,000 metric tons — or 661 million pounds — of ground beef, he noted. The U.S. brought in about 542 million pounds of ground beef in June alone, according to the USDA .

Griffith said shoppers could see lower prices for a short time, but they shouldn't expect major savings. For the typical U.S. consumer eating nearly 60 pounds of ground beef per year, a 25-cent price decrease would mean an annual savings of $15.

Food prices are a salient issue ahead of the midterms

Trump's announcement on Friday irked the U.S. cattle industry, which has been facing pressures from rising operating costs, a parasitic screwworm and foreign competition — leading to the smallest domestic cattle herd in decades.

"Undercutting American farmers and ranchers with inferior product from foreign competitors does nothing to create market confidence or encourage rebuilding the herd," the National Cattlemen's Beef Association said in a statement.

Cattle producers similarly criticized another Trump proposal last year to import more beef from Argentina.

Last week's announcement even elicited rare rebukes from Republican lawmakers, some of whom are up for reelection in a few months.

"This hurts!" said Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota, who called for better protections for domestic producers. Montana Sen. Tim Sheehy said Trump's "heart is in the right place on wanting lower prices for the American people," but said the plan will "make it more difficult for American ranchers to rebuild our herd and bring prices down."

Sponsor Message

Yet voters are increasingly looking to their elected officials to do something about skyrocketing food prices, which were up 3% in July compared to the previous year.

A survey by the University of Illinois and Purdue University in May found that nearly 41% of Republicans and 58% of Democrats said their votes in November would be strongly influenced by what candidates say about food affordability.

"I don't think it's the only issue," said Maria Kalaitzandonakes, a University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign economics professor who leads the survey, "but I think there's a large share of voters that wants politicians to convey that they have a plan to make sure that cost of living and affordability remain a top issue."

World.title: How Dolly Parton wrote the story of a changing America
World.content:
How Dolly Parton wrote the story of a changing America

toggle caption Richard E. Aaron/Redferns

Until her passing on Tuesday, Dolly Parton may have been the only living person truly worthy of that old-fashioned designation, "America's Sweetheart." Her immense musical talent guaranteed her top-tier standing in country music and propelled her into a level of mainstream success that only a handful of her peers would match. Her charm, depth, beauty, sense of humor and radiant goodness made her a star across seven turbulent decades.

She was, as many tributes published since her death have noted, the one person whose presence everyone welcomed, no matter what hostilities their politics or social status otherwise inspired. Parton was our favorite aunt, our imaginary president. She was also the composer of a career's worth of indelible hits that emblematized America's cultural life, and particularly the changing experiences of women, in ways that place her in an elite category: a songwriter whose greatest works, considered together, are their own version of the American songbook.

toggle caption Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images

The story of this country as told through Parton's best-known songs begins in the mid-1960s, when many aspects of the country she knew and loved so well were in flux. She didn't write her first charting country single, 1967's "Dumb Blonde" (that was Curly Putnam) but it set the tone for her amiable, uncompromising version of women's liberation, distilling the frustration of countless underestimated women in the home and the workplace into an actionable rallying cry.

Sponsor Message

This was one aspect of Parton, the adventurer whose insistent self-respect would carry her beyond any limitations others tried to impose on her. The other, the keeper of home truths, surfaced in 1971's "Coat of Many Colors," an expertly embroidered portrait of Appalachian rural life that also stands as one of the most powerful reminders of poor people's dignity to ever grace the airwaves. With those two singles and others that quickly followed, like 1972's cozily erotic "Touch Your Woman" and the same year's pastoral "My Tennessee Mountain Home," Parton — the rare Nashville songwriter who wrote her greatest songs alone — established the multifaceted world view that made her music so mobile, such a popular well for other artists to tap for inspiration, and so insightful about America.

toggle caption Donaldson Collection/Getty Images/Michael Ochs Archives

Parton's legend was secured in 1973, when she released "Jolene," a song that transcended its moment by perfectly capturing the primal intensity of insecure romantic desire. With a melody redolent of a century of folk ballads and, as Parton told NPR in 2008, a chorus "even a first-grader or a baby could sing," this true-ish tale of rivalry among women is fluid enough that a man could take it on, as Jack White did in The White Stripes' 2001 version. "Jolene" is a murder ballad whose victims all survive, a cry of revenge in the face of betrayal that puts a woman in charge and unexpectedly creates a bond between two rivals. Beyoncé's version of the song on her Grammy-winning country album Cowboy Carter, blessed by Parton, heated up that eroticism to show that "Jolene" is as much about one woman appreciating another as about the murderous restrictions of monogamy.

Sponsor Message

"Jolene" was, in fact, one of the less dramatic songs Parton wrote in her gothic mode, a style that allowed her to expose many of the burdens women endure under patriarchy; her early songs that never made it to the Top 40 dared to broach topics like emotional abuse, stillbirth, forced institutionalization, a birthmother's grief and a pregnant, abandoned lover's suicide. Her deep knowledge of the dark lent substance to the songs that expressed her belief in transcendence. The masterpiece that she released the following year showed her rising upward with unrivaled grace. Like "Jolene," the majestic "I Will Always Love You" is ripe with particulars and anchored in the country realm of adult dreams and regrets, but is open-ended enough to invite myriad interpretations. Parton wrote it as a forgiving farewell to Porter Wagoner, the duet partner who had helped launch her career but also tried to restrict her when her genius took her beyond their partnership.

toggle caption Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images

"I Will Always Love You" was a hit for her in 1974 and again in 1983, as part of the soundtrack to The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas, where it served as a lament about the forbidden (though ultimately triumphant) romance between the madam played by Parton and Burt Reynolds' local sheriff. The song reached its full potential, of course, in the hands of Whitney Houston, whose sublime 1992 version exposed the damage done by arbitrary divisions between Black and white radio formats, crossing into every corner of pop to become the definitive expression of the era's blockbuster-besotted grandeur. "I Will Always Love You" is the musical equivalent of Star Wars, an epic that encompasses many epochs. Houston could soar within it because Parton imbued it with a musical and sentimental purity that made room for the enormity of her expressiveness.

Even as Parton secured her status as a writer of timeless tunes with these megahits, she remained the quintessential modern woman chronicling her times, via her own songs and ones written by others. The hits that took her from the 1970s to the '80s form a vivid portrait of the power-suited working woman who enjoyed her pleasures with men from whom she demanded freedom and equality. "Here You Come Again," written by Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil, and her own "Two Doors Down" are jaunty artifacts of the era of swinging and the pill, while "9 to 5," along with the comedy film classic whose soundtrack it graced (and in which Dolly starred), became the era's working woman's anthem. These songs made Parton not just the era's most adorable embodiment of American values but a global icon, culminating in her duet with Kenny Rogers, the Bee Gees-authored "Islands in the Stream." Parton's vivacious touch on that song is the electricity that carries it beyond genre and makes it a definitive example of global pop.

toggle caption Gary Gershoff/Getty Images

After the 1980s, Parton remained musically prolific while easing into the exalted yet somehow always accessible position she maintained until her death. She won a new generation of fans at the turn of the 21st century by returning to the bluegrass that inspired her as a child and continued to build a discography that would ultimately include more than 50 solo and collaborative studio albums, and remain as eclectic as it had been in the beginning.

Sponsor Message

Continually taken up by would-be protégés to whom she was characteristically generous, she kept winning hearts on stages with the likes of Sabrina Carpenter, Lainey Wilson and Post Malone. Her final album, Rockstar, celebrated a 2022 induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame that Parton had greeted, at first, with great skepticism. In the end, though, America's sweetheart took on that quintessentially American musical form with the same let's-get-it-done energy she'd applied to every challenge she'd faced. "I just went for it," she told NPR. Luckily for every last American, we could always follow wherever she went.

toggle caption Rich Fury/Getty Images for NARAS/Getty Images North America

If you, like us, cannot get enough of Dolly, head to the NPR app for a Dolly Parton playlist from our archives, or check out the NPR Network podcast Dolly Parton's America.

World.title: Meta, states agree to $17 billion settlement in child safety trial
World.content:
Meta, states agree to $17 billion settlement in child safety trial

toggle caption Godofredo A. Vasquez/AFP via Getty Images



The social media company Meta and states suing it have agreed to settle a landmark federal child safety lawsuit in a move that state attorneys general hope will be a turning point for youth safety on social media platforms.

California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey represented a larger consortium of states that alleged in the suit that Meta designed its apps — Facebook and Instagram — to be addictive to kids and knew about the risks those platforms posed, but hid that information from the public.

In addition to claims that Meta broke state consumer protection laws, the states accused Meta of violating the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act by collecting data about children under the age of 13. Meta has a policy of not allowing kids under 13 on its platforms, but some skirt the rule by registering with false birth dates.

Sponsor Message

The settlement requires Meta to pay up to $17 billion in penalties to the states over 10 years and to make significant changes to how its platforms operate so that they are safer for minors.

"Today, we have secured a settlement with Meta that will make social media less dangerous for our kids and make a world of a difference for children and their families," California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement.

"Meta has agreed to make massive transformations that will reduce the risk of harm from its platforms — and will do it within months," he added.

Meta's chief legal officer, C.J. Mahoney, said in a statement that the framework was groundbreaking and "will empower parents to easily manage how their children access our platforms."

"But its success depends on all other social media platforms following Meta's lead," he said, making an explicit call for TikTok and YouTube to implement this same framework.

Representatives from Google (which owns YouTube), TikTok and Snap, which the settlement identified alongside the others as a "core" member of the industry, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Meta has denied the allegations brought by the states.

Bonta's office also said Meta had agreed to make changes to its platforms, including a default time limit of two hours for users under 18 and a nighttime block between midnight and 6 a.m., both of which can be lifted only by a parent; default night and schooltime notification blocks; a ban on displaying the number of "likes" or reactions to posts made by minors; a ban on cosmetic surgery image filters for minors; and an option for young users to have a "non-personalized feed" that is not run by an algorithm targeting them with content.

Sponsor Message

Meta must also bring on an independent auditor with "expansive access to information and resources" and the right to communicate with the attorneys general, the announcement said, and would also be subject to an injunction "prohibiting it from making further false, misleading, or deceptive statements around its safety features."

"I am proud to deliver this settlement that addresses the concerns at the core of our lawsuit and institutes real change, real transparency, and real enforceable protections for children on Facebook and Instagram — right now, no more waiting," Bonta wrote.

Some of the provisions in the settlement are triggered to tighten if YouTube, TikTok and Snap agree to similar steps. For instance, the two-hour default on-app time for minors would drop to one hour. The amount Meta pays ratchets up if others join the framework as well, an apparent move to cushion the competitive blow if they don't.

The settlement says a portion of the funds would go toward things like youth mental health programs, after-school programs and crisis intervention services. States including Vermont, Michigan, North Carolina, Indiana and South Dakota are set to receive parts of the settlement.

Nora Freeman Engstrom, a law professor at Stanford University, said both sides appear to have gained from the choice to settle. Some of the platform changes that Meta has agreed to, and that Meta and the states are hoping others will also adopt, would have been hard to obtain through legislation, she said.

Meta, meanwhile, is on the hook for an amount of money that she called "not exactly pocket change, but it's hardly a body blow." The company reported a net profit of around $16 billion last quarter.

But the settlement sends a signal. "Meta is clearly signaling that it would like this litigation behind it. But this is not game over," she said.

Sponsor Message

This case is one of thousands against social media companies, including Meta, for alleged harms to the mental health of minors, and experts say many of those cases will not be affected by this outcome.

Matthew P. Bergman, the founding attorney at the Social Media Victims Law Center, which has represented plaintiffs in cases against social media companies, applauded the settlement as a "watershed moment" in holding Meta accountable.

"But our work is far from over," he said in a written statement. "We will continue fighting for the individual families whose children will never come home, and for those still struggling with mental health crises caused by these platforms. Accountability to the public is important — but accountability to the families harmed must remain our focus."

The trial started last week in federal court in Oakland, Calif., and was expected to run through early October. But the settlement announcement comes only midway through the trial's second week.

Key testimony came from insiders who worked at Meta, including whistleblower Arturo Béjar, who testified that the company culture was obsessed with increasing user numbers and that Meta's internal studies showed that young users were exposed to harmful experiences at much higher rates than the company acknowledged publicly.

Tuesday, the states brought Instagram head Adam Mosseri to the stand and questioned him about the effectiveness of some features added to Instagram to try to keep teens from using it too much. They accused Mosseri of publicly touting the use of one of those safety features — called "Take a Break," a feature that nudged kids to close the app — when the reality was that it had very limited uptake by teens.

Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California approved the settlement hours after it was filed.

Sponsor Message

The case is part of a wave of lawsuits that has been compared to litigation against tobacco companies in the 1990s. Those suits led to record settlements, changes to the way the companies operate and a shift in the public discourse about cigarettes.

The case was consolidated from a series of lawsuits by attorneys general around the U.S. against Meta, and the settlement resolves the cases and claims of 51 of those, according to the California Attorney General's Office.

World.title: Trump's top trade negotiator disputes Canadian assertion that U.S. made last-minute demands
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In a Canadian exclusive interview, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer disputed Canada’s explanation about why trade talks fell apart, and told CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton there’s currently no ‘open channels’ to get both sides back to the negotiating table.

The Trump administration's top trade negotiator on Wednesday disputed Ottawa's assertion that last-minute demands from the U.S. derailed a trade deal between the two countries, saying Canadian negotiators' concerns about the deal's "implementation" led Ottawa to pull the plug.

In an interview with CBC News, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the Canadian side had new requests when his counterpart, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, returned from Ottawa after the tentative deal was struck on Aug. 18.

"We had agreed to, as I've shared before in the press, really the best deal available to any country on the planet with respect to Canada," Greer told CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton in his first one-on-one interview with a Canadian news outlet since trade talks broke down on Friday.

"When [LeBlanc] came back, they had some additional views. They had some additional requests. They had some additional things that were too much for the United States."

The ambassador said it wasn't clear when the two countries might return to the negotiation table. He confirmed he and LeBlanc were not in contact as of Wednesday.

"I would say we don't have open channels right now," Greer said. "I have a good relationship with Minister LeBlanc, but right now, I think the Canadian side is talking about their next steps."

WATCH | U.S. trade rep on whether discussions might resume: What will it take to resume Canada-U.S. trade negotiations? | Duration 3:03 In a Canadian exclusive interview, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton that the path to resume trade negotiations is unclear.

The remarks from Greer, the cabinet member in charge of delivering the president's tariff regime, make clear that the two countries disagree as to which is to blame for the breakdown in negotiations. Prime Minister Mark Carney was first to introduce the notion that last-minute changes scuttled the agreement, but said it was the U.S. that tried to make "unfair, uneconomic" adjustments that "called into question the reliability of any deal."

The White House has said Canada turned down a deal that would've included cuts to existing tariffs on steel, aluminum, lumber and Canadian-made automobiles.

On the topic of retaliation, Greer didn't rule out another tit-for-tat response from the U.S. after Canada announced dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs against hundreds of American products to take effect after Labour Day. The levies are in response to the United States' latest round of tariffs, which began last weekend.

"If there's further retaliation from the Canadian side, of course, we're not going to just sit down and take that. Our view is, 'Don't retaliate,'" he said, speaking outside the White House. "I know how people are feeling in Canada and what they think. It's unfortunate, but it is what it is."

Greer outside the White House on Wednesday. (Jonathan Austin/CBC)

At a news conference on Saturday, Carney said the deal proposed by the U.S. ultimately would've encroached on Canada's ability to pursue trade agreements with other countries, threatened key industries and undermined French language protections.

"A good deal [became] a deal we would not accept," the prime minister said.

Neither government has released the text of the draft agreement, and both LeBlanc and Greer have cited confidentiality in response to questions around wider details.

Greer said the White House was prepared to lower the tariff on the majority of steel Canada sent to the United States from 50 per cent to 25 per cent. It would have been subject to a tariff-rate quota system, a provision meaning only a portion of steel imports receive that lower rate.

WATCH | Carney's full remarks on Saturday: FULL SPEECH | Carney explains why Canada suspended trade talks with U.S. | Duration 22:59 Prime Minister Mark Carney explained why the government chose not to sign a trade deal with American counterparts as U.S. President Donald Trump's 50 per cent tariffs on almost $30 billion of Canadian goods are in effect. 'We were not prepared to compromise Canada's sovereignty or undermine our key industries,' Carney said.

On Canadian-made vehicles, Greer said the rate would've been reduced from 25 per cent down to 15 per cent, with "the possibility of going down to seven per cent."

Sources told CBC News the auto tariff could have been reduced further by having more U.S. content, taking the effective rate down to 7.5 per cent. The Canadian side believed that offer was still not good enough, sources noted.

Greer denied that the White House had asked for a say in the trade deals Canada cuts with other countries. He said the administration wanted to prioritize co-operation, referring to the Fortress North America concept floated most prominently by Ontario Premier Doug Ford.

"We didn't have any text like that," Greer said Wednesday. "We talked about, let's co-ordinate on a bilateral basis, right? It wasn't, 'Canada shall' or anything like that. It's, 'Let's talk about this.'"

WATCH | U.S. trade rep on communication with his Canadian counterpart: No open channel with Canada's trade minister, Greer says | Duration 0:17 In a Canadian exclusive interview with CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there isn’t currently any open channels of communication between him and Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc.

On the issue of discoverability of French content on streaming services, Greer said it had been "highlighted" by the White House but not as a dealbreaker.

"President Trump, myself and the U.S. government recognizes the importance and sensitivity of the French language in Canada, in Quebec, in the Maritimes and some [other] areas. We know that this is quite sensitive and quite important," he said of French language protections.

"There is no way we would let a good deal go by for something like this. This is not something where we push hard or condition or red line. It's like the farthest thing from a red line."

The new measures and deteriorating political rhetoric from both sides of the border were a marked departure from the conciliatory tone last week, when the two countries appeared closer than ever to an agreement after months of tension.

Last week, Greer and his Canadian counterpart appeared shoulder-to-shoulder in front of Greer's office, assuring the cameras they effectively only needed to cross T's and dot I's to get the agreement over the finish line. That night, U.S. President Donald Trump granted a tariff extension so negotiators could keep working for three more days.

But by Friday, the deal had fallen apart. Asked about last-minute demands in an interview with CNN this week , Trump said: "That sounds like me."

Greer said Wednesday that the president didn't interfere in the negotiations' dying days and described the remark as "off the cuff."

WATCH | An economist explains how counter-tariffs affect Canadians: Canada hits back at U.S. with $28B worth of retaliatory tariffs | Duration 1:42:33

This week, Carney said Canada will return to the negotiating table when the American side comes back with "the right attitude." LeBlanc told CBC News he and his team won't "rush back to Washington" until they see an "economically viable" deal.

The prime minister said the government will instead focus its energy on pursuing trade relationships with global allies and shoring up the economy at home, moving Canada away from its reliance on the United States.

Carney made clear he would rather bear the consequences of a painful, drawn-out trade war than concede to the terms proposed by the White House.

"Some of the biggest payoffs of this plan, of this transformation, will take time," he said.

World.title: Alberta premier to provide update on tariffs, Canada-U.S. trade war
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As the Canada-U.S. trade war heats up, the Alberta government says Premier Danielle Smith will provide an update regarding tariffs on Wednesday.

In a news release Wednesday morning, the province said Smith will “deliver brief remarks addressing the ongoing tariff dispute with the U.S.” at an unrelated news conference in Grande Prairie, Alta., just after 3 p.m. MT. You can watch it here.

Smith has been calling on the federal government to return to the negotiating table with the United States before Canadian tariffs on $27.6-billion worth of U.S. goods take effect in about two weeks.

In a statement posted online Tuesday, Smith said tariffs and counter-tariffs “ultimately risk escalation to even higher and broader tariffs that will impact even more Canadians.”

“There is still time before these counter-tariffs take effect on Sept. 8, and I am urging the federal government to use that time to get back to the negotiating table with the United States,” Smith said in the social media post.

Political scientist Elizabeth Smythe, professor emeritus at Concordia University of Edmonton, said Alberta’s reliance on the U.S. for the province’s oil exports is driving Smith’s more diplomatic approach to the trade war.

"The U.S. is not going to stop importing those fossil fuels," Smythe said. "She thinks what she's doing is the better approach. Now, whether all Albertans agree with that is another story."

More to come.

World.title: Premier Scott Moe announces retaliatory tariffs on U.S. booze, won't pull liquor from shelves
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe has announced counter-tariffs on U.S. alcohol products, matching the U.S. tariffs of 50 per cent.

At a news conference in Prince Albert Wednesday, Moe said the counter-tariffs will take effect Sept. 8.

The U.S. implemented a 50 per cent tariff on a range of Canadian alcohol products on Aug. 22.

However, the premier said the province is still not considering pulling U.S. booze from shelves. He said his government will leave the choice to buy or not buy the U.S. products up to Saskatchewan consumers.

On Tuesday, Ottawa announced counter-tariffs on $27.6 billion of U.S. goods. It also unveiled $7.5 billion in support for workers and businesses.

Sask. backs federal counter-tariffs on U.S. imports

Moe said the province supports the federal government's "focused and targeted approach in its counter-tariffs on U.S. imports," after trade negotiations fell apart over the weekend.

He said the U.S. was "encroaching on international trade agreements," and called that unacceptable. Moe said Saskatchewan has been working to build trade relationships outside of North America, and that those efforts have been successful.

The premier said the new counter-tariffs cover about $1.5 billion, or 11.3 per cent, of Saskatchewan's annual imports from the U.S. He said the province is analyzing the counter-tariff list closely and is working with "affected industries to determine its potential impact on jobs and consumer prices."

WATCH | No export tariffs on Canadian potash and oil, says Sask. premier: No export tariffs on Canadian potash and oil, says Sask. premier | Duration 2:23 Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe says while he supports Ottawa's latest plans for reciprocal tariffs on some U.S. products, he will not support export tariffs on Canadian natural resources. 'Canadians would lose jobs immediately,' said Moe.

On Wednesday Moe made it clear to reporters that export tariffs affecting potash and oil are off the table.

“What we as a province cannot and will not support is any kind of export tariff on our natural resources or any resources that are being exported to the U.S. or through the U.S. to other areas of the world," Moe said.

“We cannot in any way support the adding of export tariffs on a product like oil,” he said, calling it an unsustainable hit to the Saskatchewan and Alberta industries in particular.

Moe said Canadians would lose jobs immediately if that were to happen.

”An export tariff on oil would have a far greater impact on those that are living in Eastern Canada than it would even on those that are directly working in the energy industry," he said.

The premier also said an export tax on potash would be "devastating" for Saskatchewan's economy, adding it would lead to much higher fertilizer costs, affecting farmers all over the world.

Meanwhile, U.S. steel and aluminum are affected by the counter-tariffs. The province's steel industry wants to ensure its workers' jobs are protected.

"I welcome the announcements from the federal government that we are gonna take targeted retaliatory measures and we are going to support businesses and workers that are impacted," said Scott Lunny, Western Canada director for the United Steel Workers Union.

Agricultural equipment is also targeted by the counter-tariffs.

The Agricultural Producers Association of Saskatchewan (APAS) said farmers have no choice but to pay the price for parts and machinery.

"Going into the harvest season now, producers are going to be forced to pay a really high price for parts because they need them to keep the equipment running," said APAS president Bill Prybylski.

Province reviewing support measures for affected businesses, workers

Moe said the province is also reviewing the federal government’s support measures to ensure they work for businesses and workers.

"While this is the appropriate response to the latest round of U.S. tariffs, we can never lose sight of the fact that all tariffs hurt businesses, jobs, consumers and families on both sides of the border, and our ultimate goal must be to get back to a free and fair trade relationship with the U.S., as we have enjoyed for many years," Moe said.

Ultimately, Moe told reporters in Prince Albert that Canadians “need to have one goal”: to return to the negotiating table and make a deal with their largest trading partner.

“With all of the very intentional actions that we take, the goal has to be for both parties to return to the table,” Moe said, adding the ideal outcome would be a trade arrangement that's good for Canadians and Americans.

World.title: It's finally time to rename Ottawa's Trump Avenue, councillor says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Donald Trump's trade war against Canada heats up, an Ottawa city councillor says it's finally time to rename a street that bears the U.S. president's name.

A 2021 effort to rename Trump Avenue in the Central Park neighbourhood off Merivale Road fell through after a consultation found residents were split on the idea.

The nays Ave. it: Ottawa's Trump Avenue to keep its name

But the area's councillor, Riley Brockington, said it's now time to put an end to what he called an embarrassment in light of Trump's repeated threats to Canada's sovereignty and economy.

"I'm embarrassed that there is a street in River Ward called Trump Avenue, and I'm embarrassed that in the nation's capital we have Donald Trump honoured in this respect," he said.

Brockington said he will work with Trump Avenue residents to launch the renaming process after the next election, but he said he's set on seeing it done.

"I think the time has come when you look at the damage and carnage that the president has caused, including with our own country," Brockington said. "We're past the point of debating."

NYC-themed street names

The Central Park neighbourhood has several streets with New York City-themed names such as Staten Way and Grammercy Park.

Brockington's statement came during a debate on a motion from Mayor Mark Sutcliffe to support Ottawa businesses affected by the tariffs that the Trump administration imposed on $28 billion of Canadian exports.

Asked about the proposal to rename Trump Avenue, Sutcliffe said it could prove a "hassle" to people who live on the street who would have to change their driver's licence and notify all of their contacts to change their address.

He said those residents still need to be consulted, but he said his own position is clear.

"If it were up to me, there would be nothing named after Donald Trump in Ottawa," Sutcliffe said.

World.title: 'People are people': How Dolly Parton became an unlikely 2SLGBTQ+ icon, ally and advocate
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Dolly Parton never forgot her roots, carrying the spirit of her Tennessee mountain home wherever she went and her deep Christian faith with her until the end.

Yet the omnipresent country music legend was as celebrated for her advocacy as much as her music. She spent decades championing women's rights, civil rights and gay rights, while openly denouncing several recent anti-trans and anti-drag bills, telling the Hollywood Reporter in 2023 that "I just want everybody to be treated good."

"I think everybody should be allowed to be who they are, and to love who they love. I don't think we should be judgmental," Parton told Billboard about her gay fanbase in 2014.

"Lord, I've got enough problems of my own to pass judgment on somebody else."

Parton, 80, died Tuesday in Nashville after a brief battle with cancer. Her publicist said she died peacefully, surrounded by loved ones. And among the many, many tributes pouring in celebrating the star's life and legacy , there's a common thread: her advocacy, allyship and enduring love for her 2SLGBTQ+ fans.

Dolly Parton performs onstage during the 58th Academy Of Country Music Awards in 2023. (Theo Wargo/Getty Images)

"Before I met her, I loved her because she took a risk and accepted me (and all of us) for being gay in a time where she didn’t need to say anything," singer/songwriter Brandi Carlile posted on Instagram Tuesday.

"She never wavered on accepting anyone for who they were and who they were meant to be."

As the Guardian points out in its tribute, Parton was beloved by many, "but it was perhaps her gay fans who claimed her most vociferously and publicly."

And, as dozens of 2SLGBTQ+ writers and media publications have noted since Tuesday's announcement, the world lost an icon, but "the queer community ... lost one of its most steadfast advocates."

An Instagram post by Interview magazine quotes Dolly Parton's conversation with Andy Warhol for its July 1984 cover story. (@interviewmag/Instagram)

'Always on the right side of history'

So, how did the granddaughter of a preacher, who grew up inside a two-room Appalachian cabin, become a global advocate and icon for the 2SLGBTQ+ community?

"She was always on the right side of history," a fan commented on an Instagram post by Impact.

As an early example, in 1984 — right around the time the AIDS virus was intensifying anti-gay stigma — Parton spoke out in support of her diverse fanbase in an interview with Andy Warhol for Interview magazine.

"I got a huge gay following and some really macho-looking women," Parton said in the cover story.

"To me, people are people. … Many of my friends are gay, male and female. I don’t judge people. I don’t care what people do in their bedrooms and people shouldn’t care what I do in mine."

The Hollywood Reporter points out that a statement like that could have cost Parton a large portion of her country music audience, but " Dolly disregarded the possible consequences."

In the mid 1980s, alongside her manager, Sandy Gallin, Parton co-founded the production company that co-produced Common Threads: Stories From the Quilt. The documentary about the AIDS memorial quilt won an Academy Award in 1990.

Gallin also "openly acknowledged being gay, becoming one of the earliest Hollywood figures to do so," notes a 2017 tribute to him in the Los Angeles Blade. And he and Parton were inseparable, according to the publication, adding they considered each other "beyond best friends and almost soul mates"

In 1991, Parton released a song called Family, with the lyrics: " Some are preachers, some are gay. Some are addicts, drunks and strays. But not a one is turned away when it's family."

A screengrab of an Instagram post by Out magazine shows Dolly Parton on the cover of the magazine's 1997 July cover. (@outmagazine/Instagram)

This move, in the historically conservative world of country music, when even the word "gay" was still controversial in mainstream culture, was "gobsmacking," notes The Advocate's John Casey.

"Country music in particular didn't go near queer identity — at all," Casey wrote.

"Dolly didn't make some giant political statement or scream it from the mountaintops. Instead, she made a family portrait and put us within the frame, perhaps without listening to those who might have told her not to."

By 1997, Parton was on the cover of Out magazine.

In a tribute posted to Instagram Tuesday, Out noted that even three decades later, "the image feels like an especially poignant reminder of the joy, generosity, and unapologetic individuality she brought to the world.

"From her music and philanthropy to her steadfast message of love and acceptance, Dolly made generations of queer fans feel seen."

WATCH | Icon Dolly Parton dead at 80: Music icon Dolly Parton dead at 80 | Duration 2:32 Fans and fellow musicians shared tributes and memories of Dolly Parton after the country music legend’s death at 80.

'We are all God's children'

Her unwavering support continued over the coming decades.

In 1999, Parton collaborated with Culture Club — fronted by openly gay singer Boy George — for the song Your Kisses are Charity. In 2005, Parton wrote and performed Travelin' Through, the title song for Transamerica — a movie about a transgender woman. As the news site Wide Open Country notes, the song became "an anthem of equality."

Parton also voiced her support for gay marriage years before the U.S. Supreme Court made it a fundamental right in 2015.

"Sure, why can't they get married? They should suffer like the rest of us do," Parton told CNN host Joy Behar in 2009.

WATCH | Dolly Parton tells Larry King 'We are all God's children':

In 2011, she personally apologized to a lesbian couple after a security guard at Dollywood, Parton's namesake theme park, forced one of the women to turn her shirt inside-out before entering. The shirt had said, "Marriage is so gay."

"Everyone knows my personal support of the gay and lesbian community. Dollywood is a family park and all families are welcome," Parton said in a statement at the time.

She spoke out again about marriage equality in 2014, saying, "I think everyone should be with who they love." In 2016, Parton famously told Larry King, "We are all God's children."

"If you're gay, you're gay. If you're straight, you're straight. And you should be allowed to be how you are and who you are."

What younger fans sometimes miss, but older fans won't forget, is that Parton treated allyship "like it was no big deal," wrote the Advocate's Casey.

Parton paid for staff member to transition

In more recent years, Parton — who has famously quipped, " If I hadn’t been a girl, I’d have been a drag queen" — spoke out against Tennessee's ban on gender-affirming health care for minors, as well as the state's anti-drag laws.

"I try not to get into the politics of everything. I try to get into the human element of it," Parton told the Hollywood Reporter in 2023.

" That’s who they are. They cannot help that any more than I can help being Dolly Parton."

Dolly Parton performs during an event celebrating the Kansas statewide expansion of her Imagination Library in 2023. (Charlie Riedel/The Associated Press)

But now we know her support started more quietly decades earlier. On Tuesday, Parton's former editor at HarperCollins revealed that the singer paid the medical costs for a member of her staff to transition back in the 1990s.

" She was a profoundly good and kind person; it wasn’t an act," Elissa Altman posted on Instagram.

Parton's mere memory served to continue her advocacy work Tuesday as a federal judge cited Parton as he struck down a Texas law banning drag shows.

In his ruling, Texas District Judge David Hittner determined the law was so broad even Parton could have faced penalties under it.

"Just as many people ... chastised Dolly Parton as a voluptuous sex symbol because of her big hair, flamboyant clothes and breast exposure ... there are 'erotic' elements in countless popular performances," Hittner wrote.

World.title: 24 Canadians among hundreds missing after flash floods kill at least 157 in Nepal, Tibet
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Massive flash floods in a border area of Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday killed at least 157 people, according to Nepali police, and left hundreds of tourists — including 24 Canadians — workers and others missing after sweeping through communities and bringing travel in some areas to a halt. The Prime Minister's Office in Nepal earlier reported at least 95 dead. China's state broadcaster CCTV said a mudslide in Tibet's Gyirong County near the border killed at least three and left 265 missing. The Bhotekoshi River flooded around 9 a.m. local time Wednesday, destroying several villages as well as roads and hydropower projects, Nepali officials said. They issued warnings to residents in several of Nepal's districts and asked them to stay away from the banks of the Bhotekoshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers. "We have asked both India and China to help us with the rescue efforts," said Sasmit Pokharel, a spokesperson for the Nepali government. Sunil Sharma, officiating director of the Nepal Tourism Board's public relation and publicity department, said 403 people, including 341 foreign nationals were reported missing, including 24 Canadian citizens. Nepal's ambassador to Canada later confirmed the information about the Canadians. In an interview with CBC News, Bharat Raj Paudyal said while he cannot confirm the circumstances around the Canadians, he said the affected area is both popular with hikers and also a route often used by those on pilgrimage. Prime Minister Mark Carney called the flash flood "absolutely devastating." In a statement on social media, he asked all Canadians in the region to register with the ROCA (Registration of Canadians Abroad) system as soon as possible, and said Canada stands ready to provide support. "Canadians are thinking of all those in distress right now, those who have lost a loved one, and all those who are still waiting for answers," he added. The flash floods along Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River are absolutely devastating.

Canadians are thinking of all those in distress right now, those who have lost a loved one, and all those who are still waiting for answers.

Our government is closely following the situation and… —MarkJCarney Global Affairs Canada said it is aware there are Canadians who have been affected by the floods and while it has consular officials in the region, it may take time to establish communication due to power outages. If you or someone you know needs emergency consular assistance in the region, Global Affairs Canada's Emergency Watch and Response Centre can be reached by calling +1 613-996-8885, by text message at +1 613-686-3658, via WhatsApp at +1 613-909-8881, via Signal at +1-613-909-8087 or by e-mail at sos@international.gc.ca People tried to flee before landslide Security footage captured on the Chinese side of ⁠the Nepal-Tibet border showed many people fleeing before a wall of rock, mud and water destroyed buildings and ‌vehicles, with the people disappearing from view. Sharma said 133 of the missing are from India and on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus. Also missing are 47 from the United States, 34 from Australia and 33 from Britain. South Korean and Malaysian government officials said separately from Sharma that several of their citizens were unaccounted for. At least 62 missing Nepali citizens were among hundreds of locals trekking near the Gosaikunda lake in Rasuwa, coinciding with the upcoming local festival of Janai Purnima, Sharma added. Nepal police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle told The Associated Press that at least 28 police officials were missing. Nepal's steep valleys are economic lifelines and travel corridors but precarious ones when disaster strikes. Images showed what appeared to be the second floors of buildings in the hard-hit Nuwakot district slathered in mud after the torrent rushed by. Debris hung from tree branches and wires, vehicles were buried and stunned survivors were caked in mud. Initial reports from Nepali officials suggested an earthquake in the area could have caused the lower part of a glacier to collapse and trigger the floods. The U.S. Geological Survey later said the tremor recorded at the time was caused by the glacial rock and ice collapsing to the valley floor. The Trishuli river roughly parallels a highway north of the Kathmandu area that is used to reach one of Nepal's most popular treks in the Langtang area. WATCH | Warning: Some graphic footage: Hundreds of people, including tourists, missing after flood in Nepal | Duration 1:28 Rescue efforts are underway after an earthquake struck the mountainous Rasuwa district in Nepal. Officials say around 400 tourists and travellers — including from India, the U.K. and Malaysia — are missing as crews attempt to reach villages where homes are covered in mud. China, India prepared to help United Nations teams and partners were mobilizing supplies and personnel in Nepal to support communities affected by the disaster, UN Secretary General António Guterres said. Chinese President Xi Jinping ordered authorities to step up the efforts for people missing after the mudslide, state news agency Xinhua reported. Chinese authorities were conducting large-scale search and rescue operations in the Tibetan border area of Gyirong, according to state broadcaster CCTV. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah and offered help. "India is prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance. Our teams are closely co-ordinating on rescue and relief efforts," Modi said in a social media post. Dozens of multi-storey buildings, trucks, and vans were buried under vast quantities of mud in the district of Nuwakot, one of the worst-affected areas. Officials warned residents in several of Nepal's districts and asked them to stay away from the banks of the Bhotekoshi, Trishuli, and Narayani rivers. The same regions affected by Wednesday's disaster saw flash floods similar to those in August last year, when a glacial lake in Tibet overflowed because of high temperatures in the mountain region. Nine people were killed, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting Nepal and China, was damaged at the time. Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development say an avalanche from a glacier likely caused Wednesday's flash flood. The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River, witnessed maximum flooding Wednesday, they said. "The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in 14 months, this time triggered by an ice rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream," said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the climate research group. "In a warming Himalaya, early warning is the first line of adaptation," he added. The Himalayan region, which crosses Nepal and several nearby countries, including India, is especially vulnerable to heavy rains, floods and landslides because the area is warming up faster than the rest of the world due to human-caused climate change. Damaged houses and vehicles are seen in the aftermath of flash floods along the Trishuli River in Nepal's Nuwakot district on Wednesday. (Niranjan Shrestha/The Associated Press) Research has shown that extreme weather events, including heat waves, heavy rains and melting glaciers, have become more frequent in the region. Researchers at the Kathmandu research group found earlier this year that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region are melting at an accelerating rate, with ice loss rates doubling since 2000, primarily due to rising global temperatures and climate change.

World.title: Hamilton-born NHL prospect Matthew Mayich hospitalized after 'training incident,' OHL says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

NHL prospect Matthew Mayich, who was born in Hamilton and played junior hockey with the Ottawa 67's, is in hospital in Arizona following "an off-ice training incident," says the Ontario Hockey League.

The OHL said it's "sending thoughts, prayers and support" to Mayich, 21.

The St. Louis Blues drafted the defenceman in the sixth round of the 2023 NHL draft.

Mayich's player record says he played minor hockey with the Hamilton Huskies between 2016 and 2020 before joining the 67's.

The OHL said reports indicate he was hospitalized while preparing for the 2026-27 season in Arizona on Aug. 20.

St. Louis Blues 'pray' for Mayich's recovery

CBC Hamilton reached out to ask Arizona State University, where Mayich is listed as a player , if he was injured at the Tempe school.

The university said a student on the hockey team collapsed during an outdoor morning exercise session and remains hospitalized. It said it's not naming the student and is “reviewing the circumstances surrounding the workout.”

Doug Armstrong, the Blues' president of hockey operations, said in a news release, "The entire Blues organization is keeping Matthew Mayich close to our hearts as we pray for his comfort and recovery while he continues to undergo medical treatment in Arizona."

The organization extends its "deepest support" to his family, friends and teammates during this difficult time," Armstrong said.

OHL commissioner Bryan Crawford shared a similar message in the league's news release, saying, “Our thoughts are with Matthew, his parents John and Christina, and the entire Mayich family."

“Matthew spent four seasons in our league and earned the respect of everyone he played with and against," Crawford said. "The entire Ontario Hockey League is thinking of him and pulling for him, and we are keeping his family close in our thoughts."

The Huskies — now the Hamilton Steel Hockey Club — posted congratulatory messages to Mayich in 2021 when he signed with the '67s and in 2023 when the Blues selected him.

The Huskies said he'd played with the organization since he was nine years old.

World.title: More charges for former Manitoba MP Inky Mark after 445 guns, explosives found in home: RCMP
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Former member of Parliament Inky Mark, who was arrested on a dozen weapons offences last month, has been hit with 26 more charges, after police say they took a total of 445 firearms and 26.5 kilograms of explosives from his Manitoba home.

RCMP say the 78-year-old was rearrested on new charges on Aug. 12 after an ongoing investigation.

Mark was arrested during a July 7 search of his home near the western Manitoba city of Dauphin and was initially charged with 12 weapons-related offences , including firearms trafficking, possession of a firearm with a tampered serial number, three counts of unsafe firearms storage, two counts of careless use of a firearm and two counts of possession of a prohibited device.

Police said last month they took 439 guns from his home and seized other items, including an antique cannon and ammunition.

RCMP said in a Wednesday news release that after processing the evidence seized in July, they determined 445 firearms were taken from the home. Of those, 295 were unsafely stored, 10 were prohibited and 11 were restricted or prohibited firearms that were not registered to Mark, according to police.

RCMP also now say they seized 26.5 kilograms of explosives — more than four times the amount licensed individuals are allowed to possess, according to police.

A number of the restricted or prohibited firearms were stored with readily available ammunition, and two firearms registered to Mark could not be located, the RCMP release said.

A photo provided by Manitoba RCMP shows some of the weapons they say they found at Mark's home during a July 7 search. (Manitoba RCMP)

In total, 38 charges have now been laid against Mark.

The 26 new charges include w eapons trafficking, three more counts of possession of a prohibited weapon, nine counts of possession of a restricted firearm/prohibited weapon with ammunition, and nine counts of possession of a firearm when knowing it is unauthorized.

He's also been charged with another count of possession of a firearm with a tampered serial number, two counts of failing to report the loss of a firearm and having more than six kilograms of what RCMP called explosives.

The explosives were mostly Tannerite, a spokesperson for Manitoba RCMP said in an email to CBC News. Tannerite is a brand of explosive target used for firearms practice, and it is illegal to possess more than six kilograms of such reactive targets.

A photo provided by RCMP shows more of the guns they say they seized from Mark's home in July. (Manitoba RCMP)

A few days after the initial charges were laid in July, Mark told CBC News that he broke the law by illegally transferring three guns, but denied he trafficked any.

Mark said at that point he's been legally collecting firearms since the early 1970s, but some of those weapons are now illegal to own due to gun law changes over the years.

During the initial search of Mark's home, RCMP also seized more than $300,000 in currency. Mark told CBC the cash was from property sales in Dauphin and denied it was connected with firearms trafficking.

RCMP also now allege that sometime between December 2024 and February 2025, Mark went unprompted to the home of a friend who had made a social media post about a coyote on their property, and handed that person a firearm and ammunition, according to Wednesday's news release.

The person did not have a gun licence and did not use the weapon, which was later recovered by investigators. The friend has not been charged with any offences, while the weapons trafficking charge against Mark was related to this incident, the RCMP spokesperson said.

Mark is a former MP who represented the Dauphin-Swan River-Neepawa riding. He was first elected to Parliament in 1997 and resigned his seat in 2010, after serving first with the Reform party, and later with the Canadian Alliance and finally as a Conservative.

He ran unsuccessfully for the seat again in 2015 as an independent.

Prior to his time as an MP, he was elected mayor of Dauphin in 1994. He ran unsuccessfully for that position again in 2010.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.
