A group of his followers gathered outside the building to express their support for Braun, who finished fourth in last year’s presidential elections. Since then, his Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party has risen to around 9% in polls, making it a potential kingmaker after next year’s parliamentary elections. After meeting with Braun, IPN prosecutor Robert Janicki announced that they had presented him with charges for “publicly and contrary to the facts denying the crimes of genocide committed by officers of the Third Reich in the German concentration and extermination camp KL Auschwitz-Birkenau”. The charges relate to two interviews Braun gave in July last year. He declared that “Auschwitz with its gas chambers is unfortunately a fake” and said that claims about the use of gas chambers are part of a “propaganda narrative” supporting a “quasi-religious cult”. In fact, gas chambers were used at Auschwitz, which was located in German-occupied Poland, to kill around 900,000 people, the vast majority of them Jews. Janicki noted that Braun’s remarks “clearly contradict common historical knowledge based on documents, witness accounts, perpetrators’ statements and findings from past criminal proceedings”. Polska🇵🇱, Litwa🇱🇹, Łotwa 🇱🇻i Norwegia 🇳🇴 kupują wspólnie polskie pioruny. To 63 umowa w ramach polskiego SAFE. Dziś 8 mld zł. Mesko od maja zwiększyło zatrudnienie o 200 osób. To jak to było,… pic.twitter.com/YIDWBGBvpm — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) August 24, 2026 The deal will see the firm provide “several hundred” launchers and “several thousand” missiles for its shoulder-fired Piorun systems, which target low-flying aircraft such as planes, helicopters and drones. Over 80% will be supplied to Poland’s armed forces, with the remainder going to its three NATO allies. The purchase is being funded through SAFE, which provides loans at preferential terms for defence spending. While SAFE can be used individually by countries to make purchases for their own armed forces, some funds are designated for joint procurement by groups of countries (including non-EU member Norway). “Our partners from Lithuania, Latvia and Norway have decided to purchase from Poland,” declared deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who oversees Poland’s participation in SAFE. “We are a leader in the SAFE mechanism and are the first to create such agreements. For the first time, the [Polish defence ministry’s] Armaments Agency is making purchases not only for the Polish armed forces, but also for those of our allies.” “This is a measure of the success of the Polish arms industry,” declared defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, as the deal was announced on Monday. “This is the moment when Poland can proudly say: we are a European leader.” He noted that Mesko’s production capacity is now 2.5 times larger than it was when the current government took power in December 2023. Since SAFE launched in May, the firm’s staffing, which stood at 3,200 by the end of last year, has increased by around 200, added the minister. Poland is by far the largest recipient of SAFE funds, with around €44 billion. The government says that SAFE will not only bolster Poland’s defence capabilities but also provide a boost to the domestic defence industry, where around 90% of the funds will be spent. However, the programme has been opposed by the right-wing opposition and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who argue that it will give Brussels too much influence over Polish defence spending and burden Poland with decades of debt on uncertain terms. Wiceminister @magdasobkowiak: Dzisiaj rozpoczynamy etap wspólnych zakupów. Wiele było pytań o to, czy to zrealizujemy, a może będziemy kupować w Niemczech. I widzicie, co się wydarzyło. Nie dosyć, że te umowy realizujemy w polskim przemyśle zbrojeniowym, to jeszcze nasi partnerzy… pic.twitter.com/hFL8M2Laah — Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) August 24, 2026 In 2022, Pioruns were among the large quantities of military equipment Poland provided to Ukraine to help its eastern neighbour defend itself from Russia’s full-scale invasion. The systems were successfully used to take down a variety of Russian aircraft. In that same year, Mesko announced that the US government had ordered “several hundred” Piorun systems, while Norway also put in a similar order. Last year, Belgium and Sweden announced that they would purchase hundreds of Pioruns, while Ukraine itself also revealed that it had requested a €120 million loan from Poland to help fund the purchase of Polish-made weapons, including Pioruns. Earlier this year, Mesko, which belongs to the state defence holding group PGZ, announced the best financial results in its 100-year history. The firm’s revenues of 2.3 billion zloty in 2025 were up 33% year-on-year, driven by international demand for Pioruns. World.title: Regulation on recognising foreign same-sex marriages comes into force in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. All registry offices in Poland can now recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other European Union countries, after a government regulation issued in May went into force. The decision came in response to a ruling by the Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU) requiring Poland to recognise such unions. Deputy prime minister Krzysztof Gawkowski expressed his “great joy, because finally in Poland we have a law that gives the right to dignity”. The government’s plenipotentiary for equality, Katarzyna Kotula, warned local authorities that they will be breaking the law if they refuse to comply with the new rules. However, the mayor of one town in a conservative region has already declared that his administration will not recognise such marriages. He argues that doing so would violate Poland’s constitution, which mentions marriage as a union between a man and a woman. Od jutra polskie państwo będzie lepiej chronić godność i prawa swoich obywateli. Nowe wzory aktów małżeństwa umożliwią transkrypcję zagranicznych aktów małżeństw jednopłciowych z pełnym szacunkiem dla par. To koniec administracyjnej fikcji i niepewności, z którą przez lata… pic.twitter.com/mRZYkEg9W4 — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) August 22, 2026 Polish domestic law still does not allow any form of same-sex unions to be formed. However, last year, the CJEU ordered that the country recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other EU member states. That was followed by a similar ruling from Poland’s own Supreme Administrative Court (NSA). One obstacle to implementing those decisions was that, previously, Poland’s civil registry only allowed male-female marriages to be entered. But, under a regulation issued by the government in May, the system now allows either mixed-sex or same-sex marriages. Even before that went into force on Sunday, some Polish cities, starting with Warsaw and Wrocław, had already begun transcribing same-sex marriages conducted abroad into their registries. They simply listed one spouse in the “man” section and the other as a “woman”, even though that was not accurate for one of them. But some local authorities have refused to do so, pointing to article 18 of Poland’s constitution, which states that: “Marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, as well as the family, motherhood and parenthood, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland.” Such doubts were cited by the mayor of Zakopane, a town in southern Poland, last week when he announced that his administration did not intend to begin recognising foreign same-sex marriages after the regulation came into force. “We will not be issuing such transcriptions in Zakopane,” said Łukasz Filipowski, quoted by local news service Nasze Miasto. He argued that doing so would “not be in accordance with the constitution”, adding that, while Zakopane is “tolerant”, it “promotes the traditional family model…[as] our foundation”. Filipowski pointed to a ruling in July by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which found that the government’s regulation conflicts with the constitution’s definition of marriage. However, the government considers the TK to be improperly constituted and therefore regards its rulings as invalid. Poland's Constitutional Tribunal has ruled that a new regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriage certificates to be registered in Poland is unconstitutional. The government says it will not implement the rulinghttps://t.co/xDAzLjcJQ4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2026 In response to Filipowski’s remarks, Kotula told broadcaster TVN that officials who refuse to recognise foreign same-sex marriages “will be breaking the law”. She said that the personal views of officials cannot “translate into what [legal] actions they take” and that the government would be monitoring the situation. Gawkowski – who, like Kotula, is a leading figure in The Left (Lewica), a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition – also warned municipalities against issuing refusals. He noted that, as well as the CJEU ruling, Polish courts have also issued orders to recognise foreign same-sex marriages. “In the end, these local authorities will lose [a court battle], so why embarrass themselves? Let’s not look for legal tricks. Let’s just implement something that has been done in other, normal countries for years,” Gawkowski told Polsat News. However, even once same-sex marriages are transcribed into Polish civil registries, there remains uncertainty about what legal consequences that will have in practice, especially given that Poland’s domestic law does not allow for any legally recognised form of same-sex union. Legal experts say that it may take years – and potentially many more legal challenges by same-sex couples – for the situation to be clarified. Separately, parliament earlier this year approved a bill, proposed by the ruling coalition, that would have granted same-sex couples in Poland certain rights normally granted to married couples. However, the law was vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Ukraine to establish new national pantheon as Poland warns against honouring massacre figures
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Volodymyr Zelensky has signed a law establishing a new national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian historical heroes. While it is not yet known which figures will be honoured there, Poland has expressed concern that they will include nationalist leaders associated with massacres of Poles in World War Two. On Sunday, a Polish deputy foreign minister warned that Kyiv “will have a huge problem” integrating with the European Union if it celebrates such individuals. But Zelensky reiterated that “only Ukrainians will decide who is a hero to us”. The establishment of the pantheon has taken place against the backdrop of a diplomatic crisis triggered in May by Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”. Parts of the UPA were responsible for the so-called Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. Poland regards the episode as a genocide, though Ukraine strongly rejects that label. Many Ukrainians hold the UPA in high regard for the role that it played in fighting for independence from Moscow-backed Soviet rule. Poland condemned Zelensky’s decision and stripped him of the country’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. In response, the Ukrainian president announced in late June that he would seek to create a new national pantheon, because “no one will dictate which heroes we should honour”. A bill creating the pantheon was subsequently approved by the Ukrainian parliament in July, and, on Saturday, Zelensky signed it into law, just ahead of today’s celebrations of Ukrainian independence day. “A Ukrainian pantheon will definitely be established, and only Ukrainians will decide for themselves who our heroes are,” declared Zelensky at a meeting with military veterans on Saturday. “All our true heroes…who fought for Ukraine, for our independence…deserve due honour.” However, the introduction of the law only now begins the process of building the pantheon itself – where the remains of those chosen as national heroes will be reburied – and the establishment of an advisory body that will decide which figures should receive such an honour. It therefore remains unknown for now who will be included in the pantheon. However, on Sunday, Polish deputy foreign minister Marcin Bosacki warned against honouring figures associated with the Volhynia massacres. “Every nation and its government has the right to choose the heroes they deem appropriate,” emphasised Bosacki in an interview with broadcaster TVP. “However, if individuals responsible for mass crimes against civilians, such as [Stepan] Bandera or [Roman] Shukhevych, are included in Ukraine’s national pantheon, it would significantly worsen Ukraine’s relations not only with Poland but with Europe in general,” he added. Bandera was the leader of a faction of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN-B), which in turn founded the UPA. Shukhevych was a military leader of the UPA. Both figures continue to be honoured in Ukraine, often prompting protests from Poland. 🇵🇱 Polskie MSZ ostrzegło Ukrainę przed „ogromnymi problemami” z Europą z powodu Bandery i Szuchewycza „Ukraina wie, że z tymi, którzy zabijali nie tylko Polaków, ale także Ukraińców, Czechów, Żydów i Romów, na swoich sztandarach będzie miała ogromne problemy z integracją… pic.twitter.com/hyujMppbEw — NEXTA Polska (@nexta_polska) August 24, 2026 “Ukraine knows that, with those who murdered not only Poles, but also some Ukrainians, Czechs, Jews and Roma, on its banners, it will have a huge problem integrating with Europe,” added Bosacki. However, the deputy minister also emphasised that, “strategiaclly, the interests of Poland and Ukraine remain very close” and that Poland must continuing “supporting Ukraine in defeating the aggressive Russia”. “We do not differ much with the Ukrainians, only with certain parts of the Ukrainian authorities after their absolutely erroneious decision to name a unit after the ‘heroes of the UPA’.” The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of relations with Ukraine has risen to the highest level ever recorded by state research agency CBOS Meanwhile, the proportion who believe reconciliation with Ukraine is possible is at its lowest ever level https://t.co/YYBCFkVxNr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Polish government figures have previously made it clear that, if Ukraine honours figures associated with historical massacres, that will make it harder for the country to achieve its ambitions of joining the EU. In June, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz warned that “you can’t build a pantheon to those who destroy European cooperation”, and that countries seeking EU membership should “not build national identity…on events, people or systems that in some way raise objections or pain among EU partners”. Kosiniak-Kamysz declared that, just as Zelensky said no one will tell Ukraine who they can honour, “no one will tell us how to vote on the entry of any state into the European Union”. That was an allusion to the fact that Poland, like all other EU member states, can veto Ukraine’s accession to the bloc. Polish and Ukrainian media have widely quoted Poland's deputy PM as saying: “With Bandera, Ukraine will not enter the EU.” However, he did not actually speak those words. World.title: Rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski seeks to switch allegiance to Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A rising US track star has declared his intention to represent Poland, the country of his ancestors. Sam Blaskowski’s personal-best 100 metres sprint time of 9.89 seconds is more than a tenth of a second faster than the current Polish national record. “I plan to make Poland the finest sprinting nation in the world. I want to win medals for Poland,” the 23-year-old told Polish broadcaster TVP Sport. Sam Blaskowski przed naszymi kamerami mówi o tym, dlaczego chciałby reprezentować Polskę! 🇵🇱 Więcej o tej sprawie 👉 https://t.co/oC8MJ4moV6 pic.twitter.com/Nw1i7YqrIp — TVP SPORT (@sport_tvppl) August 23, 2026 Blaskowski says that two of his ancestors, Franciszek and Julian, left Poland in 1905, at a time when the country was still partitioned between Germany, Austria and Russia. “My last name is Polish. But for a long time, I didn’t understand that these were my roots. Everything changed recently, because my parents and I talked a lot about our roots,” he explained to TVP Sport. He was contacted by Piotr Maruszewski, coach of the Polish sprint team, after clocking a time of 9.89 seconds in May, which is the joint-ninth-best run by anyone in the world this year. The Polish 100m record is still held by Marian Woronin, who ran 10.00 in 1984. View this post on Instagram A post shared by D3 Glory Days | D3 Running Podcast & News (@d3glorydays) Maruszewski has since been persuading and helping Blaskowski to apply for citizenship, including hiring lawyers to obtain documents proving the sprinter’s heritage. Under Polish law, people who have a Polish parent, grandparent or great-grandparent who was born in or lived in Poland after January 1920 are themselves regarded as holding Polish citizenship. That means Blaskowski’s ancestry may not be enough to qualify. However, it could be enough to convince Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, who has discretion to grant citizenship to anyone he wishes. Last year, Nawrocki granted citizenship to Vladimir Semirunniy, a speed skater who fled from Russia to Poland. Semirunniy now represents the Polish national team, including at this year’s Winter Olympics, where he won a silver medal. Given that Blaskowski last represented the United States as a junior over four years ago, he is not subject to World Athletics’ mandatory waiting period for athletes transferring national allegiance. At yesterday’s Silesia Diamond League meeting in Chorzów, Poland’s biggest annual athletics event, Blaskowski told Citius Mag that he expects to be able to represent Poland at next year’s World Championships in Beijing. “I want to inspire the next generation… to make an impact on people around me, and I think the best way to do that is to go and represent Poland,” he told TVP Sport at the same event. “Not only do I have heritage there, but people [in Poland] are very aware of your talent and they give so much appreciation for our sport, and I think it’s a great place.” He added that he and his parents plan to visit their ancestors’ hometown of Sompolno in central Poland on Monday before he again competes in Szczecin on Wednesday. In Chorzów, Blaskowski came fifth in his semi-final against some of the world’s sprinters, just ahead of European champion Romell Glave. Poland’s current top male sprinter, Dominik Kopeć, finished ninth and last in 10.32. The final was won by Jamaica’s Oblique Seville in 9.83 seconds, ahead of another American with a Polish surname, Kenneth Bednarek, who was adopted as a child by a woman with Polish heritage. “The love and support I received from Poland today were truly incredible,” Bednarek wrote on social media after competing at the same event two years ago. “I’m thrilled to have run here for the first time and can’t wait to return with my mom, who has Polish roots.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kung Fu Kenny (@kenny_bednarek) Blaskowski would not be the first sprinter to switch allegiance to Poland. Belarusian runner Krystsina Tsimanouskaya received Polish citizenship in 2022, having been granted a humanitarian visa the previous year after the Tokyo Olympics. This month, high jumper Maria Żodzik, another Belarusian who was granted Polish citizenship in 2024, won silver at the European Championships, adding to another silver at last year’s World Championships. At the 2024 Summer Olympics in Paris, Poland’s athletes disappointed, finishing with just one bronze medal in track and field events and one gold and ten medals overall, the country’s worst result since 1956. ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: How will the Law and Justice split affect Polish politics?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak The biggest-ever split within Poland’s main right-wing opposition party is a serious self-inflicted wound, signalling a more fragmented conservative landscape and complicating the right’s path back to power. While it provides a tactical boost for the Tusk government, there is still every chance of a conservative comeback if the right-wing parties cooperate effectively. Radical-right challengers At the end of last month, the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party, Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, saw the biggest split in its 25-year history. The rupture was the culmination of months of increasingly open and bitter factional conflict over the party’s future direction. PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right. However, it lost power following the October 2023 parliamentary election, which led to the formation of a coalition headed up by Donald Tusk, leader of the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party. Since last autumn, PiS has seen its polling numbers decline to the party’s lowest level of support for 15 years. At the same time, it has been challenged by two radical right competitors: the free-market Confederation (Konfederacja) and the ultra-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), which together began to match, or even exceed, PiS’s level of support. Responding to declining support At the heart of this conflict was a bitter clash between longtime party leader Jarosław Kaczyński and Mateusz Morawiecki, who served as PiS prime minister from 2017 to 2023 but grew increasingly impatient with the former’s dominance. Two main factions emerged centred on a bitter dispute on how the party should respond to declining support and political competition on its right flank. The hardline traditionalist-conservative faction, often referred to as the “butter-makers” (maślarze), was more Eurosceptic and advocated a clearer right-wing agenda that included pushing ahead with radical state reconstruction and promoting a conservative vision of national identity and traditional values. In their reading, PiS lost support to its right-wing competitors because it was not radical enough and the solution was to sharpen its ideological profile and double down on hardline rhetoric. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 This group gained influence in party structures and when, in March, Kaczyński designated one of its key figures, former education minister Przemysław Czarnek, as the party’s prime ministerial candidate in the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, this was widely seen as a clear signal favouring the traditionalist-conservative faction. Morawiecki and his allies in the modernising-technocratic faction, often called the “scouts” (harcerze), also had strong conservative values and at times were very critical of Poland’s post-1989 establishment. However, they advocated a strategy of stressing economic competence, pragmatic governance and boosting Polish prosperity over hardline rhetoric on moral-cultural issues as a more effective way of appealing to voters less influenced by traditional institutions such as the Catholic church. Although they were also critical of Brussels overreach, Morawiecki’s faction preferred to avoid escalating conflict with the EU and argued that PiS had to broaden its appeal to younger, urban, more centrist-conservative Poles who found radical cultural rhetoric off-putting. Programmatic differences and personal ambitions The conflict became so destabilising because, although rooted in genuine programmatic and strategic disagreements, personalities and individual ambitions also played a major role. While Kaczyński maintained formal control of the party, his advancing age escalated debates over PiS’s direction and leadership, and these tensions intensified after the party failed to translate its presidential candidate Karol Nawrocki’s surprise summer 2025 election victory into broader momentum. For his part, Morawiecki grew increasingly impatient and frustrated as hardliners sidelined him, while his supporters were afraid that they would be excluded from PiS candidate lists at the next election. These long-simmering tensions came to a head in April, when Morawiecki announced the formation of Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), a think tank-like platform focused on economic development The association was widely interpreted by Kaczyński and PiS hardliners as a direct challenge to party unity and the leader’s authority. The leadership ruled that Development Plus violated the PiS statute, which explicitly prohibits members from joining political organisations that conflict with the party’s goals. While Morawiecki insisted that it was simply a modest intra-party policy forum, by registering an organisation with dozens of parliamentarians, he gave his faction a formal institutional shell that could potentially act as a launchpad for his own rival breakaway party. Initially, Kaczyński and Morawiecki came to a compromise agreement whereby Development Plus would work within an official party expert group. However, in July the situation escalated when the PiS leadership issued an ultimatum banning members from participating in internal political factions (clearly targeting Development Plus) and instructing parliamentarians to sign loyalty declarations confirming that they were not involved in any such groupings. Most complied, but 40 parliamentarians affiliated with Development Plus refused to do so, accusing the leadership of political blackmail. Ultimately, Kaczyński announced that, by refusing to sign, Morawiecki and his allies had effectively left the party, while Development Plus framed it as expulsion over policy differences caused by “plotters” surrounding the party leader. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. However, he categorically ruled out ever working with Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/J6mQaer4MA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 An even more fragmented right The loss of 40 deputies means that PiS is no longer the largest parliamentary caucus, thus losing procedural advantages, committee control and visibility. The departing group includes many experienced and talented politicians, particularly in the economic and foreign policy fields. The split also reduces PiS’s funding, staffing, and in some regions local organisation, as well as creating the risk of demoralisation and further defections. Even if the Polish right secures a parliamentary majority at the next election, PiS’s relative influence could be greatly reduced. Although Kaczyński’s formal party leadership remains unquestioned, the split signals to the broader right that his authority is waning and undermines his claim to be the undisputed hegemon and central broker on the right; he is increasingly now one leader among several. It also further erodes the model that Kaczyński has built over many years as the main ideologue and ultimate arbiter of internal PiS factions. In earlier crises, this personal authority and control gave him leverage to keep everyone on board so that disagreements were managed internally, and even disillusioned figures usually stayed in, or returned to, the party. Indeed, by adding a fourth distinctive player, the PiS split further compounds the divisions on the Polish right that have deepened since the last election, transforming what was once a relatively consolidated “big tent” bloc into a multi-polar competitive field. For sure, polls conducted after the split show the combined right-wing vote as competitive overall, but even if this level of support remains stable, or even increases slightly, it is now divided across more options. This is significant because Poland’s proportional electoral system uses the d’Hondt counting system that favours larger groupings. It also creates the risk that smaller right-wing parties such as Morawiecki’s new grouping could fall below the 5% parliamentary representation threshold, so their votes are excluded from seat allocation. All of this makes it harder for the right to translate raw voter support into political power. Moreover, even if the right-wing parties win a combined parliamentary majority, post-election coordination becomes much more complex with four (or more) actors whose leaders’ rivalries, different priorities and historical animosities complicate forming a stable coalition government. Nawrocki’s role will be crucial In the light of this, Nawrocki has emerged as a critical unifier with crossover appeal across the fractured Polish right. His presidential election victory showed that he could attract support well beyond traditional PiS loyalists and consolidate a broad right-wing coalition, including the vast majority of voters from both Confederations. As president, he operates outside direct party control and has cultivated an image as an authoritative unifying figure on the right, which gives him much greater moral and symbolic stature than a partisan leader immersed in day-to-day machinations. Nawrocki has also used his constitutional powers and standing, including a legislative veto that the government lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority to overturn, to position himself assertively as a powerful counterweight to the Tusk administration, and is currently Poland’s most popular politician. Nonetheless, Nawrocki’s potential to act as a possible right-wing unifier and broker is limited. For sure, he can use the presidency to set a broad conservative agenda and mediate negotiations among the various right-wing groupings to secure pre- and post-election agreements. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland's largest opposition party, PiS, has called on President @NawrockiKn to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections https://t.co/Q3BFSOSfTG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 However, Nawrocki has no formal unifying mandate and his success ultimately depends on whether the various actors are willing to be led. Without broader cooperation, even his efforts will only mitigate, not eliminate, the damage from a divided right, and personal and ideological rivalries currently run deep and cannot be easily overridden. Moreover, not only is the president expected to remain formally above the fray and not engage too openly in day-to-day politics, he also lacks the control over party organisational machinery needed to micro-manage and enforce messy backroom deals. Pivotal but not transformative? Initial polling conducted since the split suggests that Morawiecki’s new grouping would likely clear the 5% threshold and enter parliament with a small-to-medium-sized fraction; according to Politico Europe, it is currently averaging around 6% support. Although this could make it a pivotal player in coalition talks, it does not suggest that the grouping can dramatically reshape the country’s political landscape. Moreover, its support appears to be drawn mainly from PiS’s traditional electoral base, so it is simply further fragmenting the existing right-wing vote rather than drawing in a significant number of new voters who hitherto supported the governing coalition parties. For sure, Morawiecki‘s project has advantages that many newcomers lack, notably its leader’s very high name recognition and a sizeable bloc of high-profile, political heavyweight allies, much larger than any previous PiS breakaway faction. His grouping immediately became the third largest parliamentary fraction, giving it visibility, funding, and organisational backbone. However, although there are some rare exceptions that usually involve major figures with significant resources breaking from established parties, it is a familiar pattern in post-1989 Polish politics for a brand new “startup” party to show an early bounce, benefiting from initial media coverage, only to fade or disappear as voters drift back to more established groupings or abstain at the next election. Sustaining momentum requires local organisational infrastructure, reliable funding, rapid professionalisation, and a clear identity, which new parties often lack. Indeed, to be successful a new startup should really attract at least 10% support initially simply because of its “newness”. Over the years, PiS breakaway politicians have established new parties that either quickly disappeared from the political scene or were eventually reintegrated into the grouping. Temporary relief for Tusk From a short-term tactical perspective, the PiS split is a welcome political gift for the Tusk government, shifting the media focus away from criticisms of its record and recent scandals and controversies. It has for example, blunted the opposition’s ability to maintain a sustained assault over a scandal involving high earnings for, and mismanagement by, a KO-connected doctor, alleged VIP access and potential patient harm at the Warsaw South Hospital, which had previously dominated the summer news headlines. The ruling coalition is likely to survive until next year's election, but its prospects are hampered by a weak domestic record, writes @AleksSzczerbiak The government has therefore made security key to its reelection narrative, but that also carries risks https://t.co/w2UeNaTwAO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 1, 2026 However, the PiS split has not resolved the deeper image and performance problems that have dragged down the Tusk government’s approval ratings. The administration struggles with perceptions of slow delivery on promises while facing a hostile president, and if these problems persist, or new controversies reignite strongly once the PiS drama cools, the government will very quickly find itself back on the defensive. The PiS split only provides temporary relief; to win the next election, the ruling coalition needs to improve its own standing, not rely on opposition mistakes. World.title: Historic Invalidovna Building in Prague Begins Major Reconstruction
World.content:
The long-awaited reconstruction of Prague’s Invalidovna has officially begun.

The Baroque complex in Karlín will undergo a major renovation costing CZK 2.15 billion, with work scheduled for completion in 2030.

The project is the largest investment in the history of the National Heritage Institute (NPÚ). Alongside the restoration of the historic building, two new extensions will be constructed on the southern side of the complex.



One will provide facilities for the Prague Philharmonic Choir, while the other will house technical infrastructure needed to operate the site.

Much of Invalidovna will remain open to the public

Once the reconstruction is complete, the NPÚ will use part of the complex for restoration workshops, laboratories, archives and study rooms.

An underground garage with space for 50 vehicles is also planned.

Around 80 percent of the complex is expected to remain accessible to the public. The restored site will include exhibition and conference spaces, visitor routes through the Baroque interiors, a café and facilities for children’s groups operated by Prague 8.

A new multi-purpose hall in one of the extensions will be suitable for concerts, conferences and other events. The modern section will also contain technical facilities that cannot be accommodated inside the protected historic building.

The courtyard and gardens will be opened through the original entrances.

A Baroque complex with a long military history

Invalidovna was built between 1731 and 1737 based on plans by Kilián Ignác Dientzenhofer, one of the leading architects of the Czech Baroque. The institution provided accommodation and care for war veterans and their families until 1935.

The original complex was designed at a time when European armies were beginning to develop more systematic forms of care for soldiers who had been wounded or disabled in war.

Military campaigns were often accompanied by outbreaks of diseases such as cholera and typhus, which could kill even soldiers whose battlefield injuries were not life-threatening. Separate psychiatric institutions were later established for veterans suffering severe mental trauma after their military service.

World.title: PIZZA! PIZZA! POP-UP Returns to Holešovice Market on September 3

World.title: Manifesto Market’s Craft Beer Returns for Its Third Edition

Zichovec, Sibeeria, Chroust, MadCat, Fracek, Pivovar VIK and Berlin-based BRLO will each have their own pop-up tent, giving visitors the chance to explore a wide range of beer styles directly from the breweries.

The beer will be accompanied by food from more than 10 international kitchens at Manifesto. Visitors can expect everything from juicy burgers and tacos to spicy ramen and authentic Chinese roast duck, making it possible to turn the beer tasting into a full weekend meal.

World.title: More Czechs Are Living Paycheck to Paycheck, New Survey Finds
World.content:
The number of Czechs who have nothing left from their paycheck at the end of the month is rising.

This year, 13 percent say they have no money left after covering their expenses, up from 9 percent last year. Meanwhile, 84 percent have at least a small amount left over, five percentage points less than in 2025.

The findings come from a May survey conducted by loan provider Provident Financial among 1,000 respondents.



According to the survey, Czechs’ ability to save is declining. Only 43 percent of respondents have at least 20 percent of their monthly income left after covering their expenses, down nine percentage points from last year. Almost half of Czechs nevertheless regularly set aside part of their paycheck each month.

At the same time, their overall financial resilience appears to be improving. More than a quarter of respondents have enough savings to cover their expenses for more than a year, compared with just 15 percent last year. The share of people with no financial reserve at all has also fallen, from 18 percent in 2025 to 13 percent this year.

The gap between men and women in the amount of money left at the end of the month has also narrowed. This year, 45 percent of men have at least 20 percent of their paycheck left after expenses, compared with 59 percent last year. Among women, the figure has fallen from 45 percent to 39 percent.

The share of Czechs with enough savings to cover 12 months without their main source of income has increased sharply this year, rising by 11 percentage points compared with 2025. At the same time, the proportion of respondents whose savings would last less than three months fell to 12 percent, down from 17 percent a year earlier.

Men are considerably more likely than women to report having enough savings to cover at least six months of expenses. The figure is 63 percent among men, compared with 39 percent among women.

Education also appears to play an important role in financial preparedness. Seven in ten respondents with a university degree say they have enough savings to cover at least six months, compared with 43 percent among people with lower levels of education.

World.title: Tiny Steps, Big Milestones: What Really Matters When Toddlers Start Preschool
World.content:
For a one-year-old, starting preschool is not about learning letters or sitting through lessons.

It is about feeling safe without Mum or Dad nearby, discovering the joy of playing alongside other children, and slowly gaining the confidence to explore the world independently. At Tiny Tots in Prague, these small everyday moments are at the heart of the programme.

A favourite toy clutched tightly in one hand. A cautious look back at Mum or Dad from the classroom door. Perhaps a few tears (from either side).

For families with children aged one or two, the first experience of leaving a little one in someone else’s care can feel like a very big step.

And for the child, it is one too.



At this age, development happens through moments that can look almost insignificant to adults: reaching for a spoon without help, joining another child in play, recognising a familiar song, saying a new word, or feeling comfortable enough to wander a little further away from a trusted adult.

These are precisely the moments that Tiny Tots, a programme for children aged 1–2 at Nessie English Preschool, part of Park Lane International School, is designed to encourage.

Before learning comes feeling safe

For very young children, a good first preschool experience begins with something much more fundamental than an academic curriculum: trust.

“Parents often want to know how their child will cope with separation, whether we can follow the rhythm they are used to at home and, above all, whether their child will really be seen as an individual,” says Catalina Gonzalez-Got, who leads the Tiny Tots programme.

Catalina knows the feeling from both sides. An early-years educator with international experience, she is also a mother herself. Becoming a parent, she says, gave her a much deeper understanding of how emotional it can be to entrust a young child to somebody else for the first time.

That is why settling in is treated as a process rather than a test that a toddler is expected to pass on day one.

Some children may quickly become curious about their new surroundings. Others need more time, reassurance and proximity to a familiar adult before they are ready to explore.

Both are perfectly normal. The goal is to allow each child to find that confidence at their own pace.

For toddlers, play is serious business

Adults sometimes separate “playing” and “learning”. Toddlers do not.

When a child squishes playdough between their fingers, listens to a story, sings along to a familiar song, explores the garden or watches another toddler build something, they are constantly learning.

They are practising movement and coordination. They are discovering cause and effect. They are learning how to communicate, negotiate space with other children, manage emotions and make choices.

Tiny Tots therefore follows a play-based approach inspired by the English Early Years Foundation Stage framework, with activities designed around the developmental needs of one- and two-year-olds.

There are no miniature school desks or pressure to perform.

Instead, children encounter language, movement, music, creative activities, sensory experiences, stories and outdoor play as a natural part of their day.

The programme keeps the class to a maximum of eight children, allowing teachers to pay close attention to individual personalities, routines and developmental stages.

English without the flashcards

The same philosophy applies to language.

At one or two years old, learning English does not mean memorising vocabulary lists. Children absorb language through relationships and repetition: hearing the same words during snack time, listening to songs, following simple instructions, sharing a picture book or hearing an adult describe what is happening during play.

Tiny Tots provides an English-language environment, giving children regular, natural exposure to the language throughout their day.

Catalina, who raises her own child in a multilingual family, sees communication as something that should grow out of connection rather than performance.

Toddlers often understand far more than they can say, she explains. What matters is creating a positive environment in which language is associated with people, experiences and emotions that make sense to the child.

Learning to do things “all by myself”

Anyone who lives with a toddler knows how powerful those words can be.

Between one and two, children increasingly want to try things independently — even when the result is a spoon on the floor, mismatched shoes or a task that takes considerably longer than if an adult simply did it for them.

Tiny Tots gives children safe opportunities to practise that emerging independence while knowing that an adult is close by when they need help.

The milestone may be eating more independently, choosing an activity, joining a group song, approaching another child or simply becoming comfortable enough to explore a new corner of the room.

For a toddler, these are significant achievements.

And independence does not mean pushing children away from adults. In fact, the opposite is often true: children are more willing to explore when they know they have a trusted person to return to.

A small community for Prague’s smallest residents

For international families in particular, early-years programmes can provide something else that is easy to overlook: a sense of community.

Many parents raising children in Prague live far from grandparents, siblings and the wider family network that might otherwise form part of everyday life.

A nurturing preschool environment can therefore become more than somewhere a child spends part of the day. Familiar teachers, other children and their families can gradually become part of the support network that makes a new city feel more like home.

Tiny Tots is based at Nessie English Preschool in Prague 5, in a quiet residential setting with its own garden. The programme combines experienced early-years teachers, personalised attention and structured routines with plenty of room for children simply to play, discover and be little.

Because at one or two years old, success does not need to look impressive.

Sometimes it is a child who cried at the door last week walking in happily today.

Sometimes it is making a first little friend.

Sometimes it is a new word, a messy painting, a favourite song or the confidence to let go of a teacher’s hand and go exploring alone.

Those tiny steps are exactly where the big journey begins.

Tiny Tots at Nessie English Preschool is designed for children aged 1–2 years. Families interested in the programme can arrange a visit to the Prague 5 campus to see the environment and meet the team.

Enrolment for the 2026/27 school year is now open.

World.title: Not Ready for Summer to End? 3 Places to Take the Kids Before August Ends
World.content:
The end of the summer holidays is in sight. While school supplies, pencil cases and sports shoes are already making their way onto shopping lists, there are still a few days of summer left to enjoy.

Before the September school routine kicks in, here are three ways to make the most of the final days of August with the family.



Letni Letna

When: 12–31 August

Where: Prague, Letenské sady

Letenské sady is taking on a new look until 31 August, transforming into a colourful festival village. The Letní Letná Festival isn’t just about evening acrobatics for adults. It also offers a programme for younger visitors called Letní Letná for Children.

From morning until late afternoon, the huge children’s tent comes alive with fairy-tale performances and other activities. Kids can take part in creative and juggling workshops, explore an interactive play area made from recycled materials or take a ride on the iconic hand-carved wooden carousel.

Most of the children’s activities take place under the festival tents, so an unexpected rain shower won’t disrupt the day.

The festival also offers a “Night Watch” childcare service for children aged four and up. Parents can enjoy the evening programme while experienced entertainers look after their children.

When: 24–29 August

Where: Liberec and the surrounding area

Fancy a trip beyond Prague at the end of August? Head north to Liberec from 24 to 29 August, when the city hosts Crystal Valley Week, a celebration of Czech glassmaking and jewellery.

This year’s theme focuses on the interconnection of cultures, with the Czech glass bead at the centre of the programme. Children can also enjoy a free ride aboard the special Crystal Tram, which has been decorated this year to resemble a long-distance train.

There are plenty of opportunities to make your own jewellery from glass beads, with workshops and craft sessions taking place throughout Liberec for both children and adults.

When: Sunday, 30 August, 11:00–19:00

Where: Prague, Ladronka Park

On the last Sunday of the summer holidays, skip cooking lunch and head to the F.O.O.D. Picnic in Prague’s Ladronka Park. The popular event returns for its 16th edition this year.

Entry to the festival grounds is free, with 120 food and farm stalls to explore, including food trucks. There is also a large children’s zone with games and creative workshops, as well as a raffle for younger visitors.

It’s a family-friendly way to spend the final Sunday of the holidays, combining food, activities and a relaxed atmosphere before the new school year begins.

World.title: Airbnb Accounts for 1 Percent of Prague’s Housing Stock, Analysis Finds
World.content:
Prague’s short-term rental market has grown into a professional business but Airbnb accounts for only a small share of the city’s housing stock, according to a new analysis.

In June 2026, around 7,878 entire apartments and houses in Prague were actively listed on Airbnb. With roughly 720,000 apartments across the capital, that represents about 1.1 percent of the total housing stock.

The situation is very different in individual parts of the city. In Prague 1, Airbnb-listed properties account for around one-fifth of all apartments, according to the Prague Institute of Planning and Development (IPR). In Prague 2, the share is around 7 percent, while in some outer districts it is below 0.5 percent.



The concentration of short-term rentals has also changed the nature of the market. IPR data show that hosts managed an average of two apartments in 2019. By 2024, that figure had risen to three, while more than half of Prague’s Airbnb listings were operated by hosts with at least five properties.

This means short-term accommodation is increasingly being run as a business rather than as occasional home-sharing.

Prague’s housing shortage is much larger

Despite the impact Airbnb can have in central neighborhoods, the analysis points to a much bigger problem behind Prague’s housing crisis — a long-term shortage of new construction.

Since 2006, Prague has accumulated a housing deficit of more than 91,000 apartments, according to the analysis. That shortfall is about 11.5 times larger than the number of apartments currently listed on Airbnb.

Even if every Airbnb property in the city were suddenly returned to the long-term rental market, Prague would still be short more than 83,000 homes.

The accumulated construction deficit reportedly became larger than the number of active Airbnb apartments around 2009 or 2010. Since then, the gap has continued to grow.

This suggests that Prague’s housing crisis began well before short-term rentals reached their current scale.

Tourism brings other concerns

Housing availability is also not the only issue surrounding short-term rentals.

Residents in central Prague have complained about noise, disruption and visitors staying in residential buildings.

The city also collects accommodation fees from short-term stays, although payment is not automatic because apartment owners must register and pay the fees themselves.

The debate over Airbnb in Prague therefore extends beyond housing. While short-term rentals can change the character of central neighborhoods and create problems for residents, the latest figures suggest that the city’s wider housing shortage is primarily the result of years of insufficient construction.

World.title: ASEAN Plus Three Film Festival Returns to Prague for Its Fifth Edition
World.content:
The ASEAN Committee in Prague (ACP), representing the embassies of ASEAN member states, together with the embassies of China, Japan and the Republic of Korea, will host the fifth edition of the ASEAN Plus Three Film Festival (APTFF).

The festival will begin on Monday, September 7, 2026, at the Municipal Library of Prague.

Organised in cooperation with the Municipal Library of Prague, the festival will run until September 14 and feature seven full-length films, alongside a curated selection of short films from across the ASEAN Plus Three region.



Since its launch in 2022, the APTFF has introduced Czech audiences to the diverse cultures and cinematic voices of ASEAN and its Plus Three partners.

Previous editions have featured acclaimed films including Escape from Mogadishu (Republic of Korea), Father and Son (Viet Nam) and Yuni (Indonesia).

This year’s programme includes Solata: Friends Are the Family We Choose (Indonesia), Babah (Malaysia), The Beginning (Myanmar), I’m Perfect (the Philippines), 4 Tigers (Thailand), Song of the South (Viet Nam) and One and Only (China).

A selection of short films will also be screened during the opening night on September 7.

The programme includes Mbiyodo/Communal Work (Indonesia), Ninavau (Malaysia), Myanmar Be Enchanted (Myanmar), Lola Loleng/Grandma Loleng (the Philippines), Give to Getters (Thailand), Welcome to Viet Nam (Viet Nam), My Chinese Ecological Notes (China), Pukkulapottas and Hours in the Forest (Japan), and Persona (Republic of Korea).

Beyond its cultural programme, the festival is part of a broader effort by ASEAN and its Plus Three partners to introduce Czech audiences to the region, its societies and creative industries, as well as its shared identity as a community of more than 690 million people.

All screenings are open to the public and free of charge. Films will be shown in their original languages with English and Czech subtitles.

The full programme and schedule are available on the Municipal Library of Prague website.

World.title: Hungarian pilgrim missing in Nepal following flash floods – photos, update: another Hungarian missing
World.content:
A Hungarian national is being sought after flash floods in Nepal, the Foreign Ministry told the Hungarian news agency MTI on Wednesday.

A Hungarian pilgrim was in the area hit by the flash floods, and efforts to establish their identity and whereabouts are still under way, the ministry said. According to Nepal’s tourism authority, at least 384 tourists – including 291 foreign nationals – have been reported missing.

Photo: Anadolu/Safal Prakash Shrestha

Nepal’s honorary consul said that a Hungarian pilgrim had been in the affected area. Consular officials are monitoring developments closely and remain in contact with the local authorities, the Foreign Ministry said.

Flash floods swept through several villages in north-eastern Nepal on Wednesday. Authorities said the disaster had claimed more than 50 lives and damaged roads, bridges and energy infrastructure in areas close to Tibet.

Update: 24.hu wrote that another Hungarian national is missing and it cannot be excluded that there are more missing Hungarians.

Photo: Anadolu/Safal Prakash Shrestha

Death toll in Nepal-China border flash floods climbs to 97, dozens missing

The death toll from a devastating flash flood on the Nepal-China border climbed to 97 as at least 384 tourists and travelers, as well as soldiers and police, were reported missing Wednesday in Nepal after flash floods and mudslides near the Chinese border, according to officials, Anadolu wrote.

Shailendra Thapa, a spokesperson for the Armed Police, said rescuers have recovered 97 dead bodies while 54 people were rescued from the flood-affected area. Earlier, briefing parliament on the disaster, Nepalese Foreign Minister Sishir Khanal said officials, soldiers and police were among the missing after flash floods swept away their barracks. The Nepal Tourism Board said separately that it recorded 384 missing people.

Photo: Anadolu/Safal Prakash Shrestha

Authorities “are working to verify the whereabouts and safety status of the tourists and travelers who were in or traveling through the affected areas,” said the board. Khanal said 29 police officers and 44 soldiers were also missing after the floods swept away their barracks in Rasuwa district.

At least 19 bridges have been swept away, and 40 kilometers (25 miles) of road were damaged, along with 13 hydropower projects, according to government estimates. About 200 trucks were also swept away. Khanal said an earthquake struck the border area Wednesday, triggering an avalanche that “eventually caused the collapse of glacial lakes in the Tibet region of China.”

Beijing identifies the region as the Xizang Autonomous Region. “Due to the flood, a large number of hydropower projects, government offices and road facilities were erased,” said Khanal. A magnitude 4.4 earthquake struck Kodari village in Nepal, which borders Tibet in China, at 8.37 am local time (0252GMT), according to the US Geological Survey.

Photo: Anadolu/Safal Prakash Shrestha

Hungarian firefighters and vehicles sent to Serbia to aid the battle against forest fires

Massive search and rescue operations were launched on both sides of the border. Those reported missing include people from Nepal, India, the UK, South Africa, Australia and the Netherlands, while the nationalities of many others have yet to be confirmed.

Eight South Korean nationals were “unaccounted for,” while 10 others were stranded following the floods in Nepal, Seoul-based Yonhap News reported, citing the South Korean Foreign Ministry. Khanal said the floods caused widespread destruction in the Rasuwa, Dhading and Chitwan districts.

World.title: Tashkent International Media Forum brings global journalists together in 2026
World.content:
The main Tashkent sessions of the Tashkent International Media Forum (August 24-25, 2026) concluded on Wednesday after bringing together hundreds of journalists, media executives, filmmakers, researchers and digital specialists from around the world to discuss how the heritage of Islamic civilisation can be presented to modern global audiences. Daily News Hungary was also present at the event, reporting directly from Tashkent.

Held under the title Islamic Civilization: A New Perspective – New Discoveries, the forum brought together around 200 media representatives and experts from nearly 46 countries. Its main events in the Uzbek capital were hosted by the Center for Islamic Civilization in Uzbekistan, one of the country’s most ambitious new cultural institutions.

Tashkent International Media Forum focuses on a new way of telling history

Across the professional sessions in Tashkent, one theme returned repeatedly: preserving history is no longer enough. The challenge is also to make that history accessible and relevant to generations that increasingly encounter the world through smartphones, streaming platforms, social media and artificial intelligence.

The programme therefore went far beyond traditional discussions of museums and historical research. Participants examined documentary filmmaking, publishing, digital storytelling, artificial intelligence and immersive technologies, as well as new international media projects capable of bringing the intellectual, scientific and cultural achievements of Islamic civilisation to a wider audience.

The final sessions on Wednesday also addressed the media’s role in overcoming stereotypes, hate speech and Islamophobia, while stressing the importance of professional standards and objective reporting when dealing with cultural and religious issues. Participants discussed how heritage can connect different eras and how Uzbekistan can present its civilisational legacy through contemporary media.

Uzbek presidential press secretary highlights journalism’s core values

At the opening session, Sherzod Asadov, Press Secretary to the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan, addressed some of the most important challenges facing journalism today. His remarks focused on the rapidly changing information landscape, the growing role of artificial intelligence, the responsibility of journalists and the importance of presenting Uzbekistan’s rich historical heritage to international audiences.

Asadov stressed that technological change should not weaken the fundamental standards of the profession.

Press Secretary Asadov at Tashkent International Media Forum 2026

“No matter how much technology changes, the fundamental principles of journalism will remain truth, impartiality, integrity, and the interests of people,” the Presidential Press Secretary said.

He also highlighted the broader role of domestic media in the relationship between citizens and public institutions.

“National media, serving as a bridge between the state and society, is an important force that contributes to our country’s development, protects human rights, and brings our future achievements to the attention of the world,” he said.

If you missed it: Tashkent International Investment Forum 2026 opens with major investor pledges from Uzbekistan

Uzbekistan puts cultural heritage at the centre of its international image

For foreign participants, the forum also offered a closer look at the way Uzbekistan is increasingly using its historical and cultural heritage as part of the country’s international profile.

Central Asia was home to some of the Islamic world’s most influential scholars, scientists and thinkers, while cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara occupied key positions in the intellectual and commercial networks of the Silk Road. Uzbekistan is now seeking to make this legacy more accessible to international audiences through museums, research, digital technology and global media cooperation.

The Center for Islamic Civilization is central to this effort. The institution combines manuscripts and historical artefacts with interactive exhibitions and modern technologies, while also seeking partnerships with international media organisations, filmmakers and publishers.

Hungary represented at the Tashkent International Media Forum

The forum program included representatives from CNN International Commercial, Euronews, BBC Studios, TRT World, Oman TV, Oman Observer, Tunisia’s TAP news agency, Yemen’s Saba news agency, and other international media outlets.

Hungary was represented at the Tashkent International Media Forum by Alpár Kató, owner of Daily News Hungary, who participated in the professional events and discussions in the Uzbek capital. His attendance also provided an opportunity to strengthen media and professional connections between Hungary and Uzbekistan.

Alpar Kató, owner of Daily News Hungary at Tashkent International Media Forum

During his stay in Tashkent, Kató also delivered a presentation at Tashkent International University on Wednesday. His programme in Uzbekistan includes a number of business meetings aimed at developing new professional and commercial contacts alongside his participation in the international media gathering.

Kató has previously spoken publicly about Uzbekistan’s transformation and the development of Hungarian-Uzbek relations. In a recent interview with Uzbekistan’s Dunyo Information Agency, he highlighted the country’s greater openness to the outside world, economic liberalisation and expanding international cooperation.

Media cooperation expected to continue beyond Tashkent

The forum has been presented by its organisers not simply as a one-off conference, but as a platform for longer-term professional cooperation.

Asadov said the organisers viewed the gathering as the beginning of lasting dialogue between media professionals and institutions. He said the discussions and initiatives launched during the forum could help bring Uzbekistan’s civilisational heritage into the global information space.

The wider programme extends beyond the main professional sessions in Tashkent and also includes activities linked to Uzbekistan’s historical and cultural heritage, including events in Samarkand.

For the journalists and media professionals gathered in Uzbekistan, however, the central question raised by the Tashkent International Media Forum will remain relevant long after the event itself: how can rapidly changing technologies be used to reach new audiences without losing accuracy, context and the fundamental principles of journalism?

The message emerging from Tashkent was that heritage and innovation do not have to compete. Used responsibly, modern media and new technologies can instead offer new ways to bring centuries of history to a global audience.

World.title: Wizz Air sets sights on expansion – and ‘taking over’ Romania – but receives blunt rebuke from Romanian carrier
World.content:
Wizz Air is currently the largest airline in the Romanian market, but it wants to grow further. It has offered to take over the international routes operated by Romania’s state-owned carrier and, following negotiations, could even operate its domestic services in return. Tarom has now delivered a sharp response, while in Hungary the country’s “national airline” is also planning to expand – although the details remain unclear.

Romanian airline ‘not viable’, Wizz Air four times larger

József Váradi, the chief executive of Hungarian low-cost airline Wizz Air, told the Romanian news site HotNews that national airlines were not worth maintaining. He also made highly critical remarks about Malév, Hungary’s former flag carrier, and Tarom. Váradi, who was Malév’s chief executive before its collapse, argued that the market would replace any services lost in the absence of a national airline.

Maintaining such carriers merely turned them into “black holes for public money”, he said, as had happened with Malév and was still happening with Tarom.

Wizz Air CEO József Váradi. Photo: wizzair.com

Váradi said Wizz Air would be happy to take over Tarom’s international network, which is used by millions of Romanians travelling abroad to work for higher wages. Statistics suggest that as many as a quarter of Romania’s adult population may work abroad – roughly 4 million to 5 million people. There is therefore a huge market for air travel among Romanians commuting overseas.

As the state-owned airline also operates domestic services, Váradi said Wizz Air could provide those as well under a long-term agreement. He described Tarom as economically unviable and dependent on continuous state support, while claiming that Wizz Air was already four times larger in the Romanian market, according to Transtelex.

Wizz Air has operated in Romania for 20 years. From 14 airports, it runs 231 routes linking 83 destinations in 26 countries. In the autumn, it will open a tenth Romanian base in Brașov, adding to its existing nine, and employs more than 1,900 people in the country.

Váradi said the domestic model was already operating in Italy, while similar plans had been announced in Spain. He therefore believed there was potential for Wizz Air to pursue the same approach in Romania.

Boarding of a Wizz Air plane at Budapest Airport. Photo: Daily News Hungary

Tarom hits back

Tarom described Wizz Air’s proposal as “unrealistic and unserious”, while pointing out that the Hungarian discount airline had cancelled a number of Romanian routes in recent years.

The Romanian carrier warned that the withdrawal of a state-owned airline did not guarantee that the market would automatically replace the lost capacity. Several Romanian cities could, it argued, permanently lose their air links.

Central Romania’s charming Rozsnyó/Rasnov. Photo: depositphotos.com

Expansion also under discussion in Hungary

A different form of co-operation is taking shape in Hungary. Dávid Vitézy, the Minister for Transport and Investment, recently held talks with Váradi about further development by Wizz Air in Budapest and Debrecen, new air links and an expansion of the carrier’s Budapest base.

If you missed: Wizz Air launches brand new service in Budapest

The airline is open to new investment in both cities, while the Government has promised a predictable regulatory and airport environment. No further details have yet been disclosed.

The Cabinet has, however, imposed one clear condition: Wizz Air must comply with strict rules governing night flights. This is particularly contentious in Budapest, where residents in several districts have complained that heavy air traffic is disturbing their sleep.

The ministry and the airline are also to establish a joint working group tasked with reducing night-time pressure on the airspace around the capital. The Government says that, as air traffic expands, the peace and quiet of people living near the airport must also be protected.

Budget flights are getting expensive: How Ryanair and Wizz Air make money from hidden extras

World.title: Breaking: Huge explosion in Mohács facility, multiple workers died
World.content:
Two workers were killed in a fire that followed a huge explosion at a site in Mohács on Tuesday, prompting police to launch an investigation into negligent endangerment committed in the course of employment resulting in death, the Baranya County Police Headquarters said on Wednesday afternoon on the police.hu website.

Police said they received a report on Tuesday afternoon that an explosion had occurred in a wood-storage facility at an industrial site in Mohács. Powdered wood material, believed to have been near the base of the fuel-supply system, caught fire and sent flames 15 metres into the air, police.hu wrote.

Three workers caught in the path of the blaze suffered serious, life-threatening injuries. Two of them died after being taken to hospital, while doctors were still fighting to save the life of the third, police said.

Officers have launched criminal proceedings, with the assistance of experts and the occupational safety authority, to establish the precise circumstances of the workplace accident. The investigation is being conducted on suspicion of negligent endangerment committed in the course of employment resulting in death, according to the statement.
