World.title: ‘We pray together’: Georgian and Russian Orthodox churches to exchange hundreds of icons
World.content:
The Georgian diaspora in Russia has announced the launch of the “We Pray Together” project, which will involve creating hundreds of icons and exchanging them between the Orthodox churches of Georgia and Russia.

The icons created as part of the project will depict Saint Gabriel and Saint Seraphim of Sarov. The organisers say the icons will share the title “Friendship of the Peoples of Russia and Georgia”.

According to the Federal Georgian National-Cultural Autonomy in Russia (FGNCA), the first batch of icons has already been painted in Georgia and is ready to be handed over to the Russian Orthodox Church.

In a statement, the FGNCA said the project would “serve as a major civilisational response to the challenges of our time” and bring the peoples of Russia and Georgia closer through their shared faith and centuries-old traditions.

The head of the Georgian diaspora in Russia, David Tsetskhladze, described the project as “one of the largest Orthodox initiatives” in the history of Russian-Georgian relations.

“We are not simply exchanging gifts. We are bringing together the patron saints of our peoples to show that spiritual kinship is stronger than any political circumstances. The exchange of hundreds of Orthodox icons will create a historic precedent,” Tsetskhladze said.

The idea of creating the icons came from a group of volunteers led by journalist and filmmaker Konstantin Tsertsvadze.

The statement also says that the initiative received the blessing of the late Catholicos-Patriarch of All Georgia Ilia II in 2018.

Georgia-Russia icon exchange

World.title: Tourism support package: Can Azerbaijan reach its target of 3.8 million visitors?
World.content:
State support for tourism in Azerbaijan

A new state programme, approved by a decree from President Ilham Aliyev, sets out plans to develop the tourism sector in the coming years, attract more foreign visitors and expand tourism beyond Baku.

The programme comes into force as the tourism sector faces declining figures. In the first half of 2026, 1.09 million foreigners and stateless people arrived in Azerbaijan. This was 10.3% fewer than in the same period last year. Arrivals from the Gulf countries fell by 31.4%, while hotel stays declined by 8.3% and hotel revenues by 3.8%.

Target for 2030: 3.8 million tourists

Under the State Programme, the value added generated by industries directly linked to tourism — in other words, the sector’s actual contribution to the economy — should rise from 6.96 billion manats (about $4.1 billion) in 2025 to 8.51 billion manats in 2027 and 12.17 billion manats (about $7.2 billion) in 2030.

The programme targets real growth of around 40% in the tourism sector by 2030. “Real growth” means an actual increase in the volume of production and services, rather than a nominal rise caused by higher prices.

The government plans to increase the number of foreign arrivals from 2.57 million in 2025 to 3.8 million by 2030.

The target for 2026 is 2.42 million arrivals. Given the 10.3% decline recorded in the first half of the year, the figures will need to improve significantly in the second half to meet this target.

Competition is also intensifying. Azerbaijan ranks 56th among 119 countries in the World Economic Forum’s 2024 Travel and Tourism Development Index. Georgia ranks 45th, Kazakhstan 52nd and Uzbekistan 78th.

In 2025, Georgia reported 5.5 million tourist trips, Uzbekistan 11.7 million foreign tourists and Kazakhstan 15.7 million foreign visitors. The countries use different methods to count tourists and visitors, so these figures cannot be compared directly. Nevertheless, they show that Azerbaijan’s tourism sector faces strong regional competition.

Subsidies, new flights and easier visa rules

The programme provides for extensive government support. Authorities plan to offer subsidies to local tour operators that bring tourists to Azerbaijan, as well as to micro and small businesses operating in the tourism sector.

The measures also include partial compensation for charter flight costs, incentives to open additional scheduled flights to Azerbaijan from priority markets, and financial support for concerts and other entertainment events.

Another area concerns easier entry into the country. The programme provides for expanding visa-free access to citizens of 34 target markets, widening access to e-visas and introducing a “digital nomad” visa in 2027-2028. It will target people who work remotely and want to live in another country for an extended period.

The plan also calls for the development of regional tourism zones, walking routes, health tourism and gastronomic tourism. These measures could help reduce Azerbaijan’s tourism sector’s dependence on Baku, expensive hotels and major international events.

A 2026 World Bank analysis also highlights shortcomings in transport links, accommodation infrastructure, local tour operators and the quality of services in the regions.

At least on paper, therefore, the programme correctly identifies many of the sector’s existing problems.

The problem is not just a lack of subsidies

The key question is whether government support alone can make Azerbaijan a more affordable and competitive tourist destination.

The State Programme itself also highlights the high concentration of the air travel market, meaning that a relatively small number of companies provide most of the services. It also points to limited hotel supply, high prices, and problems with hygiene and service quality.

At the same time, budget airlines have expanded their presence in Baku compared with previous years. In July, Heydar Aliyev International Airport said that around 20 low-cost and hybrid airlines operated flights from Baku to more than 20 international destinations.

The problem can therefore no longer be reduced to the claim that “Azerbaijan has no budget airlines”. Other questions have become more important: how frequently do these airlines operate, which cities do they serve, and does competition between airlines actually affect ticket prices?

The position of major business groups in the tourism and hotel markets also matters in this context.

According to publicly available information from PAŞA Holding, whose shareholders include the president’s father-in-law and daughters, its wholly owned subsidiary Absheron Hotel Group operates hotels including Four Seasons Baku, JW Marriott Absheron and Ritz-Carlton Baku. Another group company, PAŞA Travel, brings tourists to the country, books hotels and provides transport services.

This means that companies belonging to the same business group operate at different stages of the tourism chain. Economists call this model “vertical integration”.

Vertical integration is not in itself illegal or necessarily harmful. However, even without complete public data on market shares, an important question remains: what rules will govern the distribution of subsidies among companies of different sizes?

The main question is this: will government support help new and small companies enter the market, or will it mainly benefit companies that already have significant resources?

Who will receive the money, and for what?

Under the presidential decree, the Cabinet of Ministers must develop rules for awarding subsidies within three months. So although the programme has already been approved, one key question remains unanswered: which companies will receive public funds, according to what criteria and in return for what results?

The Centre for Analysis of Economic Reforms and Communication has been tasked with monitoring and evaluating the programme.

However, effective oversight will depend not only on which institution is responsible for it. It will also depend on how accessible information is to the public about the companies receiving subsidies, the amounts they receive and the results they achieve.

Previous audits of other government support programmes by the Chamber of Accounts have identified problems such as insufficient justification for spending on individual projects and a lack of data needed to assess their results. These findings do not directly concern the tourism programme, but they highlight the importance of building the new subsidy mechanism around clear and measurable criteria from the outset.х.

A tourist’s decision is not based on price alone

Entry requirements also directly affect the competitiveness of the tourism sector.

At present, travellers can enter Azerbaijan by air, while crossing the land border remains largely restricted and subject to special rules. Since 25 May, exceptions have applied to rail travel with Georgia for Azerbaijani citizens and some foreign nationals who can enter the country without a visa.

The country’s overall reputation also affects tourists’ choices. The UK Foreign Office generally considers crime levels in Baku to be low, but notes that there are occasional reports of foreign nationals being asked for unofficial payments.

In Reporters Without Borders’ 2026 World Press Freedom Index, Azerbaijan ranks 171st out of 180 countries. In Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, it ranks 130th out of 182 countries.

These rankings do not directly determine whether tourists will visit Azerbaijan. However, they form part of the broader picture that shapes international perceptions of the country, assessments of the predictability of its legal and business environment, and investors’ perceptions of risk.

State support for tourism in Azerbaijan

World.title: Azerbaijan confiscates cryptocurrency in favour of state for first time
World.content:
Cryptocurrency confiscated in Azerbaijan

The Yasamal District Court in Baku has sentenced two people arrested by the State Security Service, B.H.R. and I.R.F., and ordered the confiscation by the state of virtual assets identified as the proceeds or subject of the crime.

Details of the case

The defendants were found guilty under Article 206-1.3 of the Criminal Code. The article provides for criminal liability for organising the illegal covert transfer of particularly large sums of money out of Azerbaijan or into the country using set-offs and other forms of settlement.

According to the court’s ruling:

B.H.R. received a two-year-and-five-month restriction of liberty and a fine of 3,623,568 manats (about $2.13 million);

received a two-year-and-five-month restriction of liberty and a fine of (about $2.13 million); I.R.F. received a three-year restriction of liberty and a fine of 31,399,709 manats (about $18.47 million).

The court also ordered the state to confiscate 830 units of cryptocurrency held in an account on the international virtual-asset platform Binance. Investigators had frozen the assets during the preliminary investigation.

Official reports do not specify which cryptocurrency was involved, whether Bitcoin, Ethereum or another asset.

Legal basis

Under Article 99-1 of the Criminal Code, special confiscation involves the compulsory and free transfer to the state of tools and means used to commit a crime, as well as property obtained through criminal activity.

The Law on Combating the Legalisation of Property Obtained through Crime and the Financing of Terrorism also classifies virtual assets as property obtained through criminal activity.

The court has therefore applied the same legal regime to digital assets as it does to physical property for the first time in practice.

Context and significance

In 2025, the State Security Service had already secured a court order to freeze cryptocurrency in a similar criminal case. At the time, Baku’s Sabail District Court ordered the assets to be frozen. On 24 August, the process moved to the next stage: the authorities confiscated the assets.

Azerbaijan does not yet have a separate law governing virtual assets. The Central Bank previously said it expected the relevant draft law to be adopted by the end of 2026. Against this backdrop, the court ruling shows how authorities are addressing the existing legal gap in practice and could set a precedent for future regulation.

Experts note that international exchanges generally comply with court orders promptly. However, the authorities have not yet disclosed what will happen to the confiscated assets, including whether they could be sold at auction, transferred to state reserves or used in another way.

The case marks a new stage in Azerbaijan’s fight against digital crime and expands law enforcement agencies’ ability to track and confiscate virtual assets. At the same time, it highlights the real risks faced by people operating in the unregulated cryptocurrency market.

Cryptocurrency confiscated in Azerbaijan

World.title: Is Georgia expecting a new wave of migrants from Russia?
World.content:
Upper Lars checkpoint, 2022. Photo: Mediazona

While rumours of a possible mobilisation circulate in Russia, Georgia is bracing for a new wave of Russian migrants. However, current data from the Upper Lars checkpoint on the Russian-Georgian border do not yet indicate a mass exodus from Russia.

In mid-August, Russia’s Customs Service said that Upper Lars had seen a “record flow” of travellers. The agency said more than 20,000 people crossed the border in passenger cars on 18 August.

Georgia’s Interior Ministry disputed the Russian figures. According to its data, 7,880 citizens of various countries entered Georgia from Russia between 8 and 19 August, while 8,406 people left Georgia for Russia. In total, 16,286 people crossed the border in both directions.

Russia’s customs authorities later clarified their figures, also saying that more than 16,000 people had crossed the border in both directions. This time, however, they did not describe the figure as “record-breaking”. They noted that more people were travelling towards Russia as the tourist season came to an end.

The figures nevertheless caused concern in Georgia. Many people remembered September 2022, when tens of thousands of Russians entered Georgia after Moscow announced a partial mobilisation.

That large influx drove up property prices significantly. Many people in Georgia now fear that the situation could happen again.

Why are people expecting a new wave of migrants?

Reports of a new mobilisation in Russia remain unconfirmed, but they are spreading widely. The reports claim that mobilisation could be announced after September’s State Duma elections. The Russian authorities have made no official statements to that effect.

Nikoloz Urushadze, managing partner at the consulting company G. Miller International Georgia, says that even these rumours could prompt some Russian citizens to leave the country.

“Even if Russia ultimately does not announce mobilisation, the expectation of it still affects people. They are afraid, and fear is often a powerful factor driving people to move,” he told BusinessPressNews.

Urushadze believes Georgia remains one of the most accessible destinations for Russian citizens and could face a new influx of migrants if Russia announces mobilisation.

The experience of 2022

In September 2022, immediately after Russia announced its partial mobilisation, the queue at the Upper Lars checkpoint stretched for 20-30 kilometres on the Russian side. Around 5,500 cars were waiting at the border. Authorities even set up a mobile military recruitment office in North Ossetia, where the checkpoint is located.

According to Georgia’s then-interior minister, Vakhtang Gomelauri, around 10,000 people crossed the border each day. Before the mobilisation announcement, the figure stood at about 6,000.

As a result of the influx, around 100,000 Russian citizens lived in Georgia for a period. Some local residents called on the authorities to introduce a visa regime for Russian citizens.

How could a new influx affect property prices in Georgia?

According to Nikoloz Urushadze, a new wave of Russian migrants would primarily affect the property market. Increased demand would push up rental prices again. Georgia experienced this in 2022-2023, when the arrival of large numbers of Russian citizens sharply increased rental costs in Tbilisi and Batumi.

Russian citizens, along with Ukrainians and Belarusians, are also actively buying property in Georgia. In the first half of 2026, they accounted for 18% of all buyers. A year earlier, their share stood at 13%. During the same period, the share of Georgian citizens among apartment buyers in the resort city of Batumi fell from 43% to 33%.

Urushadze points to another problem. In his view, some Russian citizens do not integrate into local society and the economy. Instead, they create their own closed infrastructure.

“Georgia is a country where 300,000 Russians could come and create a little Russia here, with their own schools and universities. They would not need the Georgian language or anything else at all,” he says.

At this stage, the situation on the Russian-Georgian border does not resemble the mass exodus of 2022. The queues in August were mainly linked to the tourist season and a temporary border closure due to bad weather. Many people were leaving Georgia rather than entering it, returning to Russia.

The real scale of any new influx will become clearer later. The decisive factor will be whether the Russian leadership officially announces mobilisation.

Russian migrants in Georgia

World.title: ‘Ice cream’ and cold showers: Keeping cool on hot days at Tbilisi Zoo. Video
World.content:
As summer temperatures rise, Tbilisi Zoo switches to a special routine. The keepers’ main task is to help the animals cope with the heat and protect them from overheating.

A range of measures is used, from cooling the enclosures to providing special diets. The first and most important rule is to ensure that all the animals have a constant supply of clean, cool drinking water.

The water is refreshed several times a day, while keepers provide additional ways for the animals to cool down in their enclosures when needed. One method is to spray the enclosures with water. Zoo staff regularly hose down the floors and surrounding areas to maintain humidity and lower the temperature.

Large animals require particular attention. For elephants, for example, water treatments are a real treat. Keepers hose them down all over their bodies, helping them cool off quickly.

The zoo also creates mud wallows specifically for the elephants and the rhinoceros. As the mud dries on the animals’ skin, it forms a protective layer against strong sunlight, possible sunburn and insects. The layer also helps keep their bodies cool.

Summer heat also affects the animals’ daily care. Keepers adjust feeding methods so that the animals receive both physical and mental stimulation. Seasonal juicy fruits are added to their diets, providing another way to help them cool down.

For primates and herbivores, keepers freeze fruit and vegetables. For the animals, this is a kind of “ice cream”, but it serves more than just a cooling purpose. The animals have to make an effort to get to the frozen food, providing both physical and mental stimulation. It also allows them to display natural behaviour.

The same principle applies to predators, for which keepers freeze meat. “Meat ice cream” helps lions and tigers cool down while also providing sensory enrichment.

It is also important that the doors to indoor enclosures, where temperatures are lower and it is cooler, remain open at all times. This allows the animals to choose where they want to stay.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

The heat at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: South Ossetia residents name region’s main problems ahead of presidential election
World.content:
South Ossetia presidential election

South Ossetia election. Illustration created by Caucasian Knot using AI

A report by Caucasian Knot

Population decline, low wages, unemployment, queues at the customs checkpoint and poor public transport. Residents of South Ossetia named these as the main problems ahead of the snap presidential election.

Murad Valiev, Kazbek Kodoev, Marat Kambolov and Zurab Kokoev have been cleared to stand in the election. The Central Election Commission plans to print 40,000 ballot papers. Khokh Chochiev, leader of the Iry Farn party, who was denied registration, called the election a sham.

On 23 August, a Caucasian Knot correspondent spoke to residents of the region. The survey is not representative and reflects individual views.

“There is no trust left in anyone”

Fatima, 45, works as a kindergarten teacher in Tskhinval. She sees the lack of jobs as the main reason people are leaving the region.

“Young people mostly leave because of this. Graduates of Russian universities return home but cannot find work. If jobs become available here, they will come back,” she says.

Fatima also wants to see higher wages. She says incomes remain low while prices continue to rise. She also names queues at the customs checkpoint as another major problem.

“They said the situation improved after Kambolov visited the customs checkpoint. But there are still queues. I am not following the campaign. There is no trust left in anyone. I have not come across any campaigning either,” she said.

Karina, 23, is unemployed and lives in Dzau. She lists wages, unemployment, environmental problems and the state of agriculture among the region’s main challenges.

Public transport is a particular concern for her. The last bus leaves Dzau at 17:00, while the last bus from Tskhinval leaves at 18:00.

“I would like buses to run at least until eight or nine in the evening. I do not have a car and cannot afford to buy one. It is also practically impossible to get a loan or mortgage in South Ossetia,” Karina says.

In her view, unless these problems are addressed, the population decline will become irreversible.

“I am used to Russia’s authorities making all the decisions”

Karina is not following the election campaign and believes the outcome has already been decided.

“I am used to Russia’s authorities making all the decisions. They would benefit from making Kambolov president. The election is just window dressing. People have not had a choice for a long time,” she said.

Karina says she has not seen campaign posters or activists in Dzau or Tskhinval.

World.title: Bookstores struggle to fill shelves after cyber attack on major publisher
World.content:
A cyber attack on one of the country's major publishing distributors has left bookshops and authors struggling to fill their shelves in the lead-up to their busiest trading period.

Hachette Australia said unauthorised activity on the computer systems of its distribution subsidiary, Alliance Distribution Services (ADS), was believed to have occurred on July 18.

The incident has severely disrupted the distribution of titles by Hachette's authors across Australia, with independent bookstores unable to fill shelves as they prepare to order stock leading up to its high-demand Christmas period.

Jaye Chin-Dusting, who is owner of Mary Martin Bookshop in Melbourne, first noticed there was a problem when books published by Hachette stopped arriving.

Jaye Chin-Dusting says new release titles have been prioritised by ADS, but supply of books already released remains limited. (ABC News: Ethan White)

"ADS would supply us 15 to 20 per cent of the books that we usually have on our shelves," she said.

"In the first couple of weeks, I think we weren't really sure what was going on.

"Certainly, books weren't arriving."

Authors left empty-handed

Children's author Danielle Binks' plans to Adelaide next month to visit schools and launch her new book, Shakespeare in the Orchard, have been thrown in doubt.

"Normally when I do any interstate visits, I'll pop into bookstores and sign copies of my book," said the Melbourne author, who publishes titles with Hachette.

"I've been told I can't for this September trip, obviously because Hachette has no way of knowing who has stock and can't supply them with more at the moment."

Danielle Binks says a planned trip to Adelaide, including presentations to school students, is in doubt without a guaranteed supply of copies of her new book. (Supplied)

Binks said the incident had affected the entire Australian publishing industry.

"My publicists and sales team at Hachette are equally gutted that they can't do their jobs to their full extent," she said.

The incident was brought to wider attention by Melbourne author Maxine Beneba Clarke, who took to social media last week sharing her experience.

"For me, this will mean the loss of a large part of my income, possibly for years, and the loss of thousands of young authors," she wrote on Instagram last week.

" My heart is broken. "

Melbourne writer Maxine Beneba Clarke brought the cyber attack to public attention. (ABC Arts: Leah Jing McIntosh )

A communication breakdown

In a statement, Hachette Australia told the ABC it was continuing to restore systems and services, following "unauthorised activity" in ADS computer systems.

"We know this has been frustrating for our authors, booksellers, readers and people, and we are sorry for the impact it has had," a spokesperson said.

Hachette, who owns Alliance Distribution Services, says it is working to ensure commitments around events are delivered where possible. (Supplied: Alliance Distribution Services)

The company said while progress is being made, it is not yet in a position to confirm a timeline for a full return to normal operations.

"Restoring full operations securely remains our top priority, and we are grateful for the patience and support of everyone across the industry while we work through this."

Ms Chin-Dusting said it had been six weeks since supply issues began, slowing down the quantity of stock her business was able to purchase.

"ADS has been pretty good at nevertheless manually pushing out the new releases. So it's the backlists — books that have been out for a little bit — that are more difficult to get," she explained.

" If it goes on for much longer, our bookshop will need to start obviously having to look at other options. "

Jaye Chin-Dusting says major book retailers can afford alternative options, leaving smaller independent stores like her own vulnerable. (ABC News: Ethan White)

Ms Chin-Dusting said in the meantime, Hachette has suggested booksellers source stock through other means, including purchasing them from the online retailer Booktopia or international suppliers.

"Of course, that then increases the cost of the book because of the freight that comes through."

Authors and booksellers who spoke to the ABC made it clear they valued the relationship with Hachette, but expressed concern at a lack of clarity from the publisher.

Book Week quiz: How well do you know Aussie kids' books? Celebrate Children's Book Week with our kids' books quiz — and grab some costume ideas at the same time.

"I think the problem for us is that we don't know how long this will go for, so it's a bit difficult to manage the expectations of customers," Ms Chin-Dusting said.

"Communication has been a little bit of a challenge."

Binks agreed that she stands by and fully supports Hachette, but that the publisher has left its clients in the dark.

"Part of me wishes that there had been more transparency," she said.

"If there had been more openness, Hachette may have received some genuine goodwill from the publishing community who knows exactly how it feels when disaster outside of your control strikes."

Cyber safety expert warns of more attacks

Director of RMIT University's Centre for Cyber Security Research and Innovation Matthew Warren hypothesised one of the possible causes of the incident was a ransomware attack.

He said this occurs when hackers exploit vulnerabilities in technology systems through malware, before contacting the organisation to demand payment to stop the attack.

"The other scenario is that the actual supply chain was the aim of the attack, which was really to disrupt the entire operations," he said.

"I imagine it may be more to do with a ransomware attack that has locked down their book distribution system at their main warehouse and they're literally trying to find alternate ways to distribute books."

Matthew Warren is concerned about the rise of ransomware cyber attacks. (Supplied: Matthew Warren)

Professor Warren said with the rise of artificial intelligence, cyber attacks are likely to become more common.

"We talk about cyber attacks as vulnerabilities in systems, and AI can identify those vulnerabilities more quickly," he said.

" You're certainly going to see an increase in these cyber incidents as these cyber attackers start to work out how to use AI to help them with their criminal activities. "

He said it is critical for businesses to maintain investment in cyber security to reduce the risk of future attacks.

"It's really a responsibility that organisations have to undertake and own themselves."

Authors ask for patience

For Danielle Binks, she remains optimistic and is asking readers to be patient while continuing to support local bookstores.

"I encourage people to buy from independent booksellers, because that's investment directly back into your local community," she said.

"Part of that human investment into small business means accepting imperfect scenarios just like this one, which require very empathetic patience and kindness, in response to events entirely beyond our control."

Danielle Binks's latest book, Shakespeare in the Orchard, had an early release last month. (Supplied)

Jaye Chin-Dusting is a little more concerned, worried that sufficient stock of Rebecca Yarros's new title Threshing Day being released in September, won't be available.

"There's a global release on that, so the expectation by our customers would be that we get it when it's possible," she said.

"They've got another month to get it sorted, otherwise it will really impact Hachette authors and booksellers."

World.title: Show families 'weigh up' whether circuits are viable amid cost squeeze
World.content:
Sideshow alley business owner Melissa Quay travels to Queensland from her home in Victoria each year with an entourage of balloons, prizes and games.

Usually Ms Quay would bring a caravan for the show circuit, but fuel costs and insurance premiums meant this year she had to leave it — and her daughter — behind.

For her "whole life", Melissa Quay has made the annual trip to Queensland for the show circuit. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

"We've spent the last four weeks and probably the next four weeks living in a truck [instead] of living in a caravan to combat the cost."

From food trucks to carnival rides, sideshow alley is an annual drawcard for the hundreds of Australians in show business.

But a triple threat of high fuel, expensive insurance and staff shortages means many operators are having to make difficult decisions.

" We normally run out and do a few little shows, but now we're weighing up whether it's viable for us to do that. "

Absorb insurance, fuel costs 'somehow'

In Ms Quay's family, the show circuit has been a multi-generational business.

Her "dad came out here before me" and "his dad came out here" before that, she said.

But the increased costs were worrying.

She said public liability insurance increased fivefold since 2020 and at one point she could not obtain any coverage at all.

"It went from being around $10,000 a year to $52,000 a year," she said.

The sideshow alley operator made staff cutbacks from three to two "just to limit our other expenses" and absorb the costs.

The Showmen's Guild of Australasia said show business had become "very challenging" particularly for those who racked up around 15,000 kilometres every year on remote circuits.

Chase Lovell is working and having fun with his family at the Charleville Show. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

"The circuit that went from Darwin and back, right through the Northern Territory, was very challenging," president Aaron Pink said.

"There's not a lot of shows in that run … and it's a long way back [home]."

But Mr Pink said he was hopeful operators would still go to smaller shows, even if it became difficult to afford.

"A show movement out in western Queensland and western New South Wales is something young families really look forward to," he said.

Recruiting staff is 'hard'

Darrell Brown alongside his pop-a-balloon stall. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

Darrell Brown, who has been running a bust-a-balloon game, said he has been in the travelling show business his entire life.

"Staff's a hard thing, mate," Mr Brown said.

"Once upon a time, in the late '90s and that, people have been coming down looking for work all the time.

" Now you ask people if you want a job, '[They say] 'nahh, we don't want a job'. "

Mr Brown said his children had graduated school and were helping "at the moment", but his brother who operates the "big machines" had struggled to find staff.

"There's only him and his wife, so he can't climb up and down the big Ferris wheel, and do all that.

"He needs some guys to help him."

Show must go on, says next gen

At a fishing stall, Chase Lovell, 9, demonstrated how to catch plastic ducks.

"There's $20 for seven ducks and then there's $10 for three," he explained.

"Depending on which duck you get, there's a number on the bottom and we count up the numbers to how many ducks you got.

"Whatever the numbers add up to, you get a prize."

The Lovell kids have been to Charleville, Longreach, Winton, Darwin and Mount Isa this year. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

Chase and his sister Peyton are seventh-generation show kids but enjoy their role in the family business.

"I like to follow all my family, and do everything my family does," Peyton Lovell said.

" You do have to put it up and put it down, but the most fun is to work it. "

That enthusiasm has continued after high school for fifth-generation show person Jayden Fraser.

Mr Fraser, 20, said he has "had other jobs in the past" but preferred the travelling lifestyle of show business.

"I just love to travel, I love to drive around Australia," he said.

Fifth-generation show person, Jayden Fraser, is keen to stay on the show circuit. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

"It is getting harder for a lot of us [and] the fuel costs are bit how-you-going.

" I don't know what the future holds, but hopefully everything still works out and the shows still stick around. "

World.title: One dead, two injured after three cyclists hit in Canberra's north
World.content:
A person has died and two others have been seriously injured after a crash in Canberra's north this morning.

ACT Policing said a car hit three cyclists on Gungahlin Drive in Palmerston about 6:30am.

The crash occurred just south of the Kosciuszko Avenue intersection.

The Emergency Services Agency (ESA) issued an alert to say Gungahlin Drive was closed in both directions from Well Station Drive to The Valley Avenue.

It said the road would be closed "for some time".

Personnel from ACT Fire & Rescue, the ACT Ambulance Service and ACT Policing were all at the scene.

ACT police later confirmed one person had died, one person was in a critical condition and another was in a serious condition.

The community has been asked to avoid the area and use an alternative route.

The death is the 10th fatality on ACT roads this year.

World.title: Homicide investigation launched after woman dies in Perth's south-east
World.content:
Police are investigating the death of a 28-year-old woman who was found unresponsive at a home in Perth's south-eastern suburbs.

The woman was found with critical injuries by paramedics at a residence on Taree Street in St James last night.

She was taken to Royal Perth Hospital where she was declared dead.

St John WA alerted police after being called to the home to help the woman and Homicide Squad detectives have launched an investigation.

WA Police said a 38-year-old man known to the woman was in custody and was assisting them with their enquiries.

Neighbour Mia Porteous described the woman's death as "really sad" and "quite scary".

"We didn't hear anything, me and my partner came home from getting food and there were about five police cars and two ambulances," she said.

Ms Porteous said they saw more marked and undercover police cars attend the house throughout the night.

World.title: AIS pays more than $3m in restoration to abused athletes
World.content:
More than 225 athletes who were abused at the Australian Institute of Sport have been paid more than $3 million.

Officials are preparing to close the sorry chapter in Australian sport, ending the four-year restoration program for AIS scholarship holders.

About 225 AIS athletes have been paid between $5,000 and $50,000 each, and more than $3 million collectively, ahead of the Australian Sports Commission (ASC) stopping the four-year program at the end of the year.

"I don't think that any amount of money restores people from the trauma that they have experienced," ASC chief executive Kieren Perkins told AAP.

Swimming great and Australian Sports Commission (ASC) chief Kieran Perkins. (Supplied: AIS)

The ASC formally apologised in 2022 to AIS scholarship holders subjected to abuse at the nation's sporting hub in Canberra.

Perkins said the money was considered only one component of the restoration program, which most importantly gave ex-athletes a voice.

"Hearing that the organisation absolutely is sorry for what occurred and acknowledges it was unacceptable — and it wasn't their [the athletes'] fault, because they were children at the time — it's extremely powerful and worthwhile," Perkins said.

"Everyone who has been involved with the restorative engagement program, their first priority, by a mile, is wanting to know that their experience isn't happening to athletes today.

"They often feel guilty that they didn't do enough to bring forward their stories … that maybe because they didn't act back in the day, this is perpetuated on to other people.

"It's an understandable feeling, but it's absolutely not right."

Perkins said the restorative program, which covered scholarship holders between 1981 and 2013 and also included counselling, would continue to influence current practices.

"When someone comes to you with a complaint and a need to share their story, the worst thing you can do is turn it into a defensive, legal, combative attempt to hide or protect image, in inverted commas," he said.

"Instead of actually acknowledging and addressing the human being who is in front of you."

Perkins's comments came as the ASC released a survey showing generally positive wellbeing in Australian sport.

A survey of 1,300 people from 43 sports found 71 per cent were "thriving'', according to the National Wellbeing Survey.

Some 24 per cent of respondents were in the "surviving'' range, and 4.9 per cent in the "struggling'' range.

Para athletes and people with disability showed lower or more variable experiences in several environments.

And First Nations respondents reported a broader spread of experiences, suggesting outcomes may be strongly shaped by the presence or absence of culturally safe and supportive environments.

"There's still heaps of work to do," Perkins said.

"At scale, things are a lot better.

"What the wellbeing survey does highlight to us is there's a good system there, but we won't let our foot off the gas, we need to embed it deeper in community sport environments."

AAP

World.title: Electrician school closure leaves more than 80 apprentices in limbo
World.content:
Rockhampton electrician Wayne Harris is not feeling optimistic about the state of vocational education in central Queensland.

Mr Harris's apprentices were completing their electrotechnology qualification with Electro Group until an email arrived in the company's inbox in April informing him that the not-for-profit training organisation would be closing its doors in Rockhampton.

Four months on there is still no clear path forward for his apprentices.

"The fourth-years [apprentices] have had to go to Brisbane. There's no other option [than] to finish their training at their cost," he said.

"The government's offered a little bit of incentive money, but it's nowhere near enough."

CQUniversity and TAFE amalgamated in 2014. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

The main provider of the Certificate III in electrotechnology in the region is Rockhampton's TAFE, now amalgamated with CQUniversity.

Mr Harris said he was told enrolments at the university for this year's intakes were full.

"We can't get the first years now into their studies and into their blocks because they [the university] can't accept them," he said.

More than 80 apprentices were left in the lurch following Electro Group's closure in Rockhampton. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Mr Harris said he knew of other small businesses facing similar challenges with securing training for their apprentices.

"We do need another RTO [registered training organisation] business here," he said.

"It just needs a good hard look at the whole situation and get an outcome for central Queensland."

Funding stoush

Electro Group was established through a joint union and industry effort and had run electrical training in Rockhampton for more than 10 years, receiving subsidies from the state government.

In a letter seen by the ABC, Electro Group advised employers in April that it would "no longer be funded" by the department to deliver its courses.

In a statement, Queensland Employment and Training Minister Ros Bates did not respond to questions about funding but said it was Electro Group's decision to stop operating in Rockhampton.

Ros Bates (second from left) at CQUniversity this month. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Ms Bates said her government supported investment in diverse training options for apprentices but would not say if the government was working to reopen Electro Group in the region.

The state government is investing in a $60 million TAFE Centre of Excellence in Rockhampton which is expected to boost enrolment capacity in electrotechnology by the end of 2028.

CQUniversity has more than 150 electrotechnology apprentices in Rockhampton. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Former educators and small businesses have told the ABC there is a strong appetite for an industry-run alternative to CQUniversity.

Jamie Wynne taught at Electro Group and CQUniversity, and said employers were often attracted to the shorter training blocks and greater flexibility offered by Electro Group.

"Employers couldn't get … their training notices on time. They couldn't get it [CQUniversity] to suit their hours and/or the times of the year when they need their apprentices to go to college," Mr Wynne said.

An e-petition calling for an inquiry into electrical apprenticeships in central Queensland has received over 900 signatures. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

"Electro Group was more tailored for like, just get in there, teach them what you've got to teach them.

" It was just easier because you're only focusing on electricians there too. I can see why employers were happy with it. "

Regional vocational training

Some industry figures within the vocational education and training (VET) sector have warned the federal government's push towards fee-free TAFE is leaving private training providers short on cash.

The initiative was introduced in 2023, waiving TAFE fees for students in select courses of national priority.

Angela Connell-Richards says private training providers have been feeling the pinch. (ABC News: Ross McLoughlin)

Angela Connell-Richards is the CEO of a consulting firm working with more than 500 RTOs over a three-decade career in the VET sector.

She said times had been tough for private training providers.

"I was seeing RTOs shut down or they were laying off staff," Ms Connell-Richards said.

" What I foresee is there will be more RTOs that will be making the decision on whether they should continue their registration or not. "

She said the government could achieve better outcomes for taxpayers by allocating funding based on course outcomes rather than prioritising TAFE.

"The small RTOs can't compete because they don't have the government funding and it's [TAFE is] fee-free," she said.

"Students do not want to pay for a course if they can get it for free."

The state government is investing $60 million in a TAFE Centre of Excellence in Rockhampton. (ABC News: Liz Pickering)

In a statement, CQUniversity said it recognised the uncertainty being experienced by apprentices impacted by Electro Group's closure and that it was working with the Queensland government to ensure training for the state's future electrical workforce.

Electro Group and the Electrical Trades Union were approached for comment.

World.title: Infantino set to receive World Cup win but loses Italy's support
World.content:
UEFA is set to drop its threat to boycott FIFA tournaments after receiving assurances that plans to sell stakes in the World Cup and other major competitions will not be revived, sources aware of the discussions have told Reuters.

It comes as Italy withdrew its support for Gianni Infantino's candidacy at next year's FIFA presidential election, with France to consider its stance as well.

Italy is the latest national football federation to distance itself from Infantino, while European leagues president Claudius Schaefer told The Athletic that the FIFA chief had no future at the organisation and that world soccer's governing body needed reform.

FIFA withdrew its proposal in July for the plan that triggered opposition from UEFA's 55 member associations to boycott FIFA competitions.

How Gianni Infantino's FIFA leadership imploded over two weeks The FIFA president has faced more than a fortnight of international turmoil, embroiled in a World Cup sell-off saga that sparked loss of confidence in his leadership.

A FIFA spokesperson said all qualified teams would participate in next month's Under-20 Women's World Cup in Poland, the first major tournament that could have been affected by the stand-off.

"FIFA is pleased that all qualified teams will be participating in the upcoming FIFA U-20 Women's World Cup," the spokesperson said.

"FIFA strongly believes that football has the power to unite, even in challenging circumstances, and looks forward to welcoming all teams and players to Poland.

"We remain committed to how we can further support the global development of the game, through our competitions, through the FIFA Forward program and through our various other initiatives, and in full dialogue with the confederations and stakeholders."

UEFA officials are expected to tell the governing body's executive committee and the presidents of most of its member associations at a meeting in Monaco on Friday that the conditions for lifting the boycott have been met, the sources said.

UEFA has sought both the withdrawal of the proposal and assurances that similar plans would not be pursued again.

"It's not a UEFA defeat, rather the reality of avoiding hurting young players' once-in-a-lifetime opportunity," a source familiar with the discussions told Reuters.

"The actions and insistence on change will continue."

Italy withdraws support for Infantino

Italy has withdrawn its support of Infantino ahead of next year's elections. (Getty Images: Claudio Villa)

The Italian Football Federation (FIGC) has withdrawn its support for Infantino's candidacy in the FIFA presidential election scheduled for March next year.

"This decision is intended to clearly and transparently express the FIGC's position — in full agreement with UEFA and its president Aleksander Ceferin — regarding the recent initiatives promoted by the FIFA president concerning the governance and development of international competitions," FIGC said in a statement.

Pressure on Infantino has continued to mount with Philippe Diallo, president of the French Football Federation, saying that the federation will determine its stance at its executive committee meeting next month.

"I believe we achieved a victory, since FIFA's project was withdrawn," Diallo told L'Equipe.

France is still weighing up whether it will support Infantino at the elections or not. (Getty Images: David Buono)

"There is now the political question, on which several federations and the UEFA president, whom I have spoken to on several occasions, have expressed their views.

"I wanted the FFF's official position to be determined at its next executive committee meeting on September 10."

Infantino is also under pressure from three confederations to resign, including UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation, and CONCACAF which represents North and Central America and the Caribbean.

The regional governing bodies have discussed a potential vote of no confidence in Infantino who is planning to seek re-election for a fourth term next year and is likely to face strong opposition.

Infantino, who retains support from the African and South American confederations, has sought to sideline the confederations and appeal directly to individual members.

Reuters

World.title: Starc hits top of ICC's Test bowling rankings for first time
World.content:
Mitchell Starc has usurped Jasprit Bumrah as the best Test bowler in the world on the International Cricket Council's (ICC) rankings.

Starc's match-winning effort in Mackay, where he claimed 10 wickets and helped Australia crush Bangladesh in a two-day Test, has been rewarded with the number one spot on the ICC's charts.

It is the first time the left-armer has ever claimed the top spot on the Test bowling rankings, which use a points system based on performances in recent years.

Starc was crowned player of the match and series after snaring 6-12 and 4-39 in the second Test.

Indian pace ace Bumrah had held top spot on the Test bowling charts for two months.

Starc now sits 10th on the list of all-time Test wicket-takers with 445 scalps, having overtaken South Africa's Dale Steyn (439) on the standings with his haul in Mackay.

The 36-year-old told AAP ahead of Australia's two-Test series against Bangladesh that a clearer head and an ability to let things go were the secrets behind his remarkable form at an age when most fast bowlers have slowed down.

"You're never as good or bad as you think or other people think you are," Starc said.

"I still moan and whinge about anything that goes wrong or feels wrong. Even heading into [last] summer, it didn't feel like it clicked until the day before the Ashes.

"But I think what's been a feature of our group and, led by 'Ron' [coach Andrew McDonald] and Pat [Cummins], is that whether it's a good day, bad day, good over, bad spell, it's done. Move on.

"When you're 36 and you've been around for 16 years, you'd like to think you've improved or got better at something. You're also around that long because you're able to develop and learn and improve."

AAP

World.title: ASX opens lower after Wall Street drifts; Qantas profit slumps
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX opens lower after Wall Street drifts; Qantas profit slumps Staff writers Updated August 27, 2026 — 10:13am ,first published August 27, 2026 — 5:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket dipped in early trade on yet another busy earnings season day, with Qantas and Wesfarmers among those reporting their results. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 30.1 points, or 0.3 per cent, at 9097.70 as of 10.09am AEST. The ASX lost 0.4 per cent on Wednesday as shock inflation figures put another interest rate hike on the table. Wall Street drifted through a quiet session overnight after a report said US inflation was also a bit worse than economists expected. Wall Street didn’t provide a lot of direction for the ASX. Bloomberg Investors had to wade again through a raft of company results released before the start of trading. Qantas said its profits have taken a hit as rising fuel costs outpaced the benefit of sustained demand for international travel. The airline posted a 13.8 per cent fall in underlying pre-tax profit of $330 million in the year to June. Underlying pre-tax profit is $2.06 billion, down from $2.39 billion in 2025. The company said its fuel bill jumped by over $600 million as it was hit hard by the ramifications of the Middle East conflict.



Retail conglomerate Wesfarmers saw its sales rise 3.4 per cent to $47.3 billion, and net profits excluding significant items grow by 8.3 per cent to $2.9 billion. Bunnings showed the biggest sales growth, up 4.1 per cent to $20.4 billion; Kmart sales grew by 2.8 per cent to $11.75 billion; and Officeworks gained 3.7 per cent to $3.7 billion. The company said Bunnings boss Mike Schneider will retire in February next year, with chief customer officer Rachel McVitty set to take over the role. Healthcare giant Sigma said its sales jumped 15.5 per cent to $10.8 billion and profits climbed 22.3 per cent to $732.2 million in its first results after taking over the Chemist Warehouse pharmacy chain. Business was boosted by demand for weightloss drugs, which will also help lift sales by double digits again in the current year, the company said. Mayne Pharma said underlying earnings had slumped 27 per cent to $34.2 million in the year to June as its management was distracted by the $672 million takeover bid by US private-equity backed drugmaker Cosette, which was eventually blocked by Treasurer Jim Chalmers on national interest grounds. “The Cosette transaction process and subsequent legal matters placed real demands on management focus and caused general disruption,” chief executive Aaron Gray said. On Wall Street overnight, yields in the bond market, the focus of Wall Street’s biggest recent worries, edged higher following America’s inflation data, weighing on sentiment. The S&P 500 edged down by less than 0.1 per cent and remains near its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 113 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.1 per cent.



Nvidia, the chipmaker at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom, delivered a sales forecast that met expectations. Its shares were up 4.3 per cent in after-hours trade. Related Article Consulting Macquarie dumps KPMG from the nation’s biggest audit contract Revenue in the current period will be $US108 billion, plus or minus 2 per cent, the company said in a statement. Though analysts had forecast $US105.2 billion on average, some projections exceeded $US110 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Stocks made relatively few big moves ahead of the earnings report from Nvidia, which arrived after trading ended for the day. Expectations were high once again for the chip giant, whose tremendous growth in profit because of the artificial-intelligence boom has made it the largest stock by value in the US market. Strong profit growth across US companies broadly has been the main reason the US stock market has run to records this year.



Abercrombie & Fitch leaped 35.7 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The retailer also raised its forecast for earnings over the full year and for how much cash it will send to investors by buying back shares of its own stock. Outside of earnings reports, Meta Platforms added 1.1 per cent after agreeing to pay up to $US18 billion ($24 billion) and to add child-safety measures to Facebook and Instagram to end a landmark trial over teen social media addiction and settle claims filed by states across the country. In the bond market, US Treasury yields ticked higher to 4.65 per cent from 4.64 per cent late on Tuesday following updates on inflation and economic growth. Yields had shot upward through the American summer on worries about high inflation and the US government’s growing and gargantuan debt, among other factors. They got so high that the US Treasury Department made a surprise announcement last week to intervene in the bond market, though analysts say its effect could be limited. The latest update on inflation released overnight said that the measure the Federal Reserve has historically preferred to use sat at 3.7 per cent last month. That was the same rate of inflation as in June and slightly worse than the 3.6 per cent that economists expected, according to FactSet. It remains far worse than the 2 per cent goal the Fed has set. Growth in spending by US consumers, which is the main engine of the economy, slowed at the same time. The overall economy grew at a 1.5 per cent annual pace in the spring, according to a revised estimate of its performance, the same amount as the government’s first estimate.



Traders didn’t change their forecasts much for what the Federal Reserve will do with its main interest rate in the short term, and they are betting on a nearly three-in-four chance the Fed will hike the federal funds rate at least once by the end of the year, according to data from CME Group. One of the factors that’s worsened inflation this year is higher oil prices, though they’ve come down recently. Related Article Updated

Supermarkets Woolworths doesn’t need Ooshies effect to beat Coles, says CEO The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, continued to swing Wednesday on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. It dropped as low as $US84.56 before settling at $US86.94. That’s down 0.4 per cent from the day before and from $US94 at the end of last week. In other international markets, indexes rose across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi climbed 1 per cent, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.6 per cent for two of the bigger moves.



With AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ‘Huge gush of mud’: Survivors tell of escape – and devastating loss – from wall of rock and water
World.content:
WorldAsiaFloods ‘Huge gush of mud’: Survivors tell of escape – and devastating loss – from wall of rock and water Liz Lee , Sahana Bajracharya and Navesh Chitrakar August 27, 2026 — 10:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Follow our live coverage of the Nepal floods here. Warning: This story contains graphic content. Trishuli, Nepal/Beijing: A wall of mud and rock collapsing into a river on the Himalayan border of Nepal and China triggered catastrophic flooding on the Nepali side, killing at least 160 people with hundreds more missing. Loading It’s the worst natural disaster to hit Nepal since the 2015 earthquake that killed 9000 and as the situation unfolds, videos of homes, roads and power projects being swept away on both sides of the border point to the number of casualties rising.



As authorities continue the grim task of recovering and trying to identify bodies, survivors are coming to terms with the tragedy. “It was a huge gush of mud coming straight towards us. As it got closer, it kept rising higher and higher,” said Keshav Prasad Baral, a 68-year-old survivor, who was being treated at a small hospital. “When I saw it enter our home, I tried to grab my wife’s hand and take her to the terrace. But she was swept away by the mud,” said Keshav Prasad Baral, a 68-year-old survivor, who was being treated at a small hospital. “Four or five hours later, a helicopter came to rescue me. My wife is still somewhere beneath the mud. She’s gone.”



It’s an experience shared by many survivors. Kalpana Malla, who saw her father, mother, sister and sister’s children caught up in the floodwaters, told the BBC her family didn’t stand a chance against the fury of the flood. Related Article Live

Floods Nepal floods live updates: Dozens of Australians missing, at least 160 dead in Rasuwa, Nuwakot regions near Tibet border; Xi Jinping calls for ‘all-out’ rescue effort “They could not escape, there was no chance at all. This flood took everything, but my son and I climbed the rooftop of a house and survived somehow,” she said. Another survivor described being saved by clinging to a mango tree as he watched the house where he had been working disappear. Twelve British tourists had just crossed through Gyirong – a border land crossing between the two countries – on a tour when a mud-filled wave more than 20 metres high hit, London’s Telegraph reported. They glanced over their shoulders – then began to run for their lives as the wall of water surged towards them down the narrow valley.



The tour was led by Alpine Eco Trek, a local service that arranges regular 10-day trips from the Nepalese capital of Kathmandu to the Tibetan mountain of Kailash. “Both guides went offline at 8.42am,” said Ram Kumar Adhikari, the manager of the tour company. “The whole area was swept away by the flood. Even the Tibet immigration office,” he said. Loading The fate of the 12, which included “young girls”, remains unknown. They were among the hundreds of tourists who remain unaccounted for, according to Nepalese authorities. A 61-year-old British woman and her 60-year-old sister were following the same route as the Alpine group when the mudslide struck. Leaf Holidays, the organiser of their trip, said it had lost contact with all 54 of its pilgrims and staff.



“My brother is the guide. He is missing. I rented a helicopter myself and went out for an hour looking for them,” Gopal Thapa, one of the company’s trek leaders, told The Telegraph. Thousands of people live in Nepali riverside settlements downstream from the flooding, including along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers. The authorities have not estimated the number of people missing and the extent of damage. Locals from the affected areas of Nuwakot and Dhading were seen gathering outside a Nepali army training centre – the base for helicopter rescue operations – seeking information about missing family members.



Police were recording the names of the missing just outside the barracks gate, using mobile phone flashlights as their only source of light as the area remained without electricity due to damaged hydropower infrastructure. In the affected areas, houses, trees and vehicles were submerged or buried in mudslides. Helicopters hovered overhead all day in the area bringing in survivors. Rescuers use an excavator to save survivors in Nepal. AFP “There is devastation everywhere we look,” Tula Bahadur BK, a health worker in Rasuwa, told Reuters. “The settlements next to the river have been completely swept away. Five of my own relatives are missing.” Security footage captured on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border showed many people fleeing before a torrent of rock, mud and water destroyed buildings and vehicles and took many lives.



China’s state broadcaster said three people were killed and 265 missing in Gyirong. It said the toll was still being verified and rescue efforts were ongoing. A rescuer interviewed by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV said they had been trying to establish contact with the Gyirong border port but “so far there haven’t been any results”. A woman consoles a relative as they wait for news of family members missing after flash flooding along the Trishuli River in Nepal. AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha All roads leading to the border crossing had been “completely destroyed” after a preliminary inspection with a drone, the rescuer added. With the deluge of muddy water sweeping down from an estimated nearly 2000 metres above sea level, flood alerts were issued in the populous northern Indian states of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, which border Nepal and where several rivers flow down the mountains into the plains.

World.title: Canaccord, Euroz Hartleys, Argonaut and Taylor Collison make the running
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Canaccord, Euroz Hartleys, Argonaut and Taylor Collison make the running Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 27, 2026 — 9:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This edition of The Cap Raise Crucible features WAM Leaders, WIA Gold and Medallion Metals. If the August 5–20 capital raising fortnight proved anything, it was that Australia’s capital markets have lost none of their appetite for writing sizeable cheques. Across the ASX, the cash calls came thick and fast as companies and funds chased fresh cash for everything from building gold mines and drilling copper projects to acquisitions, artificial intelligence infrastructure and simply putting more money to work in investment portfolios. Broking desks were humming too. Canaccord appeared repeatedly, while Euroz Hartleys and Taylor Collison landed some useful mandates. Argonaut may not have matched some rivals on transaction count but landed the senior global coordinator role on one of the biggest operating-company placements of the fortnight – Wia Gold’s monster $125 million raise.



Petra Capital also chalked up two joint lead manager and bookrunner mandates, while CPS Capital was busy clipping tickets at the smaller end with four deals. But the size of the cheque only tells part of the story. The real action was in the price companies paid for capital, the discounts brokers extracted for their investing clients and what happened once everyone walked away from the bookbuild. Three transactions in particular show just how differently the market can price fresh money. WAM Leaders (ASX: WLE) Raised: $225 million placement, plus an SPP

Price: $1.32.5

Discount: 5.0 per cent to the pre-raise close



Current Price: $1.33 WAM Leaders produced the biggest completed placement of the fortnight, raising $225 million at $1.325 per share after demand exceeded the original target. The book closed early, allocations were scaled back and the placement was upsized – three pretty good indications that finding homes for the stock wasn’t keeping anyone awake at night. The price represented a modest five per cent discount to WLE’s $1.395 pre-raise close and was almost bang on its July 31 pre-tax net tangible asset (NTA) backing of $1.3231. It was also quite a gathering around the broking table.



Commonwealth Securities, Morgans Financial, Ord Minnett and Taylor Collison acted as joint lead arrangers, while those four joined Bell Potter Securities, Canaccord Genuity, E&P Capital and Shaw and Partners as joint lead managers. Existing shareholders can also join the party through an SPP priced at the lower of $1.325 or the five-day VWAP immediately before the September 4 issue date. Getting $225 million of cash in the tin at only five per cent below the prevailing share price after scaling back investors suggests the capital markets were hardly giving WAM a hard time. Drilling at Wia Gold’s 3.7-million-ounce Kokoseb gold project in Namibia. Wia Gold (ASX: WIA)



Raised: $125 million

Price: $0.425

Discount: Nil to the pre-raise close

Current price: $0.51 – up 20 per cent If WAM demonstrated the sheer amount of money available, Wia Gold showed what happens when institutions really want a piece of the action. Wia put away $125 million at 42.5 cents – exactly where its stock had last traded and only two per cent below its five-day VWAP. No double-digit sweetener. No bargain-basement entry point. Argonaut Securities landed the senior role as global coordinator, joint lead manager and joint bookrunner, while Tamesis Partners and Stifel Nicolaus Canada acted as joint lead managers and joint bookrunners.



Together with Wia’s existing cash and proposed US$360 (A$500) million Sprott debt facility, the placement fully funds its Kokoseb gold project in Namibia through construction to targeted first gold production in the fourth quarter of 2028. At 51 cents, Wia is already trading 20 per cent above the placement price – a pretty emphatic endorsement from the aftermarket. Medallion Metals (ASX: MM8) Raised: $60 million

Price: $0.48

Discount: 7.7 per cent to the pre-raise close

Current price: $0.57.5 – up 20 per cent Medallion Metals took a more conventional route, putting away $60 million at 48 cents against a 52-cent pre-halt close.



That handed incoming investors a 7.7 per cent discount while lifting Medallion’s available liquidity to about $175 million – enough to fully fund the remaining development and ramp-up of its Ravensthorpe gold project through to commercial gold-copper production. Unified Capital Partners, Sternship Advisers and Canaccord Genuity acted as joint lead managers and bookrunners. At 57.5 cents, placement investors are 20 per cent ahead and the stock has pushed beyond its pre-raise price. These three deals neatly framed the fortnight. WAM raised $225 million at a tight discount and scaled back demand, Wia found $125 million without discounting its last trade at all and Medallion offered 7.7 per cent before delivering another 20 per cent in aftermarket gains. There wasn’t much evidence of the equity window closing.



PM Capital Global Opportunities Fund (PGF) added another heavyweight transaction, putting away $221 million at $3.07 after initially seeking up to about $175 million. The price equalled its estimated pre-tax NTA but represented a chunky 10.8 per cent discount to its previous $3.44 close, with another $20 million targeted from an SPP. E&P Capital and Morgans Financial were joint arrangers, while those firms joined Commonwealth Securities, Ord Minnett, Shaw and Partners, Taylor Collison, Bell Potter Securities and Canaccord Genuity as joint lead managers. Interestingly, PM Capital’s parent, Regal Partners, picked up all placement and SPP costs, meaning PGF shareholders won’t bear them through the fund’s NTA. True North Copper paid a little more for its money.



Morgans Corporate and Petra Capital acted as joint lead managers and joint bookrunners on an $18 million placement at 37 cents, upsized from $15 million after strong demand and priced at a 14 per cent discount. Major shareholder Tembo Capital cornerstoned the book with $2 million, while chairman Paul Cronin committed another $500,000. About $7.5 million is earmarked for the final deferred payment on the Mt Oxide acquisition, with further funds supporting Mt Oxide and Cloncurry work. At 37.5 cents, the new money has its nose in front for now. Argonaut’s clients had another reason to smile through Hamelin Gold. Chieftain Corporate and Argonaut Securities acted as joint lead managers and joint bookrunners on its roughly $8 million placement at 16 cents, a 13.5 per cent discount. At 24 cents, Hamelin has since motored 50 per cent above the placement price.



But the best percentage turn among the placements examined by the Crucible came from a deal without a broker. Mount Hope Mining raised just $1.82 million at 14.5 cents, with Ronin Metals – the investment fund backed by WA gold discovery specialists Simon Lawson, Craig Jones and David Coyne – committing $1.03 million for an 11.9 per cent holding. The trio were part of the Spartan Resources leadership team associated with the Never Never and Pepper discoveries before Spartan’s $2.5 billion merger with Ramelius Resources. There were no broker fees and the placement was struck at a 2.8 per cent premium to the 15-day VWAP. At 21cents, the new stock is sitting on a whopping 45 per cent paper gain. Sometimes the most interesting thing about a capital raise isn’t the size of the cheque. It’s whose signature is at the bottom.



Alligator Energy assembled an $18 million package comprising a $15 million placement and $3 million SPP at 4.5 cents. Canaccord Genuity and Taylor Collison acted as joint lead managers, with Shaw and Partners as co-manager. The placement came at a 15.1 per cent discount and will support drilling at Samphire and Big Lake and the Samphire feasibility study. At 4.6 cents, investors are 2.2 per cent ahead. Sports Entertainment Group put away an oversubscribed $14.6 million at 28 cents, an 8.2 per cent discount, with another $2 million sought through an SPP. Bell Potter Securities and PAC Partners Securities acted as joint lead managers and bookrunners, with the money helping fund SEG’s MediaWorks acquisition. At 28 cents, investors are square. Ionic Rare Earths raised $8 million at 26 cents, a 16.1 per cent discount, with Ord Minnett and Petra Capital acting as joint lead managers and bookrunners. At 28 cents, investors are 8 per cent ahead. Ionic Rare Earth’s Makuutu rare earths project in Uganda.



CPS Capital, meanwhile, kept its ticket machine particularly busy at the smaller end of town with Patriot Resources, Future Metals, Yari Resources and Ozz Resources. CPS acted as lead broker on Patriot’s $3 million placement at 5.5 cents, clipping a disclosed six per cent cash fee. Patriot is now at 5.6cents, putting investors 2 per cent ahead. CPS and Blue Ocean Equities were joint lead managers and joint bookrunners on Future Metals’ roughly $3.6 million raise at 1.4 cents. Subject to shareholder approval, they will also receive 25 million broker options exercisable at 2.5 cents for 24 months, split 75:25 in CPS’s favour. Future Metals is 7.1 per cent above issue at 1.5 cents. CPS was also lead manager and bookrunner on Yari Resources’ $2.2 million placement at 0.45 cents and will receive, subject to approval, 44 million broker options exercisable at 0.75 cents for two years. Yari is now 0.4 cents, 11.1 per cent underwater. Rounding out the four-ticket run, CPS provided lead manager services on Ozz Resources’ $4.81 million public offer at four cents and received 10 million escrowed shares under a Facilitation Offer. At 3.5 cents, Ozz is 12 per cent below issue.



Four deals then for CPS, but a mixed Crucible verdict – two above issue and two below. Elixir Energy raised $5 million at four cents, with Euroz Hartleys as lead manager and Sternship Advisers, Chieftain Securities and Canaccord Genuity as co-managers. The 20 per cent discounted placement will fund more testing at the company’s Lorelle and potentially Diona appraisal wells in Queensland’s Taroom Trough. At five cents, investors are 25 per cent ahead. NH3 Clean Energy raised $4 million at eight cents, an 18.4 per cent discount, with Curran & Co as lead manager and bookrunner. At 9.3 cents, the shares are 16 per cent above issue. Podium Minerals went another way with an underwritten $4 million SPP at 3.4 cents. Leeuwin Wealth is underwriter and corporate adviser, with Leeuwin and Cumulus Wealth as joint lead managers. At 3.4 cents, Podium is level with the offer price. The IPO market, meanwhile, provided another reminder that getting through the ASX front door is no guarantee of what happens next.



SCX.ai raised a fully underwritten $40 million at 30 cents, with Canaccord Genuity and Henslow as joint lead managers and underwriters. At 21.5 cents, subscribers are nursing a 28 per cent haircut. Elk Range Mining raised $10 million at 20 cents, with Inyati Capital and Euroz Hartleys as joint lead managers. At 19 cents, it is five per cent underwater. WhiteRock Lithium provided the counterpoint. Euroz Hartleys acted as lead manager on its $6 million float at $3.25 and the stock has since surged to $4.90 – a cracking 51 per cent gain. If WhiteRock was standing atop the IPO podium, SCX.ai was left holding the wooden spoon. Same capital market. Same IPO process. Two very different early verdicts.



And that is why simply counting broker mandates doesn’t tell the whole story. Canaccord appeared across some of the biggest books, Euroz Hartleys enjoyed a strong run across placements and floats, Argonaut landed senior roles on two of the fortnight’s better performers and Taylor Collison combined its senior WAM Leaders mandate with Alligator. Petra picked up two solid mandates, while CPS was busiest at the smaller end with four deals. For the brokers, the old soft-shoe shuffle continues, find enough of a discount to convince investing clients to open their wallets while convincing listed companies they haven’t given away the farm. But the fortnight also showed that the biggest discounts don’t necessarily produce the best trades. Wia offered no discount to its last trade and is 20 per cent ahead, while Mount Hope’s strategic investors paid above the 15-day VWAP and are sitting on a gain north of 45 per cent.



At the other end, SCX.ai is 20 per cent underwater, with Ozz and Yari another reminder that cash in the tin and a filled book are merely the opening act. Money talks – we know what walks. The market always gets the final say. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au
